Can. 320 . § 1 . In the case of a vacant or obstructed exarchate, government passes to the Protosincellus or, if absent, to the chief pastor by presbyteral ordination. § 2 . He to whom the government of the exarchate has meanwhile devolved, must inform the authority whose exarch is to be appointed as soon as possible, so that it may decide; meanwhile he can use all the powers and faculties, ordinary or delegated, that the Exarch had, unless they were entrusted to him by the energy of the person of the Exarch.

Can. 321 . § 1 . An exarch, who has not been ordained bishop, has during his office the privileges and insignia of the first post-episcopal dignity. § 2 . In the preservation of these privileges and distinctions, or less fulfilled, a particular right will be preserved. TITLE IX OF THE COVENANTS OF THE HIERARCHIES OF THE VARIOUS CHURCHES OF THEIR LAW

Can. 322 . § 1 . When in the judgment of the Apostolic See it seems appropriate, the Patriarchs, Metropolitans of independent metropolitan Churches, eparchial Bishops and, if so established by statutes, also other local Hierarchs of various independent Churches, including the Latin Church, exercising their power in the same nation or region, shall be summoned to periodic assemblies on fixed dates designated by the Patriarch or other authority designated by the Apostolic See, so that the common good of the Churches may be convened. to be sanctified by the lights of common prudence and experience, and by concerted counsels, a conspiracy by which unity of action may be fostered, common works may be found, the good of religion may be more speedily promoted, and ecclesiastical discipline may be more effectually maintained. § 2 . The decisions of this assembly do not have binding legal force, unless they are discussed, which cannot prejudge the ritual of each autonomous Church or the power of the Patriarchs, Synods, Metropolitans and Hierarchical Councils and at the same time approved by at least two-thirds of the voting members with a deliberative vote and approved by the Apostolic See. § 3 . A decision, even taken unanimously, that in any way exceeds the competence of this assembly, lacks all force until it has been approved by the Roman Pontiff himself. § 4 . Each meeting of the Hierarchs of the different Churches must draw up its own autonomous statutes, in which the participation of the Hierarchs of the Churches that are not yet in full communion with the Catholic Church will be encouraged, as far as possible; The statutes, to be valid, must be approved by the Apostolic See. TITLE

Can. 323 . § 1 . Faithful to Christ are clerics, who are also called sacred ministers, who are chosen by competent ecclesiastical authority and delegated by the gift of the Holy Spirit received in sacred ordination, to be ministers of the Church, taking part in the mission and power of Christ the Shepherd. § 2 . Because of sacred ordination, clerics are distinguished by divine appointment from the rest of the Christian faithful.
Can. 324 . The clergy, united among themselves by a hierarchical communion and appointed at various levels, participate in different ways in the one ecclesiastical ministry instituted by God.
Can. 325 . The clergy is distinguished by the sacred ordination of bishops, priests and deacons.
Can. 326 . The clerics are constituted in the ranks of the order by the sacred ordination itself; but they cannot exercise power except in accordance with the law.

Can. 327 . If, in addition to bishops, presbyters or deacons, other ministers appointed in a minor order and, in general, minor clergy called to the service of the people of God or to perform the functions of the sacred liturgy are admitted or instituted, these are governed solely by the particular law of their own independent Church. CHAPTER I OF THE INSTITUTION OF CLERGYmen

Can. 328 . It is the right and obligation of the Church to train its clergy and other ministers; obligation that is exercised singularly and intensely when erecting and governing the seminaries. Can. 329 - § 1 . The work of promoting vocations belongs above all to the sacred ministries of the entire Christian community, which due to its co-responsibility must be concerned with the needs of the ministry of the entire Church: 1° parents, teachers and other primary educators of Christian life ensure that children and young people in families and schools animated by the evangelical spirit can freely listen to the Lord who calls through the Holy Spirit and respond voluntarily; 2. Clergy, especially pastors, seek to recognize and encourage vocations, both in the young and in others, including those of advanced age; 3. The eparchial bishop must especially awaken and coordinate the initiatives of his flock, joining forces with other hierarchs to promote vocations. § 2 . It must be provided for by special right that in all Churches works for the promotion of vocations be instituted, whether regional or, to the extent possible, eparchial, which must be open to the needs of the entire Church, especially the missionaries.

Can. 330 . § 1 . It is up to the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church or the Council of Hierarchs to issue a plan for the training of clerics, through which the common law for seminaries located within the limits of the territory of the Church itself must be explained more precisely; In other cases, however, it is up to the eparchial bishop to complete such a system for his own eparchy with the signature Can. 150, § 3; It is also necessary to change the nature of these authorities. § 2 . The system of institution of the clerics can be, even through conventions, common to the entire region or nation, or even to other autonomous Churches, with the precaution that it does not adopt any character of rites of loss. § 3 . The procedure for the training of clerics, faithfully observed by common law and taking into account the tradition of the independent Church, must include, among other more specific regulations, on the personal, spiritual, doctrinal and pastoral training of students, as well as on the provision of individual training and the organization of courses and examinations. Art. I ON THE ESTABLISHMENT AND GOVERNMENT OF THE SEMINARS

Can. 331 . § 1 . In the minor seminary those who seem to exhibit judgments of vocation to the sacred ministries are instituted, so that they can discern it more easily and clearly and cultivate it with a devout spirit; those who, although they do not seem called to the clerical state, can be formed to carry out certain ministries or apostolic works, according to the norm of particular law. On the other hand, other institutions, which by their own statutes serve the same purposes, although they differ in their name, are equivalent to a minor seminary. § 2 . In the major seminary the vocation of those who already consider themselves qualified according to certain standards to assume sacred ministries is more fully developed, tested and confirmed.

Can. 332 . § 1 . In each eparchy a smaller seminary will be erected, if the good of the Church demands it and if strength and wealth allow it. § 2 . It is necessary to erect a larger seminary serving one of the larger eparchies, or, if not the entire independent Church, at least several eparchies of the same independent Church, or even different independent churches having an eparchy in the same region or nation, in such a way as to provide the institution, which lacks nothing, with an appropriate number of students and equals, a supply of well-prepared directors and teachers, as well as sufficient resources combined with the best forces.

Can. 333 . Although it is desirable that a seminary, especially a smaller one, be reserved for students from an independent Church, due to special circumstances, students from other independent Churches may also be admitted to the same seminary.

Can. 334 . § 1 . The seminary is erected for the eparchy itself by the eparchial bishop; a seminary common to several eparchies by the eparchial bishops of the same eparchies or by a higher authority, however, with the consent of the Council of Hierarchs, if it is the Metropolitan of an autonomous metropolitan Church, or with the consent of the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church, if it is the Patriarch. § 2 . The eparchial bishops, for whose subjects a common seminary has been erected, cannot validly erect another seminary without the consent of the authority that erected the common seminary, or, if it is a seminary erected by the eparchial bishops themselves, without the unanimous consent of those present or without the consent of a higher authority.

Can. 335 . § 1 . A legitimately established seminary is itself a legal entity. § 2 . In all legal matters, the rector of the seminary acts as the same person, unless the particular law or the statutes of the seminary establish otherwise.

Can. 336 . § 1 . The seminary is common to several eparchies and is subject to a Hierarch appointed by those who instituted the seminary. § 2 . It is exempt from parish government; For all those in the seminary, the office of pastor, with the exception of marriage matters and firm Can. 734, must be performed by the rector of the seminary or his delegate.

Can. 337 . § 1 . The seminary will have its own statutes, in which the special purpose of the seminary and the competence of the authorities will be determined; In addition, the method of appointment or election, the duration of office, the rights and obligations and the fair remuneration of the directors, officers and teachers and councils, as well as the methods by which they and the students participate in maintaining the care of the director, especially in the formation of the seminary, will be determined. § 2 . The seminary should also have its own management, in which the accounting rules for the training of clerics adapted to special circumstances are applied, as well as the priority chapters of the seminary training are determined more precisely, which refer to the enterprise established for the training of students and to the daily life and order of the entire seminary. § 3 . The seminary's statutes require the approval of the authority that established the seminary, and this authority also has the right to it. If chance brings, change them; the latter refer to the authority determined in the statutes.

Can. 338 . § 1 . In each seminary there must be a rector and, if the case warrants it, a financial director and other directors and officials. § 2 . It is the responsibility of the rector to ensure overall control of the seminary in accordance with the bylaws, to insist that the bylaws and direction of the seminary be observed by all, to coordinate the work of the other directors and officers, and to foster the unity and collaboration of the entire seminary.

Can. 339 . § 1 . There is also at least one spiritual father other than the rector, in addition to whom students can freely request any other priest approved by the rector for the same spiritual direction. § 2 . In addition to ordinary confessors, other confessors must also be appointed or invited, with the full right of students to request any confession, even outside the seminary, without prejudice to the discipline of the seminary. § 3 . When judging people it is not permitted to seek the wishes of confessors or spiritual fathers.

Can. 340 . § 1 . If the courses to be taught are organized in the seminary itself, there will be an adequate number of properly selected teachers who are truly experts in their respective fields, and in the larger seminary they will be equipped with appropriate academic degrees. § 2 . With their own preparation constantly updated, teachers must cooperate with each other and with the seminary directors in harmony for the complete formation of future ministers of the Church, among the various disciplines aimed at the unity of faith and formation. § 3 . The teachers of the sacred sciences, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers and Doctors approved by the Church, especially from the East, strive to illuminate the doctrine transmitted by them from the excellent treasury.

Can. 341 . § 1 . The authority that erected the seminary must ensure that the expenses of the seminary are also covered by taxes or offerings, as mentioned in cann. 1012 y 1014. § 2 . Religious houses are also subject to the seminary tax, unless they are supported solely by alms or have study centers there, as stated in cann. 471, § 2 and 536, § 2. Art. II OF THE INSTITUTION FOR THE MINISTRY

Can. 342 . § 1 . Only those students who, through documents, prove their eligibility in accordance with legal requirements are admitted to the seminary. § 2 . No one should be received unless he is certain that he has received the sacraments of baptism and the chrism of the holy miracle. § 3 . Those who have previously been students in another seminary or in some religious institute or society of common life analogous to religious ones, may not be admitted unless they have obtained the testimony of the rector or superior, especially for reasons of dismissal or departure.
Can. 343 . Students, even if they are admitted to the seminary of another independent Church or of several independent Churches, must be instituted according to their own rite, contrary to custom.

Can. 344 . § 1 . Adolescents and young people who live in a daycare must maintain an adequate routine with their own families and peers, necessary for healthy psychological development, especially emotional; and everything that, according to the sound principles of psychology and pedagogy, could in any way diminish the free choice of State, will be carefully avoided. § 2 . With the help of adequate spiritual direction, students must become accustomed to making personal and responsible decisions in the light of the Gospel and to continually develop their various talents, without neglecting any virtue consistent with human nature. § 3 . The curriculum for minor seminary studies must include those required in each nation to begin higher studies and, to the extent the study system allows, also those that are especially useful for exercising sacred ministries; It will generally be attended to, so that students obtain a civil degree and can also continue their studies elsewhere, if they have reached the point of choosing to do so. § 4 . Elderly students must be trained either in a seminary or in a special institute, also taking into account each person's previous training.

Can. 345 . The formation of the students of the major seminary must be completed by complementing those that perhaps in each case were missing in the formation of the minor seminary itself, with a spiritual, intellectual and pastoral formation that is integrated in such a way that they become ministers of Christ in the midst of the Church, light and salt of the world of this time.

Can. 346 . § 1 . Those who aspire to sacred ministries must be trained to worship in the Holy Spirit, family communion with Christ and seek God in everyone, so that all men, moved by the love of Christ the Shepherd, are eager to take advantage of the gift of their own life in the kingdom of God. § 2 . From the word of God and the sacraments, above all, draw strength for your spiritual life and your apostolic work day by day. 2° constantly participate in the Divine Liturgy, which seems to be a seedbed of life, as the source and summit of all Christian life; 3° they learn to regularly celebrate divine praises according to their own rite, and from them they nourish their spiritual life; 4. With great spiritual direction, learn to correctly examine your conscience and to frequently receive the sacrament of penance; 5° Follow with filial piety the ever-Virgin Most Holy Mary, Mother of God, whom Christ named Mother of all men; 6. Also encourage exercises of piety, which give strength and strengthening to the spirit of prayer and the apostolic vocation, especially those recommended by the venerable tradition of the independent Church. However much spiritual retreat and instruction on sacred ministries, exhortation in the path of the spirit, are recommended; 7° students are educated in the sense of the Church and its service, as well as in the virtue of obedience and cooperation with their brothers; 8° they are also helped to cultivate the other virtues that most contribute to their vocation, such as discretion of spirit, chastity and strength of mind; They also esteem and cultivate those virtues that are becoming more numerous among men and that they commend to the minister of Christ, such as sincerity of heart, constant concern for justice, the spirit of poverty, faith fulfilled in promises, civility in action, modesty in conversation united with charity. § 3 . The disciplinary rules of the seminary are applied according to the maturity of the students, so that they, while gradually learning to control themselves, learn to use their freedom wisely, to act with spontaneity and diligence.

Can. 347 . The objective of doctrinal training is that students, knowledgeable about the general culture of the place and time, and scrutinizing the efforts and achievements of human ingenuity, acquire a broad and solid learning in the sacred sciences, so that, educated in a fuller understanding of the faith and strengthened by the light of Christ the Master, they can more effectively enlighten the men of their time and serve the truth.

Can. 348 . § 1 . For those destined for the priesthood, the major seminary's signature studies Can. 345 include philosophical and theological courses, which can be taken successively or together; the same studies must comprise at least six full years, so that the time dedicated to philosophical studies is equal to two full years, and the time to theological studies is equal to four years. § 2 . The philosophical-theological courses begin with an introduction to the mystery of Christ and the economy of salvation, and do not conclude without showing the relationship and coherent composition of all the disciplines, taking into account the order or hierarchy of the truths of Catholic doctrine.

Can. 349 . § 1 . Philosophical training aims to complete training in human sciences; Therefore, taking into account the wisdom of both ancient and modern times, whether of the entire human family or especially of one's own culture, a strong and lasting philosophical heritage is sought above all. § 2 . The historical and systematic courses are taught in such a way that students can more easily separate truths and falsehoods with keen intellectual discernment and can adequately conduct theological research with an open mind for God to speak and become more apt to perform ministries by engaging in conversation with educated people of this age.

Can. 350 . § 1 . Theological training is taught in the light of faith in such a way that students deeply penetrate Catholic doctrine drawn from divine Revelation and express it in their own culture in such a way that it is both nourishment for their own spiritual life and a valuable tool to better carry out their ministry. § 2 . Holy Scripture must be the soul of universal theology, which must inform all sacred disciplines; so, in addition to exegesis, the main chapters of the economy of salvation must be taught, as well as the most important topics of biblical theology. § 3 . The liturgy must be taught taking into account its special importance as a necessary source of doctrine and a truly Christian spirit. § 4 . Until the unity that Christ wants for his Church is fully realized, ecumenism is one of the necessary principles of any theological discipline.

Can. 351 . The teachers of the sacred sciences, when they teach according to the mandate of the ecclesiastical authority, must faithfully transmit the doctrine expounded by it, and in everything they must humbly obey the constant teaching and control of the Church.

Can. 352 . § 1 . Pastoral formation must be adapted to the conditions of place and time, to the gifts of the students, whether single or married, and to the needs of the ministries for which they are preparing. § 2 . Students should be trained primarily in catechetical and homiletic art, liturgical celebration, parish administration, evangelizing dialogue with non-believers or non-Christians or less fervent Christians, social apostolate and social media, not after auxiliary disciplines such as psychology and pastoral sociology. § 3 . Although students are preparing to minister in their own independent Church, they must be formed in a truly universal spirit, so that they will be prepared to attend to the service of souls in all parts of the world; Therefore, let them be taught about the needs of the entire Church and especially about the apostolate of ecumenism and evangelization.

Can. 353 . According to the norm of particular law, exercises and tests must be considered that contribute to strengthening pastoral formation, such as social or charitable service, catechetical formation, especially pastoral during the course of philosophical-theological formation and diaconal formation before priestly ordination.

Can. 354 . The training of a deacon not intended for the priesthood is adapted from the norms given above in such a way that the course of study extends for at least three years, taking into account the traditions of the independent Church on the diaconate of liturgy, speech and charity.
Can. 355 . They must be properly educated about the obligations of the clergy and trained to accept and fulfill them with a big heart.

Can. 356 . § 1 . Every year the rector of the seminary sends a report on the progress of the students' formation to the respective eparchial bishop or, where appropriate, to the major superior; and about the state of the seminary to those who built it. § 2 . The eparchial bishop or major superior must frequently visit the seminary to advise on the formation of his students, especially if it involves promotion to sacred orders. Chapter II REGISTRATION OF THE CLERGY OF A PARTICULAR EPARCHY

Can. 357 . § 1 . Every clergyman must be a cleric registered in an eparchy or exarchy or in a religious institute or in a society of common life similar to the religious or in an institute or association that has obtained the right to register clergy from the Apostolic See or within the territory of the Church over which it presides, by the Patriarch with the consent of the permanent Synod. § 2 . What is decided on the registration of clerics in any eparchy and their dismissal from it is valid. with due reference also to the other legal entities mentioned above, as well as to the particular right that affects the Patriarchal Church itself, unless the law expressly provides otherwise.

Can. 358 . Through diaconal ordination, someone is registered as a clergyman of the eparchy for whose service he is ordained, unless he is already registered in the same eparchy according to the norms of the particular law of his own independent Church.

Can. 359 . In order for a clergyman already registered in an eparchy to validly transfer to another eparchy, he must obtain from his eparchial bishop a letter of dismissal signed by him and at the same time from the eparchial bishop of the eparchy in which he wishes to register, a letter of registration signed by him.

Can. 360 . § 1 . The transmigration of a cleric to another eparchy is carried out with a subscription retained for a certain period of time, which can also be renewed several times, by means of a written agreement between both eparchial bishops, by which the rights and obligations of the cleric or the parties are established. § 2 . Five years after the legitimate transmigration, the cleric is registered as a guest of the eparchy by right, if within four months neither of the two has contradicted this will, expressed in writing to both eparchial bishops.

Can. 361 . A cleric, especially for the sake of the evangelization of the entire Church, should be concerned about transition or transmigration to another eparchy suffering from a serious shortage of clergy, provided that he is ready and able to perform the ministries there, and that he should not be denied unless it is for the true need of his own eparchy or independent Church.

Can. 362 . § 1 . For just cause, a clergyman may be removed from transmigration by his own eparchial bishop or dismissed by the visiting eparchial bishop in accordance with concluded agreements and observing equity. § 2 . After his transmigration to his own eparchy, he should be saved and protected by all the rights he would have had if he had been assigned to the sacred ministry therein.

Can. 363 . They cannot validly register or remove a cleric from an eparchy or grant permission to a cleric to migrate: 1° The Administrator of the Patriarchal Church without the consent of the permanent Synod; Patriarchal Exarch and Administrator of the Eparchy without the consent of the Patriarch; 2° in other cases, the Administrator of the eparchy, except after one year has elapsed since the vacancy of the eparchial see and with the consent of the college of eparchial counselors.
Can. 364 . A cleric's enrollment in an eparchy does not cease unless he is validly enrolled in another eparchy or loses his clerical status.

Can. 365 . § 1 . For a licit passage or transmigration, just causes are required, such as the benefit of the Church or the good of the clergyman himself; but the license should not be denied except for serious and existing reasons. § 2 . By the particular law of an independent Church, it is also required for the legal transition to the eparchy of another independent Church that the eparchial bishop who deposes the cleric obtains the consent of the authority determined by the same particular law.

Can. 366 . § 1 . The eparchial bishop of his own eparchy must not enroll a foreign cleric, unless: 1. the needs or interests of the eparchy require it; 2° is convinced of the suitability of the cleric to exercise the ministries, especially if the cleric comes from another independent Church; 3° his legitimate release from the eparchy is confirmed by a legitimate document and he obtains from the eparchial bishop the delivery of appropriate proof of the career and morals of the cleric, also, if necessary, in secret. 4. The cleric declared in writing that he would dedicate himself to the service of the new eparchy in accordance with the law. § 2 . The eparchial bishop will inform the former eparchial bishop as soon as possible of the completion of the clerical register of his eparchy. CHAPTER III OF THE RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS OF CLERGYmen

Can. 367 . Clergymen have the first obligation to announce to everyone the Kingdom of God and the love of God towards people in the ministry of word and sacraments, yes and represent their entire lives in such a way that everyone, caring for each other and above all for God, is edified and grows in the Body of Christ, which is the Church.

Can. 368 . To the perfection that Christ proposes to his disciples, the clerics are obliged, for a special reason, to consecrate themselves to God in a new way through a sacred ordination, so that they may become more adequate instruments in the service of the people of God as eternal priests of Christ, and at the same time be a model for the flock.

Can. 369 . § 1 . Clergymen must dedicate themselves daily to reading and meditating on the word of God, so that they become faithful and attentive listeners of Christ and true ministers of preaching; May they be constant in prayer, in liturgical celebrations and especially in devotion to the mystery of the Eucharist; that they examine their conscience every day and frequently receive the sacrament of penance; They adore the ever-virgin Saint Mary, Mother of God, and implore her for the grace to conform to her Son, and perform other exercises of piety typical of the independent Church. § 2 . They must do great spiritual direction and take time for spiritual retreats at specific times as provided in the particular law.
Can. 370 . The clergy have a special obligation to show reverence and obedience to the Roman Pontiff, the Patriarch and the eparchial bishop.

Can. 371 . §1 . Clergymen have the right to obtain from their own eparchial bishop any office, service or function in the service of the Church, provided they are legally required. § 2 . Clergy must assume and faithfully carry out any duty, ministry or office entrusted to them by the competent authority, whenever the needs of the Church so require in the judgment of the same authority. § 3 . In order to practice the civil profession, the permission of the corresponding Hierarch is required.

Can. 372 . § 1 . Once the training required for sacred orders is completed, clerics should not stop concentrating on the sacred sciences, but should strive to acquire a deeper and more up-to-date knowledge and use of them through training courses approved by their own Hierarch. § 2 . Conferences that the Hierarch considers appropriate to promote sacred sciences and pastoral issues are also frequent. § 3 . Also of the profane sciences, especially those that are more closely related to the sacred sciences, they should not neglect to procure the supply that is suitable for cultivated men.

Can. 373 . The celibacy of clerics, chosen by the kingdom of heaven and so typical of the priesthood, must become very great everywhere, as indicated by the tradition of the entire Church. Likewise, the status of married clerics, sanctioned by the practice of the early Church and the Eastern Churches for centuries, must be honored.
Can. 374 . Clergy, celibate and married, must shine with the decorum of chastity; It is a matter of particular law to determine the appropriate means that must be used to achieve this end.
Can. 375 . By leading a family life and raising their children, married clergy must set an excellent example for the rest of the Christian faithful.

Can. 376 . A common life among celibate clergymen should be recommended and encouraged, as far as possible, so that they may assist each other in their spiritual and intellectual worship and may better cooperate in ministry.
Can. 377 . All clerics must celebrate divine praises according to the particular law of their own independent Church.
Can. 378 . Clergy must frequently celebrate the Divine Liturgy according to the norm of particular law, especially on Sundays and holidays; in fact, daily celebration is highly recommended.

Can. 379 . The clerics of every autonomous Church, united by the bond of charity, must all conspire for one thing, that is, for the edification of the Body of Christ, and therefore, whatever their condition, although they perform different duties, they must cooperate with each other and help each other.

Can. 380 . Clergy must be concerned with promoting all vocations to sacred ministries and to life in institutions of consecrated life, not only through preaching, catechesis or other appropriate means, but above all through the testimony of life and ministry.

Can. 381 . § 1 . Clergy burning with apostolic zeal must be an example to all of beneficence and hospitality, especially towards the sick, the afflicted, those suffering persecution, exiles and refugees. § 2 . Clergymen are obliged, unless detained by a just impediment, to supply with the spiritual goods of the Church, especially the word of God, and the help of the sacraments to the Christian faithful who ask for them at the opportune time, are duly willing, and are not prohibited by law from receiving the sacraments. § 3 . The clergy must recognize and promote the dignity of the laity and their appropriate participation in the mission of the Church, especially by demonstrating the multifaceted charismas of the laity, as well as by applying their competence and experience for the good of the Church in the ways specifically provided for by law.

Can. 382 . Clergymen must totally abstain from everything that dishonors their position according to the norms more precisely determined by the particular law, and also avoid those that are foreign to them.

Can. 383 . Clergymen, although not unlike other citizens, must have civil and political rights with equal rights, but: 1° they are prohibited from assuming public positions that imply participation in the exercise of civil power; 2° when military service is less compatible with clerical status, volunteers must not perform it except with the permission of their Hierarch; 3° they will take advantage of the exceptions that civil laws, conventions or customs grant in their favor for the exercise of public functions and positions by foreign clerical states, as well as for military service.

Can. 384 . § 1 . Ministers of the reconciliation of all in the love of Christ, may the clergy strive to foster peace, unity and harmony based on justice among men. § 2 . They should not take an active part in political parties or in the control of union associations, unless they are required by sentence of the eparchial bishop or by particular law of the Patriarch or other authority to protect the rights of the Church or promote the common good.

Can. 385 . § 1 . Clergymen, imbued with the spirit of Christ's poverty, must strive to be witnesses of heavenly goods before the world with the simplicity of their lives, and must remove temporal goods from their spiritual use. and the goods that are procured on the occasion of the exercise of the position, ministry or ecclesiastical service, provided by them for their adequate support and the fulfillment of the obligations of their own state, they impart and participate in works of apostolate or charity. § 2 . Clergymen are prohibited from doing business or commerce by themselves or through others, whether for their own benefit or that of others, except with the permission of the authority determined by the particular law of their own Church or of the Apostolic See. § 3 . The clergyman must be prohibited from attesting, even to his own assets, except with the advice of his own eparchial bishop or, where appropriate, the major Superior.

Can. 386 . § 1 . The clergy, even if they do not have a residential position, cannot leave their eparchy for a considerable period to be determined by particular law without the at least presumptive permission of the local Hierarch. § 2 . A cleric who resides outside his own eparchy is subject to the local eparchial bishop in those matters that reflect the obligations of cleric status himself; If you are going to stay there for a short period of time, you must inform the local Hierarch without delay.
Can. 387 . Regarding the clothing of clerics, a particular right will be preserved.

Can. 388 . Clergymen may not use the rights and insignia incident to the dignities conferred upon them outside places where the authority that granted the dignity exercises its power, or has consented in writing to the granting of the same dignity without exception, or unless they accompany the authority that granted the dignity, or dress the person thereof, or unless they have obtained the consent of the local Hierarch.

Can. 389 . Clergymen should try to avoid any conflict; However, if any discord should arise between them, it should be brought to the forum of the Church, and this, if possible, should also be done if it is a matter of discord between clergy and other Christian believers.

Can. 390 . § 1 . Clergymen have the right to adequate support and, therefore, to receive fair remuneration for the fulfillment of the office or function entrusted to them, which, in the case of married clerics, must also take care of the support of their families, unless otherwise sufficiently provided. § 2 . Likewise, they have the right that they and their families, if they are married, have adequate social and preventive security, as well as health care; In order for this right to be made effective, the clerics are bound by the obligation of the institute, of which in Can. 1021 , § 2 , to contribute to the norm of the particular law on their part.

Can. 391 . It is integral that firm Can. 578 , § 3 clerics associate with others to achieve ends consistent with clerical status; and it is up to the eparchial bishop to authentically judge this congruence.
Can. 392 . It is the right of the secretaries to determine the period of annual vacations due by particular law.

Can. 393 . The clergy, whatever their condition, must have in their hearts concern for all the Churches and, therefore, show themselves willing to serve wherever the need arises, and especially allowing or exhorting their own Bishop or eparchial Superior to exercise their ministry in missions or regions that suffer from a shortage of clergy. CHAPTER IV OF THE LOSS OF CLERICAL SITUATION

Can. 394 . A sacred ordinance, once validly performed, never ceases to be invalid; The cleric, however, loses his clerical status: 1° by judicial ruling or administrative decree, by which the invalidity of a sacred ordination is declared; 2° the penalty of deposition imposed by law; 3° in writing to the Apostolic See or to the norm of the Patriarch Can. 397; but this rewriting cannot be licitly granted by the Patriarch to deacons without serious reasons, nor to priests without very serious reasons, nor is it granted by the Apostolic See.

Can. 395 . A clergyman who loses clerical status in accordance with the law, thereby loses the rights of clerical status and is no longer subject to any of the obligations of clerical status, no matter how firm Can. 396 may be; it is prohibited to exercise the power of the order except cann. 725 y 735 , § 2 ; He is by right deprived of all positions, ministries, functions and any delegated power.

Can. 396 . Apart from cases in which the invalidity of sacred ordination has been declared, the loss of clerical status does not imply a dispensation from the obligation of celibacy, which is granted only by the Roman Pontiff.

Can. 397 . The Patriarch, with the consent of the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church or, if the danger is pending, of the permanent Synod, may grant the loss of clerical status to clerics who have a domicile or quasi-domicile within the territory of the Patriarchal Church proper, who are not bound by the obligation of celibacy or, if so, do not request dispensation from this obligation; In other cases the matter is referred to the Apostolic See.

Can. 398 . He who has lost his clerical status due to the new registration of the Apostolic See can be readmitted to the clergy only by the Apostolic See; But whoever has obtained from the Patriarch the loss of the clerical state, may also be admitted again into the clergy by the Patriarch. TITLE XI OF THE LAWS

Can. 399 . By the name of laity in this Code we understand the Christian faithful, to whom the character of secularism is proper and special, and who, living in the world, participate in the mission of the Church, and are not established in a sacred order or assigned to a religious state.

Can. 400 . In addition to the rights and obligations that are common to all Christians and those established in other canons, lay people have the same rights and obligations that are enumerated in the canons of this title.

Can. 401 . It is mainly the vocation of the laity to seek the Kingdom of God by directing temporal affairs and ordering them according to God, and therefore to be witnesses of Christ in their private, family and political-social life and to manifest it to others, to defend just laws in society and to contribute to the sanctification of the world with resplendent faith, hope and charity.

Can. 402 . It is the right of the laity that they can recognize that freedom in the affairs of the earthly state, which belongs to all citizens; However, those who make use of the same freedom take care that their actions are imbued with the evangelical spirit and pay attention to the teachings expounded by the teachings of the Church, being careful, however, not to express their own opinion on matters conceivable as teaching of the Church.

Can. 403 . § 1 . Lay people have the right to actively participate in the liturgical celebrations of any independent Church as provided in the liturgical books. § 2 . If the needs of the Church or actual benefits suggest it and there are no sacred ministers, some of the functions of sacred ministers may be entrusted to laymen in accordance with the law.

Can. 404 . § 1 . In addition to the catechetical training that they must receive from childhood, lay people have the right and obligation to acquire knowledge adapted to the gifts and condition of each of the characters of the doctrine revealed by Christ and transmitted by the authentic teaching of the Church, not only to be able to live according to its teaching, but also to be able to express it themselves and, if necessary, defend it. § 2 . They also have the right to acquire the most complete knowledge of the sacred sciences taught in universities or ecclesiastical faculties or in institutes of religious sciences, by attending lectures there and obtaining academic degrees. § 3 . Likewise, having observed the provisions regarding the required suitability of the statutes, they are eligible to receive the mandate to teach sacred disciplines from the competent ecclesiastical authority.

Can. 405 . The laity must also diligently study the liturgical, theological and spiritual heritage, so that mutual benevolence, esteem and unity of action among the laity of the different independent Churches are fostered and the variety of rituals does not harm the common good of the society in which they live, but rather leads increasingly to the same good.

Can. 406 . The laity, aware of the obligation mentioned in Can. 14, must know that it is all the more urgent in their circumstances, in which men can only hear the Gospel and know Christ through themselves.
Can. 407 . Lay people who live in a married state, according to their own vocation, have a special obligation, through marriage and family, to work for the edification of the people of God.

Can. 408 . § 1 . Lay people with due knowledge, experience and integrity are eligible to be heard as experts or consultants by ecclesiastical authorities, either individually or as members of various councils and meetings, such as parish, eparchial, patriarchal. § 2 . In addition to the ecclesiastical functions to which lay people are admitted by common law, other functions may be assumed by the competent authority, except those that require sacred order or that are expressly prohibited to lay people by the particular law of their own Church. § 3 . With regard to the exercise of ecclesiastical functions, the laity are fully subject to ecclesiastical authority.

Can. 409 . § 1 . Lay people, permanently or temporarily assigned to the special service of the Church, have the obligation to acquire the appropriate training necessary to adequately perform their function and to fulfill it consciously, intensely and diligently. § 2 . They have the right to fair compensation adapted to their situation, with which they can decently satisfy their own needs and those of their family members, also observing the provisions of civil law; They also have the right to provide themselves and their families with adequate social and preventive security, as well as health care. *AAS, vol. 82 (1990), no. 11, pp. 1061-1147 ___________________________________________________ (n: Indicates that the text corresponds to a new version or to a new paragraph) Cf.: Motu Proprio Apostolic Letters given to Iam Pride (on April 16, 2013) Previous version: Can. 66 § 1 . In the election of the Patriarch, all and only the members of the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church have an active voice.

Can. 410 . The religious state is a stable common way of life in some institution approved by the Church, in which the faithful follow Christ, Teacher and Example of Holiness, under the action of the Holy Spirit, consecrate themselves in a new and special title through public vows of obedience, chastity and poverty under the legitimate Superior to keep the norm of the statutes, renounce the world and dedicate themselves totally to achieving the perfection of charity in the service of the Kingdom of God for the edification of the Church and salvation. of the world as signs announcing heavenly glory.
Can. 411 . A religious state must be encouraged and promoted by all. 1° Of the dependence of the religious on the eparchial bishop, the patriarch and the Apostolic See.

Can. 412 . § 1 . All religious are subject to the Roman Pontiff as supreme superior, to whom they are bound by the obligation of obedience including the vow of obedience. § 2 . The better the good institutions and the needs of the apostolate are cared for, the Roman Pontiff, by reason of his primacy over the entire Church, with a view to the common benefit, can exempt the institutions of consecrated life from the eparchial rule of the Bishop, and subject himself alone or others to the ecclesiastical authority.

Can. 413 . Regarding internal government and religious discipline, religious institutions, unless otherwise provided by law, if they are of pontifical right, are subject directly and exclusively to the Apostolic See; but if they are of patriarchal or eparchial right, they are subject directly to the patriarch or the eparchial bishop under the signature Can. 418, § 2.

Can. 414 . § 1 . Regarding monasteries and congregations of eparchial law, the eparchial bishop has the right: 1° to approve the norms of the monasteries and the statutes of the congregations and the modifications introduced therein in accordance with the law, except those that have been approved by a higher authority; 2° dispensations of the same types or statutes, which exceed the power of religious superiors and are legitimately requested, to be granted to individuals in the cases and according to the form of the act; 3° visit the monasteries, including the dependencies, as well as the individual houses of congregations in their territory, whenever they carry out a canonical visit or when truly special reasons in their opinion so suggest. § 2 . These rights of the Patriarch apply to orders and congregations of patriarchal right, which have a main house within the limits of the territory of the Church over which he is in charge; Otherwise, the same rights with respect to all orders, as well as with respect to monasteries and congregations, which do not belong to eparchial law, belong solely to the Apostolic See. § 3 . If the eparchial right congregation spreads to other eparchies, nothing in the statutes themselves can be validly modified except with the consent of the eparchial bishop of the eparchy in which the main house is located, after consultation with the eparchial bishops in whose eparchies the other houses are located.

Can. 415 . § 1 . All religious are subject to the power of the local Hierarch within them, which concerns the public celebration of divine worship, the preaching of the word of God to the people, the religious and moral education of the faithful, especially the pure, the catechetical and liturgical formation, the decorum of the clerical state, as well as the various works in them that reflect the apostolate. § 2 . It is the right and obligation of the eparchial bishop to visit the different monasteries and houses of the orders and congregations located in his territory in these matters, whenever he carries out a canonical visit there or when serious reasons in his opinion so suggest. § 3 . An eparchial bishop can only with the consent of the competent superiors entrust to the religious the works of apostolate or the functions of the eparchy, in accordance with common law and observing the religious discipline of the institutes, of a specific nature and determined purpose. § 4 . Religious who have committed an offense outside the home and are not punished by their own Superior, warned by the local Hierarch, may be punished with this penalty, even if they have legitimately left the house and have returned to it.

Can. 416 . Both the patriarchs and the local hierarchs must promote meetings with the religious superiors, at specific times and when it seems convenient, so that they proceed in harmony with the plans given for the works of apostolate carried out by the members.

Can. 417 . If abuses have been introduced in the house of institutions of patriarchal or pontifical right or in their Churches and the Superior has not heeded the warnings of the local Hierarch, the same local Hierarch has the obligation to immediately refer the matter to the authority to which the institution itself is immediately subject. 2° Of the Superiors and members of religious institutes

Can. 418 . § 1 . The superiors are the president of the monastic confederation, the superior of the independent monastery, the superior of the general order or congregation, the provincial superior, the vicars of the same and others who have the same power as the provincials, and also those who, if the previous ones are absent, legitimately succeed to the office in the meantime. § 2 . On behalf of the Superior of monks and other religious, the local Hierarch and the Patriarch are not subject to the firm canons that confer the authority of the Patriarch or the local Hierarch over them.

Can. 419 . § 1 . The president of a monastic confederation, the Superior of a non-confederated autonomous monastery and the Superior of a general order or congregation must send a report on the status of the institutes over which they preside, at least every five years, to the authority to which they are directly subject, according to a formula established by the same authority. § 2 . The superiors of the eparchial or patriarchal legal institutes also send a model report to the Apostolic See.

Can. 420 . § 1 . The superior elders, whom the statutes of the order or congregation designate to the office of visitor of the monastery, will visit all the houses subject to them at the same hours that they themselves or others determine, if they are legally prevented. § 2 . Members must act in trust with the visitor, to whom they are legally obliged to respond according to truth in charity; but no one may in any way divert the members from this obligation or otherwise prevent the end of the visit. § 3 . The local hierarch must visit all religious houses if the major superior, to whom the visit is legally entitled, has not visited them within five years and has refused to visit them when warned by the local hierarch.

Can. 421 . Superiors have the heavy obligation to ensure that the members entrusted to them live their lives according to their typical or proper statutes; Superiors are to help members by example and encouragement to achieve the goal of religious status, adequately attend to their personal needs, diligently care for and visit the sick, rebuke the restless, comfort the narrow-minded, and be patient with all.

Can. 422 . § 1 . Superiors must have a permanent plan established in accordance with the norm or statutes, the work of which they use in the exercise of their position; In cases provided for by law, they are obliged to request your consent or advice in accordance with the Can. 934 standard. § 2 . It will be determined by particular law whether or not there should be a council in houses in which fewer than six members live.

Can. 423 . A monastery, a monastic confederation, an order and a congregation, and their legitimately constituted provinces and houses, are by law legal persons; but they may exclude or restrict your ability to acquire, possess, manage and dispose of typical or established temporary assets.
Can. 424 . The typical or statutory norms establish the use and administration of goods in order to promote, express and protect one's own poverty.
Can. 425 . The temporal property of religious institutions is governed by cann. 1007 - 1054, unless otherwise provided by common law or determined by the nature of the matter.

Can. 426 . Each and every one of the religious, both superior and subordinate, must not only faithfully and fully keep the vows they have made, but also organize their life according to the typical or established mentality and faithfully keeping the purposes of the founder, and thus seek the perfection of their state.
Can. 427 . Each and every religious person is subject to the obligations prescribed for clergy by common law, unless otherwise provided by law or determined by the nature of the matter.

Can. 428 . A member of a religious institute is enrolled with perpetual vows as a cleric through deacon ordination or, in the case of a cleric already enrolled in an eparchy, through perpetual profession.

Can. 429 . The letters sent by the religious to their Superiors, as well as to the local Hierarch, the Patriarch, the Legate of the Roman Pontiff and the Apostolic See, as well as the letters that they themselves receive from them, are not subject to any inspection.

Can. 430 . It is not permitted to confer merely honorific titles of dignities or religious offices, unless it is a typical matter or the statutes that allow it for the titles of the offices of Superiors of the ancestors, which the religious have already exercised.

Can. 431 . § 1 . A religious cannot be promoted from his first profession to a position or office outside his own institution without the written consent of his own superior, except those conferred by election made by the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church, and with the signature Can. 89, § 2; after completing the task he must return to the monastery, order or congregation. § 2 . The religious who becomes Patriarch, Bishop or Exarch: 1° remains bound by his vows and remains bound by the other obligations of his profession, except those that he himself wisely judges cannot be reconciled with his dignity; lacks active and passive voice in his own monastery, order or congregation; is free from the power of the Superiors and is subject to the vow of obedience only to the Roman Pontiff; 2. Once the function is fulfilled, the one who returns to the monastery, order or congregation of the rest's signature cann. 62 y 211, may have the active and passive voice, if the typical or the statutes allow it. § 3 . The religious who becomes Patriarch, Bishop or Exarch: 1° if by profession he has lost the capacity to acquire ownership of goods, he has the use, usufruct and administration of the goods that come to him; But the patriarch, the eparchial bishop, the exarch acquires the property of the patriarchal Church, of the eparchy, of the exarchy; to another monastery or order; 2° if he has not lost ownership of the assets by profession, he recovers the use, usufruct and administration of the assets he had; What happens to him afterwards, he acquires completely for himself; 3. In both cases, the goods that come to them without the person's intention are owed to the transferor according to the will of the offerors.

Can. 432 . A monastery, house or province dependent on a religious institution of any independent Church, including the Latin Church, which is registered with the consent of the Apostolic See and other independent Churches, must preserve the right of this Church, without prejudice to the typical provisions or statutes, which respect the internal government of the same institution, and the privileges granted by the Apostolic See. Art. II ON MONASTERIES

Can. 433 . § 1 . A monastery is called a religious house, in which members strive for evangelical perfection by observing the rules and traditions of monastic life. § 2 . An independent monastery is one that does not depend on another monastery and is governed by its own typology approved by the competent authority.

Can. 434 . A monastery is of pontifical right, if it is established by the Apostolic See or recognized as such by decree of the same; patriarchal law, if it is stauropegic; of eparchial law, if erected by the Bishop, the decree of recognition of the Apostolic See was not obtained. 1° On the establishment and suppression of monasteries

Can. 435 . § 1 . n It is the responsibility of the eparchial bishop to erect an independent monastery with prior written authorization within the territory of the Patriarchal Church of the Patriarch or, in other cases, of the Apostolic See. § 2 . The construction of the Stauropegian monastery is reserved for the patriarch.

Can. 436 . § 1 . Any independent monastery may have dependent monasteries, some of which are subsidiary, if by the same act of establishment or by decree according to a typical and broad approach they can tend to the status of an independent monastery, while others are subsidiary. § 2 . To validly erect a dependent monastery, the written consent of the authority to which the independent monastery is subject and the eparchial bishop of the place where this monastery is erected is required.

Can. 437 . § 1 . The license to erect a monastery, even a dependent one, carries with it the right to have a church and to perform sacred services, as well as the pious works typical of the norm of a monastery, which must be carried out in accordance with the legally imposed clauses. § 2 . To build and open a school, hospital or similar building separate from a monastery, the written consent of the eparchial bishop is required for each monastery. § 3 . For a monastery to be converted to other uses, the same ceremonies are required as for its erection, except in the case of conversion, which for the moment refers to internal government and religious discipline.

Can. 438 . § 1 . It is the duty of the Patriarch to suppress, within the territory of the Church over which he presides, a monastery of its own right or a branch of eparchial or stauropegical law for serious reasons, with the consent of the permanent Synod and at the request or consultation of the eparchial Bishop, if the monastery is of eparchial law, and with the consultation of the Superior of the monastery and the President of the confederation, if the monastery is a confederation, unless resorted in a suspensive manner to the Roman Pontiff. § 2 . Only the Apostolic See can suppress other independent or subsidiary monasteries. § 3 . A subsidiary monastery can be suppressed by decree of the Superior of the monastery on which it depends, according to the norm and with the consent of the eparchial bishop. § 4 . The property of a suppressed independent monastery is transferred to the confederation, if there is a confederation; otherwise of the eparchy or, if it were stauropegic, of the patriarchal church; and the property of the suppressed dependent monastery will be transferred to the independent monastery; Regarding the assets of the suppressed monasteries, the pontifical right to decide is reserved to the Apostolic See, without prejudice in any case to the will of the offerors.

Can. 439 . § 1 . Several independent monasteries of the same Eparchy, subject to the eparchial bishop, can form a confederation with the written consent of the same eparchial bishop, who is also responsible for approving the statutes of the confederation. § 2 . A confederation may be constituted between several independent monasteries of different eparchies or stauropegy located within the territory of the Patriarchal Church, after consultation with the eparchial bishops concerned and with the consent of the Patriarch, who also reserves the approval of the statutes of the confederation. § 3 . In other cases, the meeting of the confederation must be referred to the Apostolic See.

Can. 440 . § 1 . The aggregation of independent non-confederate conventions and the separation of confederates from the confederation is reserved to the same authority as discussed in Can. 439. § 2 . A confederation within the territory of the Patriarchal Church cannot be suppressed except by the Patriarch with the consent of the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church, in consultation with the eparchial Bishops concerned, and the President of the confederation, except by appeal in suspensive form to the Roman Pontiff; the suppression of other confederations is reserved to the Apostolic See. § 3 . It is up to the authority that suppressed the confederation, subject to the will of the bidders, to determine the assets that belong to the suppressed confederation itself. In this case the Patriarch needs the consent of the permanent Synod. 2° Of the Superiors, Synaxes and Bursars of the Monasteries

Can. 441 . § 1 . In the monasteries the Superiors and Synaxes have this faculty, which is determined by common and typical law. § 2 . The superiors in independent monasteries have the power of government, so far as it is expressly granted to them by law or by the authority to which they are subject, firmly Can. 979 . § 3 . The powers of the President of a monastic confederation, in addition to those determined by common law, must be determined in the statutes of the confederation itself.

Can. 442 . A typical undertaking of an independent monastery, which requires that most of all be qualified to hold the position of Superior of an independent monastery, one must have made perpetual profession, have professed for at least ten years, and have reached the age of forty.

Can. 443 . § 1 . The Superior of an autonomous monastery is elected in a Synax according to the typical norms collected and observed cann. 947 - 960, without prejudice to the right of the eparchial Bishop to preside over the election of the Synax by himself or through another. § 2 . In the election of the Superior of the independent monastery of the confederated Synaxis, the election is presided over by himself or by another President of the same confederation.

Can. 444 . § 1 . The office of Superior of an autonomous monastery is conferred for an indefinite period, unless otherwise typical. § 2 . Unless the type prescribes otherwise, the Superiors of dependent monasteries are appointed for a specified period in the type itself by the Superior of the monastery independently of the consent of his council, if the monastery is subsidiary, but with the same council, if it is subsidiary. § 3 . However, Superiors who have reached the age of seventy-five, or who, due to illness or any other serious reason, have become less fit to perform their duties, must present their resignation from the position of Synaxis, whose duty it is to accept it.

Can. 445 . The members of the Synaxis must strive to elect those whom they recognize in the Lord as truly worthy and suitable for the office of Superior, abstaining from all abuse and especially from manipulation of votes, both for themselves and for others.
Can. 446 . He must reside in his own superior monastery and not leave it except according to the norm of the typical.

Can. 447 . § 1 . For the administration of temporal goods there must be a financier in the monastery, who performs his duties under the supervision of the Superior. § 2 . The superior of an independent monastery must not simultaneously hold the position of financial manager of the same monastery; but the office of financier of a dependent monastery, although better distinguished from the office of Superior, may nevertheless be combined with it, if necessity requires it. § 3 . The financier is appointed by the superior of the monastery, regardless of the consent of his council, unless otherwise typical. 3° On admission to the independent monastery and on the novitiate

Can. 448 . For someone to be admitted to an independent monastery, he or she is required to be motivated by right intention, fit to lead the monastic life, and not be hindered by any obstacles established by law.
Can. 449 . A candidate, before being admitted to the novitiate, must live for a typically determined period of time in a monastery under the special care of an approved member.

Can. 450 . According to the firm prescriptions, which demand greater priority, the following cannot be validly admitted to the novitiate: 1° non-Catholics; 2° those who have been punished with canonical punishment, except the penalties mentioned in Can. 1426, § 1; 3° Those who are threatened with serious punishment for the crime of which they have been legitimately accused; 4° those who have not yet reached the age of eighteen, unless it is a monastery in which a temporary profession is made, in which case the age of seventeen will suffice; 5° those who enter the monastery by force, induced by serious fear or deception, or those who are received by the Superior after having been induced in the same way; 6th spouses during the marriage; 7° those who are bound by the bond of religious profession or another sacred bond in the institution of consecrated life, unless it is a legitimate transition.

Can. 451 . No one can be legally admitted to the novitiate of a monastery of another independent Church without the permission of the Apostolic See, unless he is a candidate who is destined for a monastery dependent, as discussed in Can. 432, on his own Church.

Can. 452 . § 1 . Eparchy clergy registered in the novitiate cannot be legally admitted except with the advice of the appropriate eparchy bishop; nor can they be lawfully admitted, if the eparchial bishop contradicts it, because their departure results in a serious loss of souls, which otherwise cannot be avoided at all, or if they are those who are detained by some impediment established by law to sacred order in a monastery. § 2 . Likewise, parents whose work is necessary to feed and educate their children, nor children who must help their father or mother, grandfather or grandmother when they are in extreme need, cannot be legally admitted to the monastery, unless the monastery provides otherwise.

Can. 453 . § 1 . The superior of the monastery is independent to admit the novitiate at his discretion. § 2 . The Superior himself must be convinced, by appropriate means, of the suitability and complete freedom of choosing a candidate for the monastic state. § 3 . Regarding the documents that candidates must provide, as well as the collection of various testimonies about their good conduct and suitability, the typical provisions are observed.

Can. 454 . In typical terms, the rules regarding dowry, if necessary, must be provided by the candidates and administered under the special supervision of the local Hierarch, as well as the full dowry, without the already ripened fruits, which must be returned to those who leave the monastery for any reason.
Can. 455 . The novitiate begins with the taking of the monastic habit or otherwise, in the typical prescribed form.

Can. 456 . § 1 . An independent monastery may have its own novices, who are initiated into the monastery itself under the guidance of a qualified member of monastic life. § 2 . For the novitiate to be valid, it must be carried out in the independent monastery itself or by decision of the Superior, in consultation with his council, in another independent monastery of the same confederation. § 3 . However, if any independent monastery, whether confederated or not, cannot comply with the provisions relating to the training of novices, the Superior has the obligation to send the novices to another monastery, in which the same provisions are religiously observed.

Can. 457 . § 1 . The novitiate, to be valid, must be completed for three complete and continuous years; but in monasteries where temporary profession precedes perpetual profession, one year of novitiate is sufficient. § 2 . In each year, the absence from the novitiate for three months, continuous or shorter, does not affect the validity, but the missing period, if it exceeds fifteen days, must be made up. § 3 . Can. 461 , § 2 should not extend the novitiate beyond three years.

Can. 458 . § 1 . The training of novices must be carried out as a teacher according to the standard of the typical member, showing prudence, charity, piety, knowledge and respect for monastic life, having professed for at least ten years. § 2 . The rights and obligations of this master, especially those relating to the method of training of novices as well as relations with the Synax and the Superior of the monastery, are determined in the typical.

Can. 459 . § 1 . During the period of the novitiate, it is constantly necessary to educate the mind of the novice under the guidance of the master through typical study, through pious meditations and constant prayer, teaching him what belongs to the vows and virtues, through appropriate exercises to eradicate vices, control emotions and acquire virtues. § 2 . During the period of the novitiate, novices should not be assigned to external work in the monastery, nor should jobs dedicated to the studies of letters, sciences or arts remain vacant.
Can. 460 . A newbie cannot validly renounce his assets in any way or bind them to the company Can. 467 , § 1 .

Can. 461 . § 1 . A novice can freely leave his independent monastery or be dismissed by the Superior or the Synaxis according to the typical just cause. § 2 . After the exact novitiate, if considered suitable, the novice is admitted to the profession; Otherwise, he is fired; If doubts persist regarding suitability, the novitiate period may be extended according to the norm, but not beyond one year. 4° Of consecration or monastic profession

Can. 462 . § 1 . The monastic state is definitively assumed through perpetual profession, which includes the three vows of perpetual obedience, chastity and poverty. § 2 . When issuing the profession, the prescriptions of the liturgy and liturgical books are observed.
Can. 463 . As for the different degrees of the monastic profession, the norm of the monastery must be preserved by the legal force of the profession according to common law.

Can. 464 . For the validity of perpetual monastic profession it is required that: 1° the novitiate has been validly completed; 2° the novice is admitted to profession by the Superior of his own monastery, independently of the consent of his council, in addition to receiving profession from the same Superior by himself or by another; 3. The profession must be expressed and not given or received by force, serious fear or deception; 4° the other requirements for the validity of the profession must be met in the typical manner.
Can. 465 . Those prescribed by common law on temporary profession also apply to monasteries in which said profession is, according to custom, preceded by a perpetual profession.
Can. 466 . Perpetual monastic profession invalidates acts contrary to the vow, if the acts can be invalidated.

Can. 467 . § 1 . The candidate for perpetual monastic profession must, within sixty days prior to profession, renounce all the property he currently possesses, which he prefers, on the condition of following profession; a resignation made before this time is automatically null and void. § 2 . Once the profession is released, all those things that are necessary must be done immediately so that the resignation can also have civil law effects.

Can. 468 . § 1 . Temporal property belonging to a member of any title after perpetual profession is acquired by the monastery. § 2 . The monastery must be responsible for the debts and obligations that the member contracted after perpetual profession with the permission of the Superior; But if he contracted fees without permission from the Superior, the member himself must respond. § 3 . It is true, however, that an action can always be brought against the party to whose object something arising from the conclusion of the contract is directed.
Can. 469 . A member who has been discharged by perpetual profession automatically loses any office, if any, and is united to his own eparchy and to the monastery as a matter of right.

Can. 470 . The document of perpetual profession issued by the member himself and by which he also received profession by delegation, will be kept in the monastery archive; The superior of his own independent monastery must inform the parish priest with whom the member's baptism was registered as soon as possible. 5° On the formation of members and on monastic discipline

Can. 471 . § 1 . The method of training the members is usually determined in such a way that they are constantly encouraged to attain a life of fuller holiness, as well as that their talents are developed through the study of sacred doctrine and the acquisition of human culture for the needs of the times and thus become more apt in the exercise of the arts and works legitimately undertaken by the monastery. § 2 . The training of monks destined for sacred orders must also be carried out according to the method of clerical training, mentioned in Can. 330, in the monastery itself, if it has a study center equipped according to the standard Can. 340, § 1, or under the direction of an approved director in another seminary or institute of higher studies approved by the ecclesiastical authority.

Can. 472 . The superior of an autonomous monastery may, according to the typical norm, give its members of perpetual vows letters of dismissal for sacred ordination; These letters must be sent to the eparchial bishop of the place where the monastery is located, even dependent, or, if it is a Stauropegian monastery, to the bishop designated by the patriarch.

Can. 473 . § 1 . In each monastery, divine praises are celebrated daily according to the norm of typical and legitimate customs; Likewise, the Divine Liturgy must be celebrated every day, except those that are excluded by the prescriptions of the liturgical books. § 2 . The Superiors of the monasteries must take care that all members conform to the norm: 1. They are not legitimately hindered by the daily praises of God and by the Divine Liturgy; When this is celebrated, they participate in the contemplation of divine things and diligently dedicate themselves to other exercises of piety; 2° to be able to go freely and frequently to spiritual fathers and confessors; 3. Every year, for several days, they are released from spiritual retreat.

Can. 474 . § 1 . Members of monasteries must frequently receive the sacrament of penance according to the norm. § 2 . With the typical firmness that encourages confession among certain confessors, all members of the monastery can receive the sacrament of penance from any priest who has the capacity to administer this sacrament and who is endowed with firm monastic discipline.

Can. 475 . § 1 . In each monastery, the spiritual fathers and confessors who exceed the number of members will be appointed by the Superior of the monastery himself, if they are priests-monks of the same monastery, who are endowed with the capacity to minister the sacrament of penance, or in other cases by the local Hierarch, after hearing the Superior of the independent monastery, who must previously consult the interested community. § 2 . For monasteries in which there are no priest-monks, the local Hierarch will likewise appoint a priest whose duty will be to regularly celebrate the Divine Liturgy in the monastery and preach the word of God with firmness Can. 612 , § 2 .
Can. 476 . Members of the monastery, both inside and outside the monastery, must wear the monastic habit prescribed by their own typical.

Can. 477 . § 1 . In the monastery, the cloister will be kept in the prescribed manner in the typical manner, except for the right of the Superior by way of act and for serious reasons to admit into the responsible parts of the cloister persons of a different sex from those who can enter according to the typical cloister. § 2 . The parts of the monastery that face the enclosure are clearly indicated. § 3 . It is up to the superior of the monastery to precisely prescribe the limits of the enclosure or change it for just cause, with the consent of his lawyer and notification to the eparchial bishop.

Can. 478 . The superior of the monastery may allow members to live outside the monastery for a certain time in the typical manner; But for absences exceeding one year, unless due to study or illness, permission is required from the authority to which the monastery is subject.

Can. 479 . If, in the opinion of the local Hierarch, the assistance of the monasteries is necessary for the catechetical instruction of the people, all the Superiors must be requested by the same Hierarch to provide it to the people in their own churches, either by themselves or through others.

Can. 480 . A parish cannot be erected in the church of a monastery, nor can monks be appointed parish priests without the consent of the Patriarch within the territory of the Church under his charge, or in other cases of the Apostolic See. 6° Of the hermits
Can. 481 . A hermit is a member of an independent monastery, who dedicates himself entirely to the contemplation of the heavens and is completely isolated from men and the world.

Can. 482 . To legitimately enter the hermit life it is required that the member has obtained the license from the superior of the independent monastery to which he belongs, with the consent of its council, and has remained at least six years from the day of perpetual profession in the monastery.

Can. 483 . The place where the hermit lives must be designated by the Superior of the monastery and be separated in a special way from the world and the other parts of the monastery; but if a place is found outside the walls of the monastery, the written consent of the eparchial bishop is also required.

Can. 484 . The hermit depends on the Superior of the monastery and is subject to the canons of the monks and the typical monastery, to the extent that they can be reconciled with the life of a hermit.

Can. 485 . The superior of an autonomous monastery may, with the consent of his council, impose the end of the hermit's life for just cause, even against the will of the hermit. 7° From the Stauropegian monastery

Can. 486 . § 1 . The patriarch, for a serious reason, after consulting the eparchial bishop and with the consent of the permanent Synod, may, in the very act of erecting the monastery, grant the status of a stauropegic monastery. § 2 . The Stauropegian monastery is directly subject to the Patriarch, so that only he has the same rights and obligations as the eparchial bishop with respect to the monastery, both of the members enrolled in it and of the people who spend long hours and nights in the monastery; but the other persons attached to the monastery are directly and exclusively subject to the Patriarch therein only insofar as their office or duty is concerned. 8. About the transition to another monastery

Can. 487 . § 1 . A member may not transfer from an independent monastery to another in the same confederation without the written consent of the president of the confederation. § 2 . For the transfer from an unaffiliated monastery to another monastery subject to the same authority, the consent of the same authority is required; but if the monastery to which the passage is made is subject to another authority, the consent of this authority is also required. § 3 . The patriarch, the eparchial bishop and the president of the confederation can only give this consent with the advice of the superior of the autonomous monastery from which the transition occurs. § 4 . Furthermore, for the validity of the transfer to a monastery of another independent Church, the consent of the Apostolic See is required. § 5 . The transition is made through the admission by the Superior of a new independent monastery granted by the consent of the Synaxis.

Can. 488 . § 1 .
