Those whose advice, consent or confirmation is required by law to dispose of ecclesiastical property must not give advice, consent or confirmation before having been accurately informed of the financial status of the legal entity whose temporal property is proposed to be disposed of, and of the disposals already made. § 2 . The advice, consent or confirmation will be deemed not to have been given, unless the application states that the disposals have already been made.
Can. 1039 . For any transfer, the consent of the interested parties is required.

Can. 1040 . If ecclesiastical property has been alienated against the provisions of canon law, but the alienation is valid under civil law, the superior authority of the person who has made such alienation, after considering everything in advance, decides whether and what kind of action, by whom and against whom should be proposed to vindicate the rights of the Church.

Can. 1041 . Unless it is a matter of minor importance, ecclesiastical property cannot be sold or leased to proper administrators and their relatives up to the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity without special authorization, as mentioned in cann. 1036 y 1037.

Can. 1042 . cann. 1035 - 1041 must be observed not only in the case of disposal, but also in any transaction in which the financial situation of the legal entity may worsen. CHAPTER IV Of pious wills and pious foundations

Can. 1043 . § 1 . He who, by natural or canon law, can freely dispose of his property, may also for pious reasons, whether by act inter vivos or by act of death, leave his property. § 2 . In the last wills, for the good of the Church, if possible, the provisions of civil law are observed; If they are not observed, the heirs must be warned of the obligation by which they are obliged to comply with the will of the testator.

Can. 1044 . The wills of the faithful who donate or leave their assets to pious causes, whether by inter vivos act or by legally accepted act of death, must be made with great care, also with regard to the form of administration and disbursement of the firm's assets Can. 1045 .

Can. 1045 . § 1 . He is the Hierarch of all pious wills, both in death and in life. § 2 . By right, the Hierarch can and must watch over him, even through visits, so that his pious wishes are fulfilled, and the other executors must give him an account of the work done. § 3 . Clauses contrary to this Hierarchical right added to the last wills will be considered not applied.

Can. 1046 . § 1 . He who has received assets for pious reasons, whether by act inter vivos or by act of death in trust, must inform the corresponding Hierarch of his trust and communicate all those assets with associated charges; but if the donor has expressly and totally prohibited it, he will not accept the trust. § 2 . The hierarch must demand that the trust assets be kept safe, and ensure according to the rule of Can. 1045, § 2, so that the pious will is fulfilled. § 3 . If these are fiduciary assets entrusted to a member of a religious institution or a society of common life analogous to religious ones, which are intended for local or eparchical churches, for the faithful who reside there, or for aid to pious causes, the Hierarch, referred to in §§ 1 and 2, is the local Hierarch.

Can. 1047 . § 1 . Pious foundations in law are: 1° autonomous pious foundations, that is, groups of things destined for works of piety, apostolate or spiritual or temporal charity, and constituted as a legal entity by the competent authority; 2° non-autonomous pious foundations, that is, temporary goods delivered in any way to a legal entity with a long-term charge, which will be determined by the particular law, charged to the annual income, within the limits mentioned in n. 1, to pursue. § 2 . The temporal goods of a non-autonomous foundation, if entrusted to legal entities subject to the eparchial bishop, after a certain time, must be assigned to the institute, about which in Can. 1021, § 1, unless the founder's will is expressly stated otherwise; Otherwise, they are transferred to the same legal entities.

Can. 1048 . § 1 . Autonomous pious foundations can only be established by an eparchial bishop or other higher authority. § 2 . For a non-autonomous pious foundation to be validly accepted by a legal entity, the written consent of the corresponding Hierarch is required; But the hierarch should not give his consent before having legitimately discovered that the legal entity can assume a new burden and satisfy those already assumed; That the same Hierarch also ensure that the income corresponds entirely to the associated charges, according to the custom of the independent Church itself. § 3 . It is a particular right to determine the other conditions without which pious foundations cannot be established or accepted.

Can. 1049 . The Hierarch who has established a pious foundation or has given his consent to accept a pious foundation, will immediately designate a safe place in which the money and movable property assigned in the name of the endowment will be deposited for this purpose, so that the same money or the value of the movable property is preserved and as soon as possible with prudence and profit, after consulting the prudent judgment of the same Hierarch and of the interested parties, and with competent advice, it is invested in favor of the same foundation with a title expressly mentioning the cargo.
Can. 1050 . One copy of the founding act will be kept in the archive of the eparchial court and the other in the archive of the legal entity.

Can. 1051 . § 1 . Having saved cann. 1044 - 1046 et 1031 from the burdens that fall on pious foundations, let a table be prepared, displayed in a clear place, so that the obligations to be fulfilled do not fall into oblivion. § 2 . A book must be kept and kept with the pastor or rector of the church, in which individual charges and their fulfillment and alms are recorded.

Can. 1052 . § 1 . The reduction of the burden of celebrating the Divine Liturgy is reserved for the Apostolic See. § 2 . If the founding document expressly provides for this issue, the Hierarch can reduce the burden of celebrating the Divine Liturgy due to reduced income. § 3 . The eparchial bishop has the power to reduce the number of celebrations of the Divine Liturgy due to a decrease in income, while the case continues, to the number of legitimately valid offerings in the eparchy, provided that there is no one who is bound by an obligation and can usefully be forced to make an increase in the offerings. § 4 . The eparchial bishop also has the power to reduce the charges for the celebration of the Divine Liturgy, which burden ecclesiastical institutions, if the income is insufficient to reach what could be obtained from them at the time of acceptance of the charges. § 5 . The powers mentioned in §§ 3 and 4 are also held by the general superiors of religious institutes or societies of common life, similar to religious clerics of pontifical or patriarchal right. § 6 . The powers mentioned in §§ 3 and 4, the eparchial bishop can only delegate to the coadjutor bishop, the auxiliary bishop, the protosyncello or the syncelli excluding any subdelegation.

Can. 1053 . The same authorities, mentioned in Can. 1052, have the power to transfer, for no other reason, the duties of celebrating the Divine Liturgy to days or institutions other than those established in the foundation.

Can. 1054 . § 1 . The voluntary reduction, control and exchange of the faithful who donate or leave their property to pious causes, if the founder has expressly granted this power to the Hierarch, can only be done by the Hierarch himself upon request and for a necessary cause. § 2 . If the execution of the imposed charges has become impossible due to a reduction in income or for any other reason, without fault of the administrators, the Hierarch, after consulting the interested parties, and with a competent plan and respecting as best as possible the will of the founder, may also reduce the same charges to the company Can. 1052. § 3 . In other cases, the matter must be addressed to the Apostolic See or the Patriarch, who acts with the consent of the permanent Synod. TITLE XXIV OF SENTENCES IN GENERAL

Can. 1055 . § 1 . The purpose of the ruling is: 1° to pursue or vindicate the rights of natural or legal persons or to declare legal facts; 2nd Crimes, which refer to the imposition of punishment. § 2 . However, in controversies arising from the act of the executive branch, only the authority higher than the cann. 996 -1006 standard is competent.
Can. 1056 . In cases reserved to a department of the Apostolic See, the courts must follow the rules issued by that department.
Can. 1057 . In the case of the servants of God, in order for them to be counted among the saints, special norms established by the Roman Pontiff are observed. CHAPTER I. OF THE COMPETENT FORUM
Can. 1058 . The Roman Pontiff is not judged by anyone.

Can. 1059 . § 1 . Due to the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, it is essential that every Christian faithful refer his case, in any state and level of judgment, to the same Roman Pontiff, who is the supreme judge for the entire Catholic world and who pronounces the law by himself or by the courts of the Apostolic See or by judges delegated by him. § 2 . However, this challenge presented to the Roman Pontiff does not suspend, except in the case of appeal, the exercise of the power of the judge who has already begun to hear the case and who can, therefore, continue the trial until the final sentence, unless it is established that the Roman Pontiff has appealed the case to himself.

Can. 1060 . § 1 . Only the Roman Pontiff has the right to judge: 1. The patriarchs; 2° Bishops in criminal cases; 3° those who hold the highest position in the State; 4° other cases, which he himself invoked for his sentence. § 2 . With the exception of bishops who exercise their authority within the territory of the Patriarchal Church, other bishops are judged in contentious cases by a court appointed by the Roman Pontiff, except Can. 1066 , § 2 . § 3 . A judge cannot see an act or document specifically confirmed by the Roman Pontiff, unless he has preceded him.

Can. 1061 . Persons who do not have authority higher than that of the Roman Pontiff must appear before the courts of the Apostolic See, whether they are natural persons not established in the order of the episcopate or legal persons, with the exception of Can. 1063 , § 4 , nos. 3 and 4

Can. 1062 . § 1 . The Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church, subject to the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, is the highest court within the territory of the Church itself. § 2 . The Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church must elect by secret ballot, for a period of five years, from among its members a General Moderator of the administration of justice, as well as two Bishops, who with him will constitute a tribunal; but if one of these three bishops is involved in the case or cannot be present, the Patriarch, with the consent of the permanent Synod, may substitute another bishop; Likewise, in case of refusal, let the Patriarch take care of the consent of the current Synod. § 3 . It is up to this court to judge contentious cases of eparchies or bishops, including titular bishops. § 4 . The appeal in these cases is made to the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church, and another appeal is eliminated, except Can. 1059 . § 5 . The general director of the administration of justice has the right to supervise all courts located within the territory of the Patriarchal Church, as well as the right to issue an objection decision against any judge of the ordinary court of the Patriarchal Church.

Can. 1063 . § 1 . The Patriarch must establish an ordinary court of the Patriarchal Church distinct from the court of the Patriarch's Eparchy. § 2 . This court will have its own president, judges, promoters of justice, defenders of the bond and other necessary administrators appointed by the Patriarch with the consent of the permanent Synod; The president, the judges, the promoter of justice as well as the defenders of the bond cannot be removed except by the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church, but only the Patriarch can accept the resignation of office. § 3 . This court is the court of appeal in the second and subsequent stages of the trial, with the participation of successive judges, for cases already defined in the lower courts; This court also has the rights of the metropolitan court for them in the areas of the territory of the Patriarchal Church, where no provinces have been established. § 4 . This court is competent to judge, with the help of successive judges, in the first and subsequent stages of the process: 1° of the Exarchs and delegates of the Patriarch, who are not bishops; 2° of the natural or legal persons directly subordinate to the Patriarch; 3rd institutes of consecrated life of pontifical right; 4° of the higher institute of consecrated life of pontifical right, which in the same institute does not have a superior endowed with judicial power; 5° of the provisions of particular law reserved to the same court.

Can. 1064 . § 1 . The metropolitan court, which is not different from the metropolitan eparchial court, is the court of appeal from the sentences of the eparchial courts. § 2 . From cases judged in the first degree of trial before the Metropolitan or other eparchial bishop, who has no higher authority than that of the Roman Pontiff, an appeal must be made to a tribunal designated by him on a permanent basis with the approval of the Apostolic See under the signature cann. 139 y 175.
Can. 1065 . The third degree court is the Apostolic See, unless expressly provided otherwise in common law.

Can. 1066 . § 1 . In each eparchy and for all cases not expressly excluded by law, the judge of first instance is the eparchial bishop. § 2 . If these are temporal rights or assets of a legal entity represented by the eparchial bishop, the court of appeal decides in the first instance under the signature Can. 1062 , § 3 .

Can. 1067 . § 1 . The Patriarch, with the consent of the eparchial bishops concerned, may constitute a court of first degree for several eparchies of the same independent Church, if they are eparchies located within the territory of the patriarchal Church; in other cases by the eparchial bishops themselves, who accepted it with the approval of the Apostolic See. § 2 . This court must be established if individual eparchial bishops are unable, for any reason, to establish their own court; within the limits of the territory of the Patriarchal Church, if the case warrants it, this tribunal will be constituted by the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church. § 3 . In the eparchies for which such a court has been established, a collegiate eparchial court cannot validly be established. § 4 . The group of eparchial bishops who have consented to such a tribunal, or the eparchial bishop elected by it, are entitled to the powers which the eparchial bishop has with respect to his tribunal; but if this tribunal has been constituted by the Synod of Bishops of the Patriarchal Church or by the Apostolic See, the norms established by the Synod or the Apostolic See must be observed. § 5 . The appeal from this court is made within the territory of the Patriarchal Church to the ordinary court of the Patriarchal Church; in other cases, however, to the court permanently by the group of bishops, as mentioned in § 4, with the approval of the Apostolic See or appointed by the Apostolic See itself.

Can. 1068 . § 1 . The eparchial bishops of different independent Churches that exercise their power in the same territory may agree among themselves to establish a common court to hear cases, whether contentious or criminal, of the Christian faithful subject to any of the same eparchial bishops. § 2 . If competent judges and other court officials are lacking, the eparchial bishops will ensure that a common court is established. § 3 . The eparchial bishops, who have agreed on a common court, must designate one of their own, to whom the powers that the eparchial bishop has with respect to his own court are competent. § 4 . The sentences of the general court are appealed in the first degree before a court permanently designated by the Apostolic See.

Can. 1069 . § 1 . Disputes between natural or legal persons of the same institution of consecrated life, with the exception of secular institutions, in which the Superiors are endowed with the power of government, must be resolved by a judge or a court determined by the typical or statutory institution. § 2 . If a dispute arises, with the exception of secular institutions, between natural or legal persons of different institutions of consecrated life or even of the same eparchial or other legal institution, in which the Superiors are not endowed with the power of government, or between a member or legal person of an institution of consecrated life and any other natural or legal person, the eparchial court decides in the first instance.

Can. 1070 . The authority establishing any court shall ensure that the court has its own statutes approved by the same authority, which shall determine the manner of appointment, duration of office, remuneration and other legal requirements of the court and other administrators.
Can. 1071 . Each court has the right to call upon the aid of another court of any Church to carry out certain procedural acts, except, however, those acts involving decisions of judges.

Can. 1072 . In the cases mentioned in cann. 1060, 1061, 1062, § 3 and 1063, § 4 the incompetence of the lower judges is absolute; Likewise, the incompetence of the judge is absolute, if the competence established by the sentencing level is not observed.

Can. 1073 . § 1 . No one can be summoned in the first degree of trial except before a judge who is competent for one of the titles determined by common law. § 2 . The incompetence of a judge who is not endorsed by any of these titles is said to be relative. § 3 . Unless otherwise expressly provided by law, the plaintiff is governed by the jurisdiction of the defendant; But if the defendant has multiple jurisdiction, the option of jurisdiction is granted to the plaintiff.
Can. 1074 . Any person can be summoned before a domicile or quasi-domicile court.

Can. 1075 . § 1 . The homeless man has a market in the place where he actually resides. § 2 . The person whose domicile, quasi-domicile or place of residence is unknown may be heard in the plaintiff's forum, provided that no other legitimate forum exists.

Can. 1076 . Due to the fact that the thing is located, the party can be brought before the court of the place where the thing in dispute is located, provided that the action is directed to the thing or to the question of plunder.

Can. 1077 . § 1 . A party to a contract may be sued in the court of the place where the contract was made or is to be performed, unless the parties have agreed to another court. § 2 . If these are obligations arising from another title, the party may go to the court of the place where the obligation arose or must be fulfilled.
Can. 1078 . In criminal cases the accused, even if absent, may be brought before the court of the place where the crime was committed.

Can. 1079 . A party may be summoned: 1° in cases that refer to administration, before the court of the place where the administration took place; 2° in cases that refer to inheritances or pious legacies, before the court of the last domicile or quasi-domicile or firm residence Can. 1075, § 2 of the person whose inheritance or pious legacy is in question, except in the case of the mere execution of the legatee, which must be assessed according to the ordinary rules of jurisdiction.

Can. 1080 . If none of the previous titles are supported by the judge and the case is still submitted to his knowledge, he obtains jurisdiction if the parties and the authority to which the court is directly subject agree.
Can. 1081 . On the basis of connection, related cases must be recognized by the same court and in the same process, unless otherwise provided by law.
Can. 1082 . On the basis of prevention, if two or more courts are equally competent, you have the right to hear the case, because you first legitimately summoned the defendant.

Can. 1083 . § 1 . Conflicts between judges regarding which of them is competent for a given task will be resolved by the court of appeal of the judge before whom the action was first filed through the document presenting the case. § 2 . However, if one of the courts is the court of appeal of the other, the conflict must be resolved by the third degree court of the court in which the action was first filed. § 3 . Decisions in these conflicts are not subject to appeal.

Can. 1084 . § 1 . The collegiate court of three judges is reserved: 1° cases relating to the bond of sacred ordination; 2nd cases relating to the firm marriage bond cann. 1372 - 1374; 3° criminal cases for crimes that carry the penalty of major excommunication, deprivation of office, reduction to a lower rank or deposition; 4° the cases determined by the particular law of the Church itself by its own right. § 2 . Other cases are heard by a single judge, unless the eparchial bishop reserves a specific case for a three-judge court. § 3 . In the first stage of the process, if a college cannot be established, while this impossibility persists, the Patriarch, consulted by the Permanent Synod, may allow the Bishop to entrust the eparchical cases to a single clerical judge, who, if possible, will provide him with an advisor and an auditor; the same can be granted by a Metropolitan who presides over an autonomous Metropolitan Church, or even by a Metropolitan of a patriarchal Church appointed outside the territorial limits of the same Church, each of them having consulted two eparchial Bishops of major episcopal ordination; In other cases you must go to the Apostolic See.

Can. 1085 . § 1 . The collegiate court must proceed collegially and make decisions by majority vote, including for their validity, if it involves: 1° the rejection of the request for counter-conventional action or incident case; 2° on the definition of the appeal against the president's decree; 3. Of the sentence, even if it is interlocutory, as well as of the decrees that have the force of a final sentence. § 2 . Carry out the rest of the procedural acts, unless the school has reserved any, not even for its validity. § 3 . If the case was heard collegially at the first trial level, it must also be resolved collegially at the appeal level and not by a smaller number of judges; but for him it must be determined by a single judge, even at the appeal level by a single judge, except the case mentioned in Can. 1084, § 3. CHAPTER II OF THE COURT ADMINISTRATORS Art. I OF THE JUDICIAL VICAR, OF THE JUDGES AND OF THE ACCOUNTS

Can. 1086 . § 1 . The eparchial bishop is obliged to establish a judicial vicar with ordinary judicial power distinct from the Protosyncello, unless the smallness of the eparchy or the paucity of cases suggests otherwise. § 2 . The judicial vicar constitutes a single court with the eparchial bishop, but cannot judge cases that the eparchial bishop has reserved for himself. § 3 . Assistants to the Judicial Vicar may be appointed, who are called Deputy Judicial Vicars. § 4 . Both the Judicial Vicar and the Deputy Judicial Vicars must be priests of perfect reputation, doctors in canon law or at least graduates, proven prudence and zeal for justice, over thirty years of age.

Can. 1087 . § 1 . In the eparchy, the eparchial judges are appointed by the eparchial bishop, who are clerics. § 2 . The Patriarch, consulted by the Permanent Synod, or the Metropolitan, who presides over the independent Metropolitan Church, may, after consulting the two eparchial Bishops by episcopal ordination, allow other Christian judges to also be appointed, of whom it may be assumed that one of them will form a college if necessary. In other cases you must go to the Apostolic See for this matter. § 3 . Judges must be honorable, doctors or at least licensed in canon law, demonstrated prudence and zeal for justice.

Can. 1088 . § 1 . The judicial substitute, the judicial substitute and the other judges are appointed for a specific period. § 2 . If the designated time has elapsed and the eparchial see is vacant, they cannot be removed, but continue in office until a new eparchial bishop has taken care of the matter. § 3 . If the administrator of the eparchy appoints a judicial vicar, he needs confirmation from the new eparchial bishop.
Can. 1089 . A single judge in any process may obtain two advisors from among proven faithful to advise him.

Can. 1090 . § 1 . The two judges who, together with the president, constitute the collegiate court, will be appointed by the Judicial Vicar from among the eparchial judges, by order, unless the eparchial bishop, out of his prudence, has considered otherwise appropriate. § 2 . The Judicial Vicar may not replace the designated judges except for the most serious cause that the decree expresses its validity.

Can. 1091 . § 1 . The collegiate court is presided over, if possible, by a Judicial Vicar or an Associate Judicial Vicar. § 2 . The president of the collegiate court must designate one of the judges of the same court as rapporteur, unless he wishes to fulfill this function. § 3 . The same president can replace another for just cause. § 4 . At the meeting, the judge reports on the case and makes a written decision.
Can. 1092 . The rights of the court and the president belong to the sole judge.

Can. 1093 . § 1 . The judge or the president of the collegiate court may appoint an auditor to carry out the investigation of the case, choosing him from among the judges of the court or among the faithful admitted to this position by the eparchial bishop. § 2 . The eparchial bishop may admit to the position of auditor those who are of good reputation, prudence and doctrine. § 3 . It is the auditor's duty, according to the judge's order, only to collect the evidence and deliver it to the judge; but he may, unless prevented by the judge's order, decide in the meantime what and how the evidence is to be collected, if by chance any doubt arises on this matter in the exercise of his duty. Art. II OF THE PROMOTER OF JUSTICE, OF THE BOND DEFENDER AND OF THE NOTARY

Can. 1094 . For contentious cases in which the public good may be questioned, and for criminal cases, a promoter of justice is appointed in the eparchy, who has the obligation to ensure the public good.

Can. 1095 . § 1 . In contentious cases, it is up to the eparchial bishop to judge whether the public good can be questioned or not, unless the intervention of the promoter of justice is prescribed by law or is clearly necessary by the nature of the matter. § 2 . If the promoter of justice intervenes in the previous stage of the trial, in the subsequent stage this intervention is presumed necessary.

Can. 1096 . In cases involving the annulment of a sacred ordination or the annulment or dissolution of a marriage, a defender of the bond is appointed in the eparchy, who has the obligation to propose and explain everything that can reasonably be challenged against the annulment or dissolution.

Can. 1097 . In cases where the presence of the promoter of justice or the defender of the bond is required, there is no procedure unless they have been summoned, unless, although not summoned, they were actually present, or at least able to perform their functions after inspecting the proceedings before the verdict.

Can. 1098 . Unless expressly provided otherwise in common law: 1. Whenever the law orders that the judge hear the parties or the other, the promoter of justice and the defender of the bond must also be heard, if they are present at the trial; 2° Whenever a party's request is required for the judge to decide something, the request of the promoter of justice or the defender of the bond, who intervene in the sentence, has the same force.

Can. 1099 . § 1 . It is the duty of the eparchial bishop to appoint the promoter of justice and the defender of the bond; In non-eparchial courts they are appointed in accordance with the statutes of the court, unless otherwise provided by law. § 2 . The promoter of justice and the defender of the bond must be Christians of unbreakable reputation, doctors in canon law or at least licensed and proven prudent and zealous for justice.

Can. 1100 . § 1 . The same person, but not in the same case, can perform the role of promoter of justice and defender of the bond. § 2 . The promoter of justice and the defender of ties may be appointed for all cases or for individual cases; but they can be removed by the eparchial bishop for just cause.

Can. 1101 . § 1 . A notary is involved in every procedure, so there are no minutes if they are not signed by him. § 2 . Diaries prepared by journalists give public credit. 3 ON THE ADMINISTRATIVE COURTS OF DIFFERENT EPARCHIES OR CHURCHES THAT ASSUME THEIR RIGHTS

Can. 1102 . § 1 . Judges and other officials of the courts may be recruited in any eparchy, religious institute or community of common life, in the manner of its own religious or even of another independent Church, with the written consent of its own eparchial bishop or major superior. § 2 . The delegated judge, unless otherwise instructed by the delegation, may resort to the assistance of administrators who reside in the territory of the principal. CHAPTER III OF THE OBLIGATIONS OF JUDGES AND OTHER COURT ADMINISTRATORS

Can. 1103 . § 1 . All the faithful of Christ, and especially the bishops, are diligently alerted so that, in the interests of justice, disputes among the people of God may be avoided, as far as possible, or settled peacefully as soon as possible. § 2 . At the threshold of the case, and also at any other time, whenever he perceives the hope of a good result, the judge will not fail to encourage and assist the parties, so that they can develop a common plan to seek an equitable solution to the dispute, and will indicate to them the appropriate means to achieve this end, including important persons employed as mediators. § 3 . However, if the case concerns the private property of the parties, let the judge decide whether the dispute can usefully be resolved by compromise or by a compromise between the arbitrators.

Can. 1104 . § 1 . The competent judge must provide his service to the legally requesting party. § 2 . A judge cannot recognize any case, unless it has been requested in accordance with the canons by the interested party, or by the promoter of justice.

Can. 1105 . A person who participated in a case as a judge, promoter of justice, bail advocate, solicitor, solicitor, witness or expert cannot subsequently validly determine the same case at another judicial level as a judge or act in the same role as an appraiser.

Can. 1106 . § 1 . The judge must know that he will not accept a case in which by reason of consanguinity or kinship in any degree of direct line and up to and including the fourth degree of the collateral line, or by reason of protection and guardianship, habits of intimate life, close coexistence, or obtaining gain or avoiding loss, he has interest. § 2 . In the same circumstances, the promoter of justice, the defender of the bond, the appraiser and the auditor must refrain from exercising their position.

Can. 1107 . § 1 . If a judge, whether in an ordinary or delegated court, although competent, is rejected, the authority to which the court is directly subject will define this exception with the exception of Can. 1062, §§ 2 and 5. § 2. If the eparchial bishop is a judge and any objection is raised against him, he should refrain from judging. § 3 . If the objection is raised against the other administrators of the court, the president of the collegiate court or the judge, if he is the only one, must deal with this exception.
Can. 1108 . Once the refutation is admitted, the people must be changed, but not the degree of sentence.

Can. 1109 . § 1 . The question of recusal should be resolved as soon as possible after hearing the parties. § 2 . The acts dictated by the judge, before being rejected, are valid; and those that have been placed after the challenged refusal, must be rescinded, if the party so requests, within ten days from the acceptance of the refusal; are invalid after the admitted denial.

Can. 1110 . § 1 . In a matter that only interests individuals, the judge can only proceed at the request of a party; but the judge can and must proceed in a legally initiated case, even ex officio, in criminal cases and in other cases that refer to the public good of the Church or the salvation of souls. § 2 . Furthermore, the judge may compensate for the negligence of the parties in the taking of evidence or in the opposition, whenever he considers it necessary to avoid a seriously unjust sentence.

Can. 1111 . Judges and courts will ensure that all cases are concluded as soon as possible with the preservation of justice, so that they do not last more than one year at the first trial level, and no more than six months at the appeal level.
Can. 1112 . All who establish the court or assist it must make a promise to faithfully carry out the task.

Can. 1113 . § 1 . Always in criminal proceedings, but in litigation, if the disclosure of any procedural act may cause harm to the parties, judges and assistants are obliged to maintain secrecy. § 2 . They are obliged always and in front of everyone to keep secret the discussion that takes place between the judges in the collegiate court before the verdict is handed down, as well as the various votes and opinions expressed there; All others to whom information on the matter reaches in any way are also bound by this secrecy. § 3 . Rather, when the nature of the case or evidence is such that the publication of the acts or evidence endangers the reputation of others or provides a loophole for disagreement or causes a scandal or other such inconvenience, the judge may bind the witnesses, experts, the parties and their lawyers or agents by oath to maintain secrecy.
Can. 1114 . The judge and all other court officials are prohibited from accepting gifts on the occasion of court proceedings.

Can. 1115 . § 1 . Judges who, although they are certainly and clearly competent, refuse to administer justice, or declare themselves competent without any legal provision to support them and to hear and resolve cases, or violate the secrecy prescribed by law, or cause damage to the parties through fraud or gross negligence, may be punished with appropriate penalties by the competent authority, without excluding deprivation of office. § 2 . The same penalties may also be imposed on other officials of the court and their assistants, if they have failed in their duties, as indicated above; all of whom the judge can also punish.

Can. 1116 . If the judge foresees that the petitioner will probably ignore the ecclesiastical ruling, since it may be contrary to it, and therefore the rights of the defendant will not be sufficiently consulted, he may, at the request of the defendant or even ex officio, impose on the petitioner an adequate guarantee for compliance with the ecclesiastical ruling. CHAPTER IV OF THE ORDER OF KNOWLEDGE

Can. 1117 . The cases will be recognized in the order in which they were proposed and registered on the list, unless one of them requires a faster campaign than the others, which, in addition, must be determined by special decree based on reasons.

Can. 1118 . § 1 . The defects for which the nullity of the sentence can be considered may be found at any stage or level of the process, and may also be declared by the judge ex officio. § 2 . But dilatory exceptions, especially those that refer to the persons and the form of the process, must be proposed before the challenge of the lawsuit, unless they have already arisen in the competition, and must be defined as soon as possible.

Can. 1119 . § 1 . If an exception is proposed against the judge's jurisdiction, he must deal with this matter. § 2 . In the case of the exception of relative incompetence, if the judge declares himself competent, his decision does not allow an appeal, but it can be challenged by means of a request for annulment, total restitution or opposition from a third party. § 3 . However, if the judge declares himself incapable, the party that considers itself aggrieved may, within fifteen business days, challenge it before the court of appeal.
Can. 1120 . A judge, at any stage of the process, recognizing that he is absolutely incompetent, must declare his incompetence.

Can. 1121 . § 1 . Exceptions to res judicata, compromise and other peremptory orders, which are called closed cases, must be proposed and known before the case is challenged; The one who objected later will not be rejected, but must pay the legal costs, unless he proves that he did not maliciously delay the opposition. § 2 . Other peremptory exceptions are proposed in the challenge of the case and will be processed in due course according to the rules relating to the issues in question.

Can. 1122 . § 1 . Compensatory actions cannot be validly filed unless they are counted within thirty days following the date of the contested claim. § 2 . Counterclaims must be recognized together with the main action, that is, at the same procedural level as this, unless it is necessary to recognize them separately or the judge considers it more convenient.

Can. 1123 . Issues relating to the granting of a security to cover legal costs or the granting of free legal aid, which were requested immediately from the beginning, and other similar issues should be reviewed periodically before the case is challenged. CHAPTER V OF THE PERIOD, EXTENSIONS AND LOCATION OF THE JUDGMENT

Can. 1124 . § 1 . The expiration periods of the rights established by law may not be validly extended or restricted except by the applicants. § 2 . But the other deadlines, before they have expired, may be extended for just cause heard by the judge or at the request of the parties, but never reduced without agreement of the parties. § 3 . However, the judge must be careful that the trial does not become too long due to the extension.
Can. 1125 . If the law does not establish deadlines for carrying out procedural acts, the judge must determine them taking into account the nature of each act.
Can. 1126 . If the court is on a holiday on the day of the judicial act, the period is understood to be extended until the first day following the non-holiday.
Can. 1127 . The headquarters of the court must be established, if possible, and must be open at the designated hours, observing the rules established by the particular law on the matter.

Can. 1128 . § 1 . A judge expelled from his territory by force or prevented from exercising judicial power there may exercise his power outside the territory and issue a decision, notifying the local eparchial bishop of the matter. § 2 . Furthermore, the judge may, only for the cause and after hearing the parties, leave his own territory to obtain evidence, but with the authorization of the eparchial bishop of the place where he goes and at the headquarters that he designates. CHAPTER VI ON PERSONS ADMITTED BEFORE THE COURT AND THE FORM OF MAKING AND KEEPING MINUTES

Can. 1129 . § 1 . Unless expressly provided otherwise in the particular law of the autonomous Church, while cases are being processed before the court, only those who the law or the judge have determined necessary to expedite the process are present in the court. § 2 . To all those present at the trial who seriously lack the respect and obedience due to the court, the judge may sanction them with a reprimand in cases with appropriate penalties, and may also suspend lawyers and attorneys from the exercise of their functions in the ecclesiastical courts.

Can. 1130 . If any person to be interrogated uses a language unknown to the judge or to the parties, a sworn interpreter designated by the judge will be used; However, the statements should be written in the original language and a translation added; An interpreter must also be used if a deaf or mute person is to be questioned, unless the judge prefers that the questions asked by him be answered in writing.

Can. 1131 . § 1 . All judicial orders, whether those that refer to the substance of the matter, or the case files, or those that refer to the form of the procedure, or the process files, must be reduced to writing. § 2 . The individual sheets of the minutes were numbered and protected by a seal of authenticity.

Can. 1132 . When the signature of the parties or witnesses is required in judicial acts, if the party or witness cannot or does not want to sign them, it will be recorded in the minutes themselves, and at the same time the judge and the notary will certify that the record itself has been read word for word to the party or witness and that the party or witness could not or did not want to sign it.

Can. 1133 . § 1 . At the end of the trial, the documents in the possession of individuals must be returned, preserving their copies. § 2 . The chancellor and notaries are prohibited from delivering copies of the judicial acts and documents acquired in the process without a court order. § 3 . Anonymous letters should be destroyed and no mention of them should be made in the records; In the same way, any other writings and signed letters that do not contribute anything to the merit of the case or are definitely slanderous must be destroyed. CHAPTER VII. ABOUT THE ACTOR AND THE PART CONSIDERED

Can. 1134 . Anyone, baptized or not, can act in judgment; and the defendant must legally respond. Can: 1135 - Even if the plaintiff or the defendant appoints a representative or lawyer, he is always obliged to be present in court as prescribed by law or by the judge.

Can. 1136 . § 1 . Minors and those who have lost the use of reason can only appear in court through their parents or guardians or guardians. § 2 . If the judge believes that their rights conflict with the rights of the parents or guardians or guardians, or that they cannot sufficiently protect their rights, then they appear in court through a guardian or conservator appointed by the judge. § 3 . But in spiritual causes and those related to spiritual causes, if minors have reached the use of reason, they can act and respond without the consent of their parents or guardians, and even by themselves, if they have reached the age of fourteen; Otherwise, by a guardian appointed by the judge. § 4 . Prohibited persons and those of less firm spirit can only appear in court on their own to answer for their own faults or for the judge's precepts; In the rest they must act and respond through their curator.

Can. 1137 . Whenever there is a guardian or tutor appointed by the civil authority, he or she may be admitted by an ecclesiastical judge, after hearing, if possible, the eparchial bishop of the place to which he was delivered; but if he is not present or does not appear admitted, the judge himself will appoint guardian or curator of the case.

Can. 1138 . § 1 . Legal entities appear before the courts through their legal representatives. § 2 . Provided that property is involved, the disposal of which requires the consent or advice or permission of a person, the same consent or advice or permission is also required to initiate or challenge proceedings. § 3 . But in case of lack or negligence of the representative, the Hierarch himself can appear before the courts on his own behalf or on behalf of another on behalf of the legal entities that are under his authority. CHAPTER VIII CONTRACTING FOR CLAIMS AND LAWYERS

Can. 1139 . § 1 . He is equally free to appoint a representative and a lawyer for himself, but he may also act and respond for himself, unless the judge has deemed the service of a representative or lawyer necessary. § 2 . In a criminal proceeding, however, the accused must always have a lawyer appointed by him or her or provided by the judge. § 3 . In the contentious trial, if minors are involved or in a case in which the public good is questioned, with the exception of matrimonial cases, the judge will appoint a lawyer ex officio for the missing party.

Can. 1140 . § 1 . A party may appoint an agent for itself, who may not replace it with another, unless authorized to do so in writing. § 2 . But if for just cause the same party appoints several attorneys, they will be appointed in such a way that there is room for prevention between them. § 3 . Several lawyers may be appointed at the same time.

Can. 1141 . The administrator and lawyer must be of legal age and of good reputation; Furthermore, the lawyer must be Catholic, unless the authority to which the court is directly subject allows otherwise, and a doctor of canon law or another truly expert and approved by the same authority.

Can. 1142 . § 1 . The administrator and the lawyer, before taking office, must deposit an authentic mandate with the court. § 2 . However, to prevent the extinction of the right, the judge may admit the agent even without the mandate being presented, whenever the case warrants it, with adequate guarantee; and the judge's act lacks any force if the attorney does not present the mandate determined by the judge within the peremptory period.

Can. 1143 . Unless he has a special mandate, the agent cannot validly waive the action, suit or judicial act, nor transfer, negotiate, settle in arbitration and in general do those things for which the law requires a special mandate.

Can. 1144 . § 1 . For the removal of the agent or lawyer to take effect, it is necessary that they be informed and, if the case has already been contested, that the judge and the opposing party have been informed of the removal. § 2 . It is widely believed that the ultimate right and obligation to appeal remains with the manager.

Can. 1145 . The agent and the lawyer may be removed by decree issued by the judge, either ex officio or at the request of a party, for serious reasons, and always with recourse to the court of appeal.

Can. 1146 . § 1 . The agent and the lawyer are prohibited from buying a lawsuit or negotiating for themselves an excessive profit or a claimed part of the contentious thing; that if they have done so, there is no agreement and they can be sanctioned by a judge with a financial penalty; In addition, the lawyer may be suspended from his position or even, if he has reoffended, dismissed by the authority to which the court directly reports, and may be removed from the list of lawyers. § 2 . In the same way, agents and lawyers who withdraw cases from the competent courts in fraud of law can be sanctioned, so that they are defined more favorably by others.

Can. 1147 . Agents and lawyers who have betrayed their position by gifts or promises or for any other reason, will be suspended from the practice of law and will be punished with a monetary penalty or other appropriate penalties.

Can. 1148 . In each court, to the extent possible, permanent guardians are appointed, receiving remuneration from the court itself, who act as attorneys or defenders, especially in matrimonial cases, for the parties who prefer to elect them. CHAPTER IX ACTIONS AND EXCEPTIONS
Can. 1149 . Every right is protected not only by action, unless expressly provided otherwise, but also by exception, which is always applicable and is by its nature perpetual.
Can. 1150 . Any action is extinguished by prescription according to law or in any other legitimate manner, except actions relating to the status of persons, which are never extinguished.

Can. 1151 . Contentious actions, unless expressly provided by law to the contrary, are extinguished by prescription five years from the date on which the action could be proposed for the first time, counting the companies where they act in this matter of the Personal Statutes. Can. 1152 n - § 1 . All criminal action is extinguished by the death of the subject, by the condonation of the competent authority and by prescription. § 2 . The criminal action is extinguished by prescription in three years, except in the case of: 1º crimes reserved to the Apostolic See, which are subject to special regulations; 2nd firm provision no. 1, on the action for the crimes mentioned in cann. 1449 , 1450, 1451 et 1453 §§ 1 -4 and 6-7, 1463, 1464, 1466, which expires by prescription in seven years, or on that of the crimes mentioned in Can. 1453 § 5, which is prescribed within a period of twenty years; 3rd of infractions that are not punishable by common law, if the particular law establishes a different limitation period. § 3 . If the accused is summoned in accordance with Can. 1474 or in the manner provided for in Can. 1190 § 3, having been informed of the presentation of the indictment according to Can. 1472 § 1, the prescription of the criminal action is suspended for three years, a period in which expired or interrupted by the suspension of the cessation of the criminal process, the time that is added to the time already elapsed by the prescription runs. again. The same suspension is equally valid if, observing Can. 1486 § 1 , n. 1, impose a penalty by extrajudicial decree. § 4 . Unless otherwise provided by law, the statute of limitations runs from the day the crime was committed or, if the crime is permanent or habitual, from the day it ceased.

Can. 1153 . § 1 . If within the deadlines mentioned in Can. 1152, from the date on which the conviction became res judicata, the execution decree of the judge notified to the defendant is not computed, the action to execute the sentence is extinguished by prescription. § 2 . The same applies to preservation, if the penalty was imposed by extrajudicial decree.

Can. 1154 . The criminal action is extinguished by prescription: 1° the contentious action that may arise from a crime to repair damages is not extinguished by it; 2° if the public good demands it, the Hierarch may use appropriate administrative measures, without excluding the suspension of the exercise of the sacred ministry or dismissal from office.

Can. 1155 . A plaintiff can sue someone for several actions at the same time, which, however, do not conflict with each other, whether on the same issue or on different issues, if they do not exceed the jurisdiction of the court.

Can. 1156 . § 1 . The defendant may file a counterclaim against the plaintiff before the same judge in the same court, or for causes related to the main action, or to suppress or reduce the plaintiff's claim. § 2 . A new trial is not allowed.
Can. 1157 . The counterclaim must be brought before the judge before whom the main action was brought, even if he is only delegated for one case or is relatively incompetent for other reasons.

Can. 1158 . § 1 . He who demonstrates with at least probable proof that he has the right to a thing in the possession of another and is threatened with losing it, unless the thing itself is delivered for safekeeping, has the right to obtain from the judge the seizure of the same thing. § 2 . In similar circumstances, it is possible to obtain that the exercise of the right in favor of someone be inhibited.

Can. 1159 . § 1 . For the security of a creditor, the seizure of something is also allowed, provided that the creditor's right is sufficiently proven. § 2 . The embargo can also extend to the debtor's assets, which are in any capacity in the possession of other people, and to the debtor's debts.

Can. 1160 . In no case may the seizure of property and the inhibition of the exercise of the right be ordered, if the damage feared can be remedied in another way and adequate guarantee of its repair is offered.

Can. 1161 . The judge may impose on whoever is granted the seizure of the property or the inhibition of the exercise of the right, a preliminary guarantee of reparation for the damage, if he has not proven his right.
Can. 1162 . Regarding the nature and force of the possessory action, the civil law of the place where the thing whose possession is involved is located.

Can. 1163 . § 1 . Whenever a petition is filed to obtain a provision for the maintenance of a person, the judge, after having heard the parties, may immediately execute the decree and, if necessary, prescribe the necessary guarantees, so that in the meantime the necessary maintenance is provided, without prejudice to the law determining the sentence. § 2 . Upon hearing the facts from one party or at the request of the promoter of justice to obtain this decree, the judge will resolve the matter as quickly as possible, but never more than ten days; When these have been concluded in vain or the petition has been rejected, recourse will be made to the authority to which the court is immediately subject, provided that it is not a judge, or, if preferred, to the judge of appeal, who will also determine the matter in the most expeditious manner. CHAPTER X METHODS TO AVOID THE SENTENCE Art. ME IN THE TRANSACTION
Can. 1164 . The civil law of the place where the transaction is concluded will be observed in the transaction.

Can. 1165 . § 1 . A transaction cannot be validly carried out in cases that refer to those things or rights that concern the public good, and others, with respect to which the parties cannot freely dispose. § 2 . But if it is about temporary ecclesiastical property, the transfer may be made, observing, however, if the matter so requires, the solemnities established by law for the alienation of ecclesiastical property.
Can. 1166 . Each party will pay equally half of the expenses required by the transaction, unless expressly provided otherwise.
Can. 1167 . The judge is not personally in charge, at least regularly, of managing the matter of the transaction, but entrusts it to other legal experts. Art. II OF THE COMMITMENT OF THE REFEREES

Can. 1168 . § 1 . Those who have a conflict between themselves may agree in writing that it be resolved by arbitrators. § 2 . Those who enter into or have entered into a contract between themselves may agree in writing on any disputes that may arise from said contract.
Can. 1169 . They cannot validly be entrusted to arbitrators for disputes in respect of which a transaction is prohibited.

Can. 1170 . § 1 . One or more arbitrators may be appointed, even if they are unequal in number. § 2 . In the commitment itself, if they are not nominally appointed, at least their number must be determined and at the same time the reason for their appointment and replacement must be established.

Can. 1171 . There is no commitment if: 1° the rules established for the validity of contracts, which go beyond ordinary administration, are not respected; 2° it was not done in writing; 3° the administrator has committed the referees without a special mandate or the provisions of cann. 1169 or 1170 have been violated; 4° the dispute has not arisen nor will it arise from a specific contract in accordance with Can. 1168, § 2.

Can. 1172 . The role of referee cannot be valid: 1st minors; 2° the penalty of excommunication, even minor, suspension or deposition; 3° members of a religious institution or of a society of common life as religious without permission from the Superior.
Can. 1173 . The appointment of an arbitrator is not valid unless he or she accepts the position in writing.

Can. 1174 . § 1 . If the arbitrators were not designated in the compromise, or if they were sufficient and the parties elsewhere who were requested to appoint them disagree in the election of all or some of the arbitrators, each party may entrust it to the court competent to resolve the case in the first instance of the trial, unless the parties have agreed otherwise; The court, after hearing the other parties, will issue a decree. § 2 . The same rule must be observed if one or the other party refuses to appoint an arbitrator, provided that the party that went to court has appointed, at least twenty days in advance, its own arbitrators, if necessary.

Can. 1175 . But the court deals with the refusal of the arbitrators, about which in Can. 1174 , § 1 , which after hearing the rejected arbitrators and by decree of the parties, resolves the issue; If you accept the refusal, the other arbitrators will suffice, unless otherwise provided in the agreement.

Can. 1176 . § 1 . The obligations of the arbitrators will be determined in the commitment itself, including those related to the preservation of secrecy. § 2 . Unless the parties have decided otherwise, the arbitrators freely choose the method of the procedure; but this must be simple and the deadlines short, respecting equity and due respect for procedural law. § 3 . Arbitrators lack coercive power; If necessary, they must go to the competent court to hear the case.

Can. 1177 . § 1 . Any incidental issues that may arise will be decided by the referees themselves. § 2 . But if a prejudicial question arises on which it is not possible to engage the arbitrators, the arbitrators must suspend the proceedings until they have obtained from the judge the parties on that question and have notified the arbitrators of a ruling that has become res judicata, or, if the condition of persons is involved, a ruling that may be ordered to be executed.

Can. 1178 . Unless the parties have decided otherwise, the arbitral award must be rendered within six months from the date on which all arbitrators accepted their position; The period may be extended by the parties.

Can. 1179 . § 1 . The referee's decision is adopted by a majority of the votes cast. § 2 . If the matter is accepted, the arbitration award is drawn up by the arbitrators themselves in the manner of a judicial decision and is signed by each arbitrator; but for its validity it is necessary and sufficient that a greater number of them subscribe to it.

Can. 1180 . § 1 . Unless the arbitration award is void due to the serious fault of the arbitrators, the arbitrators are entitled to payment of their expenses; in which case they may require adequate guarantees. § 2 . It is recommended that referees do their work for free; Otherwise, the remuneration must be provided for in the commitment itself.

Can. 1181 . § 1 . The complete text of the arbitration decision must be deposited within fifteen days in the chancery of the eparchial court where the decision was issued; Within five days following the deposition, unless it is certain that the arbitration decision is affected by nullity, the Judicial Vicar may issue an order of confirmation by himself or by another decision and immediately notify the parties. § 2 . If the Judicial Vicar refuses to issue this decree, the interested party may appeal to the court of appeal, by which the issue must be resolved as quickly as possible; However, if the Judicial Vicar remains silent for a continuous month, the same party may insist that he himself perform his function; If, however, it remains silent, after five days, the party may file an appeal with the court of appeal, which will also resolve the issue as quickly as possible. § 3 . If it is certain that the arbitration award is null and void due to non-compliance with the provisions established for the validity of the commitment, the Judicial Vicar will declare the nullity and notify the parties as soon as possible of any appeal against this declaration. § 4 . The arbitration award becomes res judicata as soon as the confirmation decision is issued by the Can. 1182 firm.

Can. 1182 . § 1 . An appeal against an arbitration decision will only be allowed if the parties have agreed in writing that it will be subject to this appeal; in which case the appeal must be filed within ten days following the date of confirmation of the decree, to be computed before the same judge who made the decree; But if there is another judge competent to hear the appeal, the accusation must be brought before him within one month. § 2 . The arbitration award, with respect to which the appeal is admitted, becomes res judicata in accordance with the Can. 1322 rule.

Can. 1183 . Regarding the claim for annulment against the arbitration decision, which has become res judicata, regarding full restitution, the injustice of the same decision is clearly evident, both regarding the opposition of the third party and regarding the correction of the material error of the decision, the judge who made the confirmation decision abides by the ordinary rule of law.

Can. 1184 . § 1 . The execution of an arbitration award may be carried out in the same cases in which the execution of a judicial award is permitted. § 2 . The arbitral decision must be executed by himself or by another eparchial bishop of the eparchy where it was issued, unless the parties have appointed another executor. TITLE XXV OF THE CONTENTIOUS JUDGMENT CHAPTER I OF THE ORDINARY CONTENTIOUS JUDGMENT Art. I ON THE INTRODUCTORY BOOK OF LITIGATION
Can. 1185 . Anyone who wishes to sue someone must present the competent judge with a document introducing the case, proposing the object of the dispute and requesting the judge's attention.

Can. 1186 . § 1 . The judge may admit the oral request as long as the plaintiff is prevented from presenting the document presenting the case or the case is easy to investigate and of minor importance. § 2 . In both cases, however, the judge orders the notary to draw up a written record, which must be read in the presence of the petitioner and approved by him, and which takes the place of the introductory document drawn up by the petitioner for all legal purposes.

Can. 1187 . The draft presentation of the case must: 1° express, before the judge before whom the case is brought, what is requested and from whom it is requested; 2° indicate what right the plaintiff relies on and, at least in general, what facts and evidence prove what he claims; 3° signed by the petitioner or his representative on the day, month and year, as well as the place where the petitioner or his representative resides or said he resides, in favor of the recipients of the documents; 4° indicate the domicile or quasi-domicile of the defendant.

Can. 1188 . § 1 . The single judge or the president of the collegiate court, after having verified that this is a matter within his jurisdiction and that the plaintiff does not lack a legitimate person to appear before the court, must, by means of his decision, as soon as possible, admit or reject the document presenting the case. § 2 . The bill that introduces the case can only be rejected if: 1° the judge or court is incompetent; 2° it is evident without a doubt that the petitioner lacks a legitimate person to appear before the court; 3rd was not saved Can. 1187, nos. 1 - 3; 4° it certainly appears from the document presenting the case that the petition lacks any basis and it is not possible for any basis to emerge from the process. § 3 . If the project that introduces the lawsuit is rejected due to correctable defects, the plaintiff can resubmit the modified project before the same judge. § 4 . In the event of a total rejection of the introduction project, the party must always present within the useful period of ten days the reasons for appeal supported by the court of appeals or, if the project has been rejected by the president, before the college; but the question of rejection must be defined very quickly.

Can. 1189 . If the judge has not issued a resolution within the month following the presentation of the draft presentation of the case, by which he admits or rejects the draft, the interested party may insist that the judge fulfill his role; but if, however, the judge remains silent, after ten days have elapsed without use since the computation of the instances carried out, the order will be considered admitted. Art. 2 OF THE SUMMONS AND OF THE INTIMATION OR NOTIFICATION OF JUDICIAL ACTIONS

Can. 1190 . § 1 . In the decree that admits the petition of the plaintiff who introduces the claim, the judge or the president of the court must call or summon the other parties to the court to challenge the claim, deciding whether they should respond in writing or appear before it to agree on the doubts; but if from the responses given in writing he perceives the need to convene the parties, he may establish it by means of a new decree. § 2 . If the project for presenting the case is considered admitted according to the Can. 1189 rule, the decision to summon the court must be made within twenty days following the occurrence of the instance mentioned in that canon, to be counted. § 3 . However, if the parties actually appear before the judge to hear the case, no summons will be required, but the notary will record in the minutes that the parties were present at the trial. Can. 1191 - § 1 . The decision of the summons must be immediately communicated to the defendant and at the same time made known to the others who must appear. § 2 . The document presenting the claim will be attached to the summons, unless the judge considers for serious reasons that the document should not be notified to the party before its presentation to the court. § 3 . If an action is filed against someone who does not have the free exercise of his rights or the free administration of the things about which it is disputed, he must be summoned, and he must appear in court in accordance with the law.

Can. 1192 . § 1 . The summons or notification of summonses, decrees, sentences and other judicial acts must be done by public mail with receipt signatures or in another way that is more secure, observing the provisions of the particular law. § 2 . The act of summons or notification and its form must be recorded in the minutes. § 3 . The defendant who refuses to receive the summons or prevents it from reaching him will be considered legally summoned.
Can. 1193 . If the summons is not duly served, there is no record of the process, unless, however, the party appears to carry out the procedure.

Can. 1194 . If the summons has been legally served or the parties have appeared before the judge to hear the case: 1° the matter is no longer complete; 2° the case becomes the jurisdiction of the competent judge or court before which the action was filed; 3° in the delegated judge, the delegated power becomes firm in such a way that it is not lost when the right of the delegate is resolved; 4° the prescription is interrupted, unless otherwise provided; 5° the start of the litigation occurs, so the principle according to which nothing is new during the pending litigation occurs immediately. Art. 3 ABOUT THE LITIGATION OF THE LITIGATION

Can. 1195 . § 1 . It is considered a controversy when the object of the dispute is determined by the judge's decision based on the requests and responses of the parties. § 2 . The requests and responses of the parties, except in the introductory writing of the case, may be expressed either in the response to the summons or in oral statements made before the judge; But in the most difficult cases the parties must be summoned by the judge to agree on a doubt or doubts, which must be answered in the ruling. § 3 . The judge's decree must be communicated to the parties; which, unless they have already agreed, may return within ten days to the same judge, so that the decree may be modified; but the issue must be resolved as quickly as possible by decree of the same judge.

Can. 1196 . The object of the controversy, once defined, cannot be validly modified except by a new decree, for serious reasons, at the request of one of the parties and after hearing the others and considering their arguments.

Can. 1197 . The owner of another's property who is in possession of a contested lawsuit ceases to be in good faith, and therefore, if he is sentenced to return the property, he must also return the profits from the date of the contested lawsuit and repair the damages.
Can. 1198 . In disputed cases, the judge will allow the parties adequate time to present and complete evidence. Art. IV OF THE SUSPENSION, TERMINATION AND TERMINATION OF THE LITIGATION

Can. 1199 . If a party dies or changes status or resigns from the position for which he or she is acting: 1° the cause of action is not yet closed until the heir or successor of the deceased or the interested party resumes the action; 2° Once the case is concluded, the judge must proceed to the new summons of the attorney, if present, or, if not, of the heir or successor of the deceased.

Can. 1200 . § 1 . If the guardian or conservator or administrator or lawyer, who are necessary according to the Can. 1139 regulation, ceases to function, the judicial instance is suspended in the meantime. § 2 . But the judge will appoint another guardian or conservator as soon as possible; but may appoint a representative or lawyer for the case, if the party has failed to do so within the short period established by the judge himself.
Can. 1201 . If the parties do not present a procedural act despite any obstacle for six months, the present case is lost.

Can. 1202 . The cancellation is effective by law and against everyone, even minors, and must also be declared ex officio, except for the right to claim compensation against guardians, curators, administrators, agents who have not proven that they were not at fault.

Can. 1203 . The annihilation extinguished the records of the trial, but not those of the case; What's more, these things can have force even in another sentence, as long as the cause intervenes between the same people and on the same matter; but with respect to foreigners they do not obtain any other force than that of the documents.
Can. 1204 . Once the trial is over, each party must pay the expenses incurred.

Can. 1205 . § 1 . At any stage and level of the process, the plaintiff may renounce the lawsuit; Likewise, both the plaintiff and the defendant may withdraw from the procedure, either from all of them or only from some of them. § 2 . Guardians and administrators of legal entities, in order to renounce the judicial instance, need the advice or consent of those whose participation is required to impose acts that exceed the limits of ordinary administration. § 3 . For the resignation to be valid, it must be made in writing, and must be signed by the same party or by his or her attorney, but with a special mandate, it must be communicated to the other party, and it must be accepted by the latter or not contested and admitted by the judge.

Can. 1206 . The waiver accepted by the judge for the actions that have been waived produces the same effects as the destruction of the lawsuit, and also obliges the waiver to pay the expenses of the actions that have been waived. Art. V OF TESTS

Can. 1207 . § 1 . The burden of proof falls on the person who claims. § 2 . They do not need proof: 1° those that are presupposed by the law itself; 2nd facts affirmed by one of the contenders and admitted by the other, unless, however, the law or a judge requires proof.

Can. 1208 . § 1 . Evidence of any kind may be presented that appears useful to support the case and is admissible. § 2 . If a party insists that the evidence rejected by the judge be admitted, the judge himself will determine the issue as quickly as possible.

Can. 1209 . If a party or a witness refuses to appear to answer before the judge, it is permitted to hear him or her by a person designated by the judge or to require his/her testimony before a public court reporter or in any other lawful manner.
Can. 1210 . The judge should not proceed to collect evidence before challenging the case unless there is a serious reason. 1° Of the statements of the parties
Can. 1211 . The judge can always question the parties to better discover the truth; in fact, he must put them beyond doubt at the request of the party or to prove a fact that is of public interest.

Can. 1212 . § 1 . The party legitimately questioned must answer and confess the whole truth, unless the answer reveals the crime committed by him. § 2 . However, if he refused to respond, it is up to the judge to assess what may be derived from this in order to prove the facts.

Can. 1213 . In cases where the public good is at stake, the judge, when questioning the parties, must swear to tell the truth, or at least convey the truth of what was said, unless serious reasons suggest otherwise; In other cases it may be due to its prudence.
Can. 1214 . The parties, the promoter of justice and the defender of the bond may present to the judge articles about which the party may be questioned.
Can. 1215 . As for the questions of the parties, they remain in accordance with the relevant canons regarding the examination of witnesses.

Can. 1216 . A judicial confession is the affirmation of a written or oral fact before a competent judge by a party against itself on the subject matter of the process, either voluntarily or by questioning the judge.

Can. 1217 . § 1 . The judicial confession of one of the parties, if it involves a private matter and no public good is at stake, frees the others from the burden of proof. § 2 . But in cases that concern the public good, the judicial confession and other statements of the parties may have the force of evidence to be appreciated by the judge together with the other circumstances of the case, but they cannot be given the force of full evidence, unless other elements are added that completely corroborate them.
Can. 1218 . Regarding the extrajudicial confession brought to trial, it is up to the judge to assess, considering all the circumstances, how much should be done.

Can. 1219 . A confession, or any other statement by either party, has no force if it is evident that it was made by mistake of fact, or was twisted by force or great fear. 2° Of the documentary evidence
Can. 1220 . In all types of trials, evidence is admitted through documents, both public and private.

Can. 1221 . § 1 . Public ecclesiastical documents are those that a person has completed on the occasion of his or her public position in the Church, observing the solemnities prescribed by law. § 2 . Civil public documents are those that are considered such according to civil law. § 3 . Other documents are private.

Can. 1222 . Public documents give credence to what is stated in them directly and mainly, except for contrary and obvious arguments that prove otherwise, by the firm civil law of the place that refers to civil documents, establishing otherwise.

Can. 1223 . The private document, whether recognized by a party or reviewed by a judge, has the same probative force against the author of the document or against the person who signed it, and against those who have a case and an extrajudicial confession from them; but against strangers it can have the force of proof that must be appreciated by the judge together with the other circumstances of the case, but it cannot be given the force of full proof, unless other elements are added that completely corroborate it.

Can. 1224 . If it is proven that the documents are scratched, corrected, interpolated or infected with any other defect, it is up to the judge to evaluate whether said documents should be presented and to what extent.

Can. 1225 . The documents do not have the force of evidence before the court, unless they are originals or are presented in an authentic copy and deposited in the chancery of the court, so that they can be examined by the judge and the parties.
Can. 1226 . The judge may order that a document common to both parties be presented to the court.

Can. 1227 . § 1 No one is obliged to present documents, even if they are common, which cannot be shared without risk of damage, as mentioned in Can. 1229 , § 2 , n. 2, or without risk of breach of confidentiality. § 2 . However, if at least part of the document can be described and presented in copy without the aforementioned inconveniences, the judge may decide that it be presented. 3. About witnesses and testimonies
Can. 1228 . The testimony of witnesses is admissible in any case under the supervision of a judge.

Can. 1229 . § 1 . Witnesses must confess the truth when legally questioned by the judge. § 2 . By signing Can. 1231, the following are exempt from the obligation to respond: 1° the clerics, regarding those things that have been revealed to them due to the sacred ministry; state magistrates, doctors, midwives, lawyers, journalists and others, who are obliged to preserve secrecy even by virtue of the established policy, with regard to businesses subject to secrecy; 2° those who, by their testimony, fear infamy, dangerous trips or other serious harm to themselves or to their spouse or to their family or relatives. a) Who can be witnesses?
Can. 1230 . Everyone may be witnesses, unless expressly excluded by law, whether in whole or in part.

Can. 1231 . § 1 . Minors under fourteen years of age and the mentally ill should not be admitted to testify as witnesses; They may, however, be heard from the judge's decree, by which it is declared appropriate. § 2 . The following are considered incapable of testifying: 1° those who are parties to the process or act on behalf of the parties, the judge or his assistants, the lawyer and others who assist or have assisted the parties in the same case; 2° the priests, with respect to all those things that they themselves have known through sacramental confession, even if the penitent has requested their manifestation; On the contrary, what anyone and in any way hears on the occasion of sacramental confession cannot even be accepted as an indication of the truth. b) Regarding the presentation and exclusion of witnesses
Can. 1232 . The party who presented the witness may refuse to cross-examine him; but the opposing party may demand that the witness be questioned nonetheless.

Can. 1233 . § 1 . If witnesses require evidence, their names and addresses will be given to the court. § 2 . The evidence on which the interrogation of witnesses is requested must be presented within the period set by the judge; Otherwise the request will be considered abandoned.
Can. 1234 . It is up to the judge to restrict an excessive number of witnesses.

Can. 1235 . Before examining witnesses, their names will be communicated to the parties; but if, in the judgment of a prudent judge, this cannot be done without great difficulty, it should at least be done before the publication of the evidence.
Can. 1236 . Under TOK1, a party may request that a witness be excluded, if good cause is shown, before questioning him or her.
Can. 1237 . The summons of the witness is made by decree of the judge, the witness having been duly notified.
Can. 1238 . The witness summoned by the judge in accordance with the law must appear or inform the judge of the reason for his absence. c) Regarding the interrogation of witnesses

Can. 1239 . § 1 . Witnesses must be questioned in court, unless the judge thinks otherwise. § 2 . The bishops and those who enjoy similar favor by right of their state must be heard in the place chosen by them. § 3 . The judge decides where to listen to those who, due to distance, illness or other impediment, find it impossible or difficult to go to the court headquarters, signature cann. 1071 y 1128.

Can. 1240 . The parties will not be able to attend the interrogation of witnesses, unless the judge, especially when it involves private interest, has decided to admit them; However, their representatives or lawyers may attend, unless the judge, due to the circumstances of the facts and people, has decided that the procedure must be confidential.
