Can. 1241 . § 1 . The witnesses will be questioned individually. § 2 . If witnesses disagree with each other or with one of the parties on a serious matter, the judge can compare the differences between them, eliminating, as far as possible, disagreements and scandal.

Can. 1242 . The interrogation of the witness is done by the judge or his delegate or by a hearing, which the rapporteur must attend; Therefore, the parties, or the promoter of justice, or the defender of the bond, or the lawyers, who take part in the interrogation, if they have other questions to ask the witness, must propose them, not to the witness, but to the judge or the judge or his substitute, so that he himself can ask them, unless otherwise provided by particular law.

Can. 1243 . § 1 . The judge will remind the witness of the serious obligation to tell the entire and only truth. § 2 . The judge will bring the witness to swear in accordance with Can. 1213; but if the witness refuses to reveal it, he must be declared guilty.

Can. 1244 . The judge first verifies the identity of the witness; He must investigate his relationship with the parties and, when asking specific questions about the case to the witness, also let him know the sources of his knowledge and, within the designated time, find out what he states.

Can. 1245 . The questions should be brief, adapted to the interrogation, not involving several things at the same time, not intelligent, not subtle, not suggesting an answer, far from offending anyone and relevant to the case in question.

Can. 1246 . § 1 . Questions should not be shared with witnesses beforehand. § 2 . But if the things to be testified are so far removed from memory that, unless previously remembered, they cannot be stated with certainty, the judge may admonish the witness of certain things, if he considers that it can be done without danger.
Can. 1247 . Witnesses must testify orally and not read what is written, unless it concerns calculations and accounts; because in this case they can consult the records they bring with them.

Can. 1248 . § 1 . The response must be immediately written down by the rapporteur, who must report the words of the testimony, at least with regard to those that directly affect the object of the trial. § 2 . The use of technical inventions through which voices are reproduced may be permitted, provided that the responses are recorded in writing and signed, if possible, by those who gave them.

Can. 1249 . The notary will mention in the minutes the oaths taken, submitted or refused, the presence of the parties and others, the questions added by the office, and in general everything worth remembering that happened while the witnesses were being questioned.

Can. 1250 . § 1 . At the end of the interrogation before the witness, the statements that the journalist has reduced to writing about his answers must be read, or the witness who has been cut off must be listened to with the help of technical conclusions about his answers, granting the same witness the right to add, delete, correct and vary. § 2 . Finally, the witness, the judge and the notary must sign the record.

Can. 1251 . Witnesses, even if they have already been questioned, may, upon request or ex officio, be called again for questioning, before the evidence is published, if the judge considers it necessary or useful, provided, however, that there is no danger of collusion or corruption.

Can. 1252 . Witnesses must be paid, according to the judge's fair assessment, the expenses they have incurred and the profits they have lost, in order to testify. d) On the reliability of the evidence

Can. 1253 . When evaluating the required evidence, the judge, if necessary, must consider the following: 1° what is the condition of the person and what is their honesty; 2° if he testifies to his own knowledge, especially his own sight and hearing, or his own opinion, reputation or hearing of others; 3° whether the witness is constantly and firmly attached to himself or variable, uncertain or wavering; 4° whether or not it has contradictory evidence or is supported by other elements of evidence.

Can. 1254 . The testimony of a single witness cannot give full credibility, unless it is a qualified witness, who testifies about things done in his or her position, or the circumstances of the things and people suggest otherwise. 4° About the experts

Can. 1255 . The services of experts must be used whenever, by law or the judge, their examination and ruling based on precepts of art or science is required to verify a fact or determine the true nature of something.
Can. 1256 . It is up to the judge to appoint experts to hear or propose to the parties or, where appropriate, to assume reports already prepared by other experts.
Can. 1257 . For the same reasons as a witness, experts can also be excluded or rejected.

Can. 1258 . § 1 . The judge, taking into account the allegations of the parties, must define through his decree the different chapters on which the expert's work must focus. § 2 . The files and other documents and resources that he may need to carry out his duties must be sent to the expert. § 3 . The judge, after hearing the expert himself, will determine the period within which the examination must be completed and the report submitted.

Can. 1259 . § 1 . Each of the experts will prepare their report separately from the others, unless the judge orders that it be written and signed by each one; which, if it occurs, differences of opinion, if any, should be carefully noted. § 2 . Experts must clearly indicate by what documents or other appropriate means they have been informed about the identity of persons, things or places, in what manner and method they have proceeded in carrying out the task entrusted to them and on what other arguments they base their conclusions. § 3 . The judge may call an expert to give the explanations he considers necessary.

Can. 1260 . § 1 . The judge must not only carefully evaluate the conclusions of the experts, even if they agree, but also the other circumstances of the case. § 2 . When you state the reasons for your decision, you should indicate why you accepted or rejected the experts' conclusions in the motion.
Can. 1261 . The experts will be paid the expenses and remuneration determined by the judge on a good and equitable basis, subject to the particular law.

Can. 1262 . § 1 . The parties may appoint private experts who will be approved by the judge. § 2 . Private experts, if the judge allows it, can inspect the proceedings of the case, to the extent necessary, participate in the execution of the expert opinion, but they can always present their report. 5° Access and judicial control

Can. 1263 . If for the definition of the case the judge has been taken to approach some place or inspect some matter, he will preside over it by decree, in which he will summarily describe what is to be done in the approach or in the judicial review.
Can. 1264 . Once judicial access or review is completed, the document must be prepared. 6. Of presumptions

Can. 1265 . The judge, in order to reach a fair decision, can reject presumptions that are not established by the law itself, as long as he does so based on a certain and determined fact, which is related to the object of the controversy.
Can. 1266 . Whoever adheres to the things that the law assumes is free from the burden of proof, which falls on the adverse side. Art. VI OF THE CAUSES OF INCIDENTS

Can. 1267 . An issue is considered to be incidental when an issue is proposed at the beginning that, although not expressly contained in the document presenting the issue, is nevertheless so relevant to the issue that it normally must be resolved before the main issue.
Can. 1268 . Incidental cases are presented in writing or orally in a connection intervening between them and the main case, before a judge competent to determine the main case.

Can. 1269 . § 1 . The judge, having received the request and heard the parties, must determine as quickly as possible whether the proposed issue appears to have foundation and connection with the main issue or whether it should in fact be dismissed at the threshold, and if admitted, whether it is of such seriousness that it must be resolved by interlocutory ruling or by decree. § 2 . However, as it indicates that the issue of the incident should not be resolved before the final ruling, it decides that the same should be taken into account when determining the main cause.

Can. 1270 . § 1 . If the issue in question must be resolved by ruling, the canons of contentious summary judgment are observed, unless, considering the seriousness of the matter, the judge thinks otherwise. § 2 . But if it must be paid by decree, the court may entrust the matter to the comptroller or the governor.

Can. 1271 . Before concluding the main case, the judge or court may revoke or reform the decision or the interlocutory sentence precisely for the cause, either at the request of the party or ex officio by hearing the parties. 1° Of the non-appearing parties

Can. 1272 . § 1 . If the aforementioned defendant did not appear and did not present an adequate excuse for her absence or did not respond to the rule Can. 1190 , § 1 , the judge will declare her absent from the court by decree and will decide that the case be preserved until the final sentence and its execution. § 2 . Before this decision is made, it must also be verified by a new summons, if necessary, that the legally issued summons has reached the defendant in time.

Can. 1273 . § 1 . If the defendant later appears in court or gives a response before the definition of the case, he can provide conclusions and evidence before the signature Can. 1283; But let the judge take care that the trial is not intentionally prolonged by longer and unnecessary delays. § 2 . Even if the defendant did not appear or did not respond before the definition of the case, he may object to the sentence; But if he proves that he was detained due to legitimate impediment, which he could not previously prove without his own fault, he may appeal to the annulment claim.

Can. 1274 . If on the day and time indicated for the answer to the case the plaintiff does not appear or present an adequate excuse: 1° the judge will summon him again; 2° if the petitioner has not appeared at the new summons, it is presumed that he has given notice of the present lawsuit; 3° if you want to intervene later in the process, Can. 1273 will be saved.

Can. 1275 . § 1 . The party absent from the court, who has not proven a just impediment, is obliged to pay the judicial expenses incurred due to his absence, as well as, if necessary, to pay compensation to the other party. § 2 . If both the petitioner and the respondent are absent from court, each of them will be personally responsible for paying all legal costs. 2° Of the intervention of a third party in the case

Can. 1276 . § 1 . The interested party may be admitted to intervene in the case at any stage of the trial, either as a party defending his or her own right, or as an accomplice to assist another party. § 2 . But to be admitted you must, before the conclusion of the case, present a document to the judge, in which you briefly demonstrate your right to intervene. § 3 . The person who intervenes in the case must be admitted in the state of the trial in which he is, having been assigned the same short and peremptory period to present his evidence, if the case has reached the evidentiary period.
Can. 1277 . The judge, after hearing the parties, must call the third party whose intervention seems necessary. 3. About the pending litigation

Can. 1278 . It is the attempted act by which, while awaiting trial, something is innovated by one of the parties against the other or by a judge against one or both to the detriment of the party and the latter disagreeing about the object of the process or procedural rights, unless the innovation is admitted by the law itself.

Can. 1279 . By law there is no attempt, so the judge must decide on its revocation; However, it is corrected by the law itself if within one month from the date of the information about the attempted calculation the question about it is not presented to the judge.

Can. 1280 . Questions about attempts must be resolved as quickly as possible by the judge in the main case, if one of the parties committed the attempts; but if the judge himself committed the attempt, by the court of appeal. Art. VII OF THE PUBLICATION OF THE PROCEDURE, THE CONCLUSION OF THE CASE AND THE DISCUSSION OF THE CASE

Can. 1281 . § 1 . Once the evidence is obtained, the judge must by decree allow the parties and their lawyers, under penalty of nullity, to inspect in the chancery of the court the minutes not yet known to them; that even lawyers who request it can be given a model of the minutes; But in cases that have the public good as their objective, the judge, to avoid the most serious dangers, may decide that a certain act is not revealed to anyone, with the precaution, however, that the right of defense always remains intact. § 2 . To complete the evidence, the parties may propose other things to the judge; therefore, if the judge has led to necessity, the place is acquired again by decree, of which in § 1 .

Can. 1282 . § 1 . Once everything related to the production of evidence is completed, a conclusion is reached in the case. § 2 . This conclusion is sustained whenever the parties have declared that they have nothing more to allege, or the time allowed by the judge for the presentation of useful evidence has elapsed, or the judge has declared that he has sufficiently prepared the case. § 3 . Once the case is concluded, however it occurs, the judge must make a decision.

Can. 1283 . § 1 . Once the process is concluded, the judge may still call the same witnesses or others, or have other evidence that has not been previously requested, only: 1° in cases in which the only private property of the parties is at stake, if all the parties agree; 2° in other cases, after hearing the parties and provided that there is a serious reason and also that any risk of fraud or bribery is eliminated; 3° in all cases, provided that it is probable that, unless new evidence is admitted, the sentence is unjust for the reasons mentioned in Can. 1326, § 2, nos. 1 - 3. § 2 . But the judge may order or admit the presentation of a document that perhaps could not be presented before through no fault of the interested party. § 3 . New tests are published by saving Can. 1281 , § 1 .
Can. 1284 . Once the case is concluded, the judge must reserve an adequate period to present defenses or observations.

Can. 1285 . § 1 . Defenses and observations must be formulated in writing, unless the discussion before the judge on duty is considered sufficient by consent of the parties. § 2 . If the defenses are printed with key documents, the judge's prior authorization is required without prejudice to the obligation of confidentiality, if any. § 3 . Regarding the extension of the defenses, the number of copies and other similar circumstances, the statutes of the court are observed.

Can. 1286 . § 1 . Once defenses and observations have been alternately communicated, both parties may present their responses within the short period established by the judge. § 2 . This right is granted to the parties only once, unless the judge considers that for serious reasons it should be granted again; and then the concession made to one party is considered also made to the other. § 3 . The promoter of justice and the defender of the bond have the right to reply again to the responses of the parties.

Can. 1287 . § 1 . It is absolutely prohibited to give information to the parties' judge or lawyers or even other information that is outside the case file. § 2 . If the discussion of the case has been done in writing, the judge may decide that a moderated discussion be held orally so that the panel in session can clarify some issues.

Can. 1288 . The oral argument, which is discussed in cann. 1285 , § 1 and 1287, § 2 , is assisted by a reporter, so that, if the judge orders it or a party demands it and the judge agrees, he or she may immediately report in writing what was discussed and the conclusions.

Can. 1289 . If the parties have neglected to prepare the defense within the time allotted to them, or if they submit to the judge with knowledge and conscience, the judge, if based on the documents and evidence he has a clear vision of the matter, can immediately issue a sentence with the requirements, but with the observations of the promoter of justice and the defender of the bond, if they are present at the trial. Art. VIII OF THE JUDGE'S PRONUNCIATION

Can. 1290 . The case that has been processed judicially, if it is the main one, is determined by the judge through a final ruling; If it is incidental, by means of an interlocutory sentence I confirm Can. 1269, § 1.

Can. 1291 . § 1 . The pronouncement of any sentence requires in the mind of the judge a moral certainty about the matter that will be defined by the sentence. § 2 . The judge must extract this certainty from the records and evidence. § 3 . But the judge must evaluate the evidence based on his knowledge of the firm provisions of the law regarding the effectiveness of certain pieces of evidence. § 4 . The judge, who could not obtain that certainty, will rule that the petitioner's right is not proven, and will reject the defendant at all, unless it is a case in favor of the law, in which case he must rule in favor of it.

Can. 1292 . § 1 . In the collegiate court, the day and time in which the judges will meet to deliberate will be determined by the president of the college and, unless a special reason suggests otherwise, the meeting will be held at the headquarters of the court itself, where only the judges of the college may be present. § 2 . On the day appointed for the meeting, each of the judges had to bring in writing, but retaining their name, their conclusions on the merits of the case and the reasons, both legal and factual, why they reached their conclusion; whose conclusions, with a note of their authenticity, signed by all the judges, will be attached to the case file, which will be kept secret, under the signature § 4. § 3 . Once the conclusions of each of the judges have been presented in order according to their precedence, so that they always begin with the person presenting the case, a discussion will take place under the direction of the president of the court, especially to establish what is decided in the operative part of the sentence. § 4 . However, in the discussion it is permissible for each one to deviate from his original conclusion; but the judge who refused to accede to the decision of others may demand that, if appealed, the conclusions of all the judges, with the names of all the judges, be sent to the higher court. § 5 . If, on the other hand, the indexes are unwilling or unable to reach a decision in the first discussion, the decision may be postponed to a new meeting for no more than one week, unless the case instruction is completed in accordance with the Can. 1283 standard.

Can. 1293 . § 1 . If the judge is the only one, he reduces the sentence. § 2 . In a collegiate court, the decision must be narrowed down by taking from among them the reasons that the individual judges brought to the discussion, unless the majority of the judges determined that the reasons were preferable; The decision must then be submitted to the individual judges for approval. § 3 . The sentence must be issued no later than one month after the date on which the case was resolved, unless in the collegiate court the judges have provided a longer period for serious reasons.

Can. 1294 . The ruling must: 1° define the controversy raised before the court, giving an appropriate response to each question; 2° define what the obligations of the parties derived from the sentence are and how they should be fulfilled; 3° explain the reasons or motives, both in law and in fact, on which the operative part of the sentence is based; 4° decide on legal costs.

Can. 1295 . § 1 . The sentence after the Divine Name must express in order the invocation, who is the judge or what is the court, who is the plaintiff, the defendant, the agent, with well-designated names and addresses, the promoter of justice, the defender of the bond, if they took part in the process. § 2 . Then you must briefly report the appearance of the fact with the conclusions of the parties and the formulation of the doubts. § 3 . This is followed by the operative part of the decision with the previous reasons, on which it is based. § 4 . It is closed with an indication of the place and day on which it was issued, and with the signature of the judge or, if it is a collegiate court, of all the judges and the notary.
Can. 1296 . The rules established on the final sentence are valid with due reference also on the interlocutory sentence.

Can. 1297 . The sentence is announced as soon as possible within the indicated limits, within which an appeal against the sentence can be filed, and has no effect before the announcement, even if the operative part of the sentence has been notified to the parties with the authorization of the judge.
Can. 1298 . Notification of the decision may be made either by delivering a copy of the decision to the parties or their representatives, or by sending the same copy to the Can. 1192 standard.

Can. 1299 . § 1 . If in the text of the sentence, either an error has been made in the calculations, or a material error has occurred in the transcription of the operative part of the sentence, or in the list of the facts or requests of the parties, or those required by Can. 1295, § 4 have been omitted, the sentence must be corrected or completed by the court that made it, either at the request of the party or ex officio, always after hearing the parties and placing a decree at the bottom of the sentence. phrase. § 2 . If any part is rejected, the issue concerned will be determined by decree.

Can. 1300 . The other pronouncements of the judge, apart from the sentence, are decrees, which if not merely directive, have no force unless they at least briefly express the reasons or refer to the reasons expressed in another act.

Can. 1301 . An interlocutory ruling or a decree has the force of a final ruling if it prevents the process or puts an end to the process itself or any of its stages, at least with respect to a part of the process. Art. 9 OF THE CHALLENGE OF THE SENTENCE 1° Of the complaint of annulment of the sentence

Can. 1302 . If it is a case that concerns only individuals, the nullity of the judicial acts established by law, which, although they were known to the party filing the annulment claim, were not announced to the judge before the ruling, is corrected by the ruling itself.

Can. 1303 . § 1 . A sentence suffers from an incurable vice of nullity, if: 1° it has been issued by an absolutely incompetent judge; 2° it was issued by someone who lacks the power to judge in the court in which the case was resolved; 3° the judge made the decision under great coercion or fear; 4° the judgment was issued without a judicial petition, as referred to in Can. 1104 , § 2 , or was not filed against any defendant; 5° it is passed between the parties, at least one of whom has no person who can appear before the court; 6° that he acted on behalf of another without a legitimate mandate; 7° the right of defense was denied to any of the parties; 8. The dispute has not even been partially resolved. § 2 . In these cases, the claim for annulment may be proposed by way of permanent exception, but through action before the judge who made the decision, which will be counted within ten years from the notification of the decision.

Can. 1304 . § 1 . The sentence can be cured by virtue of its nullity, if: 1° it was issued by an illegitimate number of judges contrary to the provisions of Can. 1084; 2° it does not contain the reasons or reasons for the decision; 3° it lacks the signatures prescribed by law; 4° it does not include the indication of the place, year, month and day on which it was issued; 5° it is not based on any indexical act whose nullity has not been corrected according to the Can. 1302 standard; 6° is issued against a legally absent party according to Can. 1273, § 2. § 2 . In these cases, the annulment application may be filed within three months following notification of the decision.

Can. 1305 . The judge who handed down the sentence considers the complaint null and void; But if the party fears that this judge may be prejudiced and therefore considers him suspicious, he may demand that another judge be substituted in his place according to the Can. 1108 rule.
Can. 1306 . The application for annulment may be presented together with the appeal within the period established for the appeal.

Can. 1307 . § 1 . The annulment claim can be filed not only by the parties who consider themselves aggrieved, but also by the promoter of justice or the defender of the bond, provided they have the right to intervene. § 2 . The judge may review or modify ex officio any decision that has been issued within the terms of action of the statutes cann. 1303, § 2 and 1304, § 2, unless in the meantime an appeal has been filed together with a request for annulment.
Can. 1308 . Cases requesting annulment may be processed in accordance with the canons of contentious summary judgment. 2° About the appeal

Can. 1309 . The party that considers itself aggrieved by a decision, as well as the promoter of justice and the defender of the bond in cases where their presence is required, have the right to appeal the decision before a superior judge, except Can. 1310.

Can. 1310 . There is no appeal: 1° against the decision of the Roman Pontiff himself or the Apostolic Signature; 2° by a judgment vitiated by a defect of nullity, unless it is combined with a claim for annulment according to the Can. 1306 standard; 3rd of the sentence, which became res judicata; 4° by order of a judge or by interlocutory ruling, which do not have the force of a final ruling, unless combined with an appeal for a final ruling; 5° by sentence or decree in a case with respect to which the law provides that the matter must be resolved as quickly as possible.

Can. 1311 . § 1 . The appeal must be filed before the judge who handed down the sentence, within the peremptory period of fifteen business days from notification of the sentence. § 2 . If it is done orally, the notary must write it down in the presence of the appellant.
Can. 1312 . The call is not made by the delegate to the delegate, but to his immediate superior, unless the delegate is the Apostolic See itself.
Can. 1313 . If doubt arises about the right to appeal, the appeal court will resolve the matter as expeditiously as possible in accordance with the canons of contentious summary judgment.

Can. 1314 . The appeal must be continued before the judge to whom it is addressed, within the month following its filing, unless the judge from whom the resolution was issued grants the party a longer period of time to continue it.

Can. 1315 . § 1 . To proceed with the appeal, it is necessary and sufficient for the party to invoke the services of the superior judge to correct the contested decision, attaching a copy of this decision and indicating the reasons for the appeal. § 2 . Meanwhile, the judge who handed down the sentence must send a copy of the documents made by the notary regarding their authenticity to the higher court; If the proceedings are written in a language unknown to the court of appeal, they will be translated into another language known to the same court, taking precautions to ensure a faithful version.
Can. 1316 . If the appeal period has expired unnecessarily, either before the judge who issued the sentence, or before the judge to whom the appeal is directed, it will be considered abandoned.

Can. 1317 . § 1 . The appellant may file an appeal with the effects described in Can. 1206. § 2 . If the appeal is filed by the defender of the bond or by the promoter of justice, the waiver may be made, unless otherwise provided by common law, by the defender of the bond or by the promoter of justice of the court of appeal.

Can. 1318 . § 1 . An appeal filed by the petitioner also benefits the respondent and vice versa. § 2 . If there are several defendants or plaintiffs and the decision is challenged by one or against only one of them, the challenge is considered made by all and against all, provided that the thing is claimed individually or the obligation falls on all of them individually. § 3 . If it is filed by one of the parties on any point of the sentence, the opposing party, even if the appeal period has elapsed, may incidentally appeal on the other points within the peremptory period of fifteen days counted from the day on which the main appeal was notified. § 4 . Unless otherwise agreed, the appeal is presumed to have been filed against all aspects of the decision.
Can. 1319 . The appeal suspends the execution of the sentence.

Can. 1320 . § 1 . With the exception of Can. 1369 at the appellate level, a new cause of action cannot be admitted, even by way of useful consolidation; and therefore the dispute of the case can only center on it, so that the previous ruling is confirmed or reformed, whether in whole or in part. § 2 . Retests are supported only in accordance with Can. 1283.

Can. 1321 . At the appeal level, the same procedure must be followed as at the first level of trial, referring to the relevant facts; but, unless by chance the evidence must be completed, immediately after the complaint is answered, the case will go to discussion and verdict. Art. 10 OF THE MATTER JUDGED, OF THE INTEGRAL RESTITUTION AND OF THE OPPOSITION OF A THIRD PARTY 1° Of the matter judged

Can. 1322 . Firmly Can. 1324 the matter is considered resolved, if: 1° a double vote has been issued between the same parties in accordance with the same claim and for the same cause of the claim; 2° the appeal of the sentence was not filed within the useful period; 3rd at the appeal level, the case was dismissed or dismissed; 4° A final sentence is issued, against which there is no appeal.

Can. 1323 . § 1 . Res judicata is legally established in such a way that it can only be challenged by request for annulment, total restitution or opposition from a third party. § 2 . Res judicata creates a right between the parties and grants an action to the court and an exception to the tried case, which the judge can also declare ex officio to prevent a new introduction of the same case.
Can. 1324 . Cases relating to the status of persons, except cases relating to the separation of spouses, never become res judicata.

Can. 1325 . § 1 . If a double sentence has been issued in a case relating to the status of persons, it may be challenged at any time before the court of appeal, presenting new and serious evidence or arguments within the peremptory period of thirty days counted from the proposal to challenge; and the appeal court must decide within the month following the presentation of the new evidence and arguments, whether or not to admit the new presentation of the case. § 2 . Recusal before a higher court, in order to obtain a new ruling on the case, does not suspend the execution of the sentence, unless otherwise provided by common law or the court of appeals orders the suspension in accordance with Can. 1337 , § 3 . 2° About the restoration in its entirety

Can. 1326 . § 1 . In the face of a decision that has become res judicata, as long as its injustice is clearly established, full restitution is granted. § 2 . But injustice is not considered manifestly evident, unless: 1° the sentence is based in such a way on evidence that is later discovered to be false, that without it the operative part of the sentence cannot be sustained; 2° later documents were discovered that undoubtedly proved new facts and demanded a contrary decision; 3° the decision was made through fraud on the part of one party to the detriment of the other; 4° the non-merely procedural provision of the law was clearly violated; 5. The sentence is contrary to the previous decision, which became res judicata.

Can. 1327 . § 1 . Full restitution for the reasons mentioned in Can. 1326 , § 2 , nos. 1 - 3, must be requested by the judge who issued the decision, within three months following the date of knowledge of the same reasons. § 2 . Full restitution for the reasons mentioned in Can. 1326 , § 2 , nos. 4 and 5, must be requested by the court of appeal within three months following notification of the ruling; yes indeed in the case that in Can. 1326 , § 2 , n. 5, the information of the previous decision is considered subsequently, the deadline runs from this information. § 3 . The aforementioned terms do not apply while the injured party is a minor.

Can. 1328 . § 1 . The request for restitution suspends the complete execution of the sentence that has not yet begun. § 2 . If, on the basis of probable evidence, it is suspected that a request to delay execution has been made, the judge may decide that the penalty of execution be required, however, assigning full restitution to the petitioner with adequate guarantee so that, if he is returned in full, he will be compensated.
Can. 1329 . By granting full restitution, the judge must rule on the merits of the matter. 3. Of the opposition of the third party
Can. 1330 . Anyone who fears injury to their rights due to a final ruling issued among others, which may be ordered to be executed, may challenge the ruling itself before its execution.

Can. 1331 . § 1 . The third party's opposition can be made either by requesting a review of the decision by the court that made it, or by challenging it before the court of appeal. § 2 . If the application is admitted and the opponent acts at the appeal level, he is bound by the laws established for appeal; If before the court that made the decision, the rules given for the judicial definition of incidental cases must be observed.

Can. 1332 . § 1 . The opponent must in any case prove that his right has been effectively injured or will be injured. § 2 . But the damage must arise from the decision itself, to the extent that it is the cause of the damage or, if execution is ordered, it affects the opponent with serious harm.
Can. 1333 . If the opponent has proven his right, the previously issued decision must be amended by the court in accordance with the opponent's request. Art. XI ON FREE SPONSORSHIP AND COURT EXPENSES
Can. 1334 . The poor, who are in no way able to bear legal costs, are entitled to free legal aid, even if only in part, to reduce costs.

Can. 1335 . The statutes of the court must regulate: 1° on the payment or compensation of judicial costs by the parties; 2° on the remuneration of lawyers, defenders and interpreters and the compensation of witnesses; 3° grant free sponsorship or reduction of expenses; 4° on the reparation of damage, which corresponds to those who not only succumbed in court, but also litigate recklessly; 5° on the deposit of money or guarantee that must be provided on the expenses to be paid and the damages to be repaired.

Can. 1336 . There is no separate appeal from the ruling regarding expenses, remuneration and damages, but the party can return within fifteen days to the same judge, who can correct the assessment. Art. XII ON THE EXECUTION OF THE SENTENCE

Can. 1337 . § 1 . The sentence, which has become res judicata, can be ordered executed with the exception of Can. 1328 . § 2 . The judge who handed down the sentence, and, if an appeal has been filed, also the judge of appeal, whose sentence has not yet become res judicata, may order provisional execution ex officio or at the request of a competent party, if the case entails, provided that they are guaranteed, if it involves provisions for necessary food or another just cause is urgent. § 3 . But if a sentence is challenged that has not yet become res judicata, the judge, who must hear the challenge, if he sees that it is probably founded and that irreparable damage may result from the execution, may suspend the execution itself or subject it to a warning.

Can. 1338 . There can be no place for execution before the execution decree of the judge is made, by which it is dictated that the execution of the sentence itself must be ordered; that the decree, due to the different nature of the cases, or due to the very tenor of the sentence, must be included or issued separately.
Can. 1339 . If the execution of the sentence requires a preliminary statement of reasons, the relevant issue is considered resolved by the judge who ordered the execution of the sentence.

Can. 1340 . § 1 . Unless the particular law of the independent Church establishes otherwise, the sentence must be executed by himself or by another eparchial bishop of the eparchy where the sentence was issued in the first instance of the process. § 2 . However, if it is rejected or neglected, the interested party, immediately or even ex officio, refers to the authority to which the court of appeal is subject. § 3 . In the controversies mentioned in Can. 1069, § 1, the execution of the sentence corresponds to the Superior in the norm or determined by statute.

Can. 1341 . § 1 . The executor, unless his discretion is permitted by the wording of the sentence itself, must execute the sentence according to the meaning of the words. § 2 . It is permissible for him to deal with the exceptions relating to the form and force of the execution, but not with the substance of the case; but if he has discovered from another source that the decision is void or manifestly unjust according to the rule cann. 1303, 1304 et 1326 , § 2 , he must refrain from executing it and refer the matter to the court that issued the decision, returning the parties to the informed facts.

Can. 1342 . § 1 . When a thing has been awarded to the plaintiff, it must be delivered to the plaintiff as soon as the thing is considered awarded. § 2 . If a party is sentenced to provide movable property or to pay money or to give or do something else, the judge in the very wording of the sentence or the executor, according to his discretion and prudence, will set a period for compliance with the obligation, which, however, may not be limited to less than fifteen days or exceed six months. CHAPTER II OF THE CONTENTIOUS SUMMARY JUDGMENT

Can. 1343 . § 1 . All cases not excluded by law can be resolved by summary judgment, unless a party requests a regular judgment. § 2 . If summary judgment is used in cases excluded by law, the judicial acts are void.

Can. 1344 . § 1 . In addition to those listed in Can. 1187, the bill introducing the case must: 1° briefly, completely and clearly state the facts on which the petitioner's claims are based; 2° the evidence with which the petitioner intends to demonstrate the facts and that he cannot provide at the same time, so as to indicate that it can be collected immediately by the judge. § 2 . The documents on which the claim is based must be attached to the document presenting the case, at least in an authentic copy.

Can. 1345 . § 1 . If the attempt at conciliation according to the Can. 1103, § 2 rule has proven useless, the judge, if he considers that the introductory document of the claim has some basis, within three days will order a decree attached to the foot of the document, so that a copy of the petition is immediately notified to the defendant, having the right to send a written response to the chancery of the court within fifteen days. § 2 . This notification has the effect of a subpoena, as described in Can. 1194.

Can. 1346 . If the objections of the defendant so require, the judge will set the deadline for the petitioner to respond in such a way that, from the elements presented by both parties, he himself has an idea of ​​the object of the controversy.

Can. 1347 . § 1 . After the deadlines to respond, mentioned in cann. 1345, § 1 and 1346, the judge will determine the formula of the doubt after looking at the record; then to hold a hearing no later than thirty days, summons all those who must participate in it, adding a formula for the parties in doubt. § 2 . The summons must inform the parties that they may submit to the court at least three days before the hearing a brief written statement to substantiate their claims.
Can. 1348 . At the hearing, the questions discussed in cann. 1118, 1119, 1121 et 1122 are first discussed.
Can. 1349 . § 1 . The testimonies are collected in the hearing save Can. 1071. § 2 . A party and its attorney may assist in the examination of other parties, witnesses and experts.

Can. 1350 . The responses of the parties, witnesses, experts, requests and objections of the lawyers must be reduced to writing by the notary, but in summary form and only those that refer to the substance of the disputed matter, and signed by them.

Can. 1351 . The judge may only admit evidence that is not provided or requested in the petition or response according to the Can. 1110 rule; but after even a single witness has been heard, the judge can only decide on new evidence according to the Can. 1283 rule.
Can. 1352 . If all the evidence could not be collected during the hearing, it is decided to hold a second hearing.
Can. 1353 . An oral discussion is carried out in the same auditorium with the evidence collected.

Can. 1354 . § 1 . Unless in the investigation of the case there is something to add to the discussion, or there is something else that prevents the decision from being made in accordance with the law, the judge, once the hearing is over, immediately decides the case; The operative part of the sentence is read immediately in the presence of the parties present. § 2 . But the court may, due to the difficulty of the case or for any other just reason, postpone the favorable decision until the fifth day. § 3 . The full text of the ruling with the reasons expressed will be communicated to the parties as soon as possible and, ordinarily, no later than fifteen days.

Can. 1355 . If the appeals court determines that summary judgment has been used at a lower level of trial in a case excluded by law, it must declare the decision void and return the case to the court that made the decision.

Can. 1356 . In the rest, which concern the way of proceeding, the canons of the ordinary contentious trial are observed; and the court may, by its reasoned decision, not observe procedural rules that are not established for the validity of the statute, so that justice is done quickly. TITLE XXVI OF CERTAIN SPECIAL PROCEDURES CHAPTER I OF MARRIAGE PROCEDURE Art. 1. CAUSES FOR DECLARING THE NULLITY OF THE MARRIAGE 1. In the competent forum
Can. 1357 . Every case of marriage of a baptized person has its own right before the Church.

Can. 1358 . According to the signature, personal statutes, when they are in force, cases relating to the purely civil effects of marriage, if they are of primary processing, belong to the civil judge, but, if they are incidental and accessory, they can also be recognized and resolved by the ecclesiastical judge by his own authority.

Can. 1359 . In cases of annulment of marriage, which are not reserved to the Apostolic See, the following are competent: 1° the court of the place where the marriage was celebrated; 2° the court of the place where the defendant has a domicile or quasi-domicile; 3° the court of the place where the petitioner has his domicile, provided that both parties reside in the territory of the same nation and the Judicial Vicar of the domicile of the defendant consents to said hearings; 4. the local court, where most of the evidence must be collected, provided that the Judicial Vicar of the defendant's domicile consents to said hearings. 2° The right to challenge the marriage Can. 1360 - The following are competent to challenge the marriage: 1° the spouses; 2° the promoter of justice, if the annulment has already been declared and the marriage cannot be validated or is not convenient. Can. 1361 - § 1 . A marriage that has not been persecuted while both spouses were alive cannot be persecuted after the death of one or both spouses, unless the question of validity is preliminary to the resolution of another dispute, either in the ecclesiastical forum or in the civil forum. § 2 . But if the spouse dies while the case is pending, Can. 1199 will be preserved. 3. Of the obligations of judges and courts

Can. 1362 . The judge, before accepting the case and whenever he sees hope for a good result, must use pastoral means, so that the spouses, if possible, can be brought to validate the marriage and reestablish the partnership of conjugal life.

Can. 1363 . § 1 . Once the introductory brief of the case is admitted, the president or the petitioner will proceed to notify the summons decision in accordance with the Can. 1191 standard. § 2 . After the period of fifteen days counted from the date of the notification, the president or the depositary, unless any of the parties has requested a session to challenge the case, must, within the period of ten days, define ex officio the formula of the doubt or doubts by means of a decree that informs the parties. § 3 . The formulation of the doubt not only asks if it is established that the marriage is void in the case, but must determine in which chapter or chapters the validity of the marriage is questioned. § 4 . Ten days after notification of the decree, if the parties have not objected, the president, or by issuing a new decree, decides the investigation of the case. 4th of tests

Can. 1364 . §1 . The defender of the bond, the guardian of the parties and, if he is before the court, also the promoter of justice, has the right: 1° to be present during the interrogation of the parties, witnesses and experts, except Can. 1240; 2° visit the files, even if they have not yet been published, and review the documents provided by the parties. § 2 . To the question about which one in § 1, n. 1, the parties cannot attend.

Can. 1365 . Unless the evidence from other sources is considered complete, the judge should use, if possible, in addition to other evidence and supporting evidence, to evaluate the statements of the parties, as mentioned in Can. 1217 , § 2 , the witnesses on the credibility of the parties themselves.

Can. 1366 . In cases of impotence or lack of consent due to mental illness, the judge may resort to the services of one or more experts, unless the circumstances show that it is useless; in other cases Can. 1255 will be maintained.

Can. 1367 . If during the investigation of the case a very probable doubt has arisen about the non-consummation of the marriage, the court may, with the consent of the parties, suspend the case for the annulment of the marriage and complete the investigation to obtain the solution of the unconsummated sacramental marriage; then sends the proceedings to the Apostolic See together with the request for this solution made by one or both spouses and with the will of the court and the eparchial bishop. 5. About the sentence and the appeal

Can. 1368 . § 1 . The ruling that declared for the first time the annulment of the marriage, together with the appeals, if any, and the rest of the judicial proceedings, will be sent ex officio to the court of appeal within twenty days following notification of the ruling. § 2 . If the ruling for the annulment of the marriage is issued at the first level of the trial, the appeals court, after considering the observations of the defender of the bond and, if any, also the decree or decision of the parties, will continuously confirm or admit the case to ordinary examination at the second level of the trial.
Can. 1369 . If a new chapter of marriage annulment is filed at the appeal level, the court can admit it as at the first level of trial and decide on the matter.

Can. 1370 . § 1 . After the ruling that first declared the nullity of the marriage has been confirmed at the appeal level, whether by a decree or another ruling, those whose marriage has been declared void may celebrate a new marriage as soon as the decree or other ruling has been intimated to them, unless this is prohibited by the prohibition of the ruling itself or by a decree attached to or established by the local Hierarch. § 2 . Can. 1325 must be observed, even if the ruling declaring the marriage null and void was not a second ruling, but was confirmed by decree.

Can. 1371 . Once the executive decision has been made, the Judicial Vicar must notify the Hierarch of the place where the marriage was celebrated; Here, however, the Hierarch must ensure that as soon as possible mention is made of the declared nullity of the marriage and of the prohibitions that may have been established in the books of marriages and baptisms. 6° Of the documentary process

Can. 1372 . § 1 . Once the petition is admitted, the Judicial Vicar or the judge designated by him may, skipping the formalities of the ordinary process, but summoning the parties and with the intervention of the defender of the marriage bond, declare the nullity of the marriage bond by means of a ruling, if from a document that is not subject to any contradiction or exception, it is certain that there is an impediment to remedies or the lack of the form of celebration of the marriage prescribed by law, provided that it is stated with equal certainty that the dispensation was not given, or about the lack of a valid mandate. of the attorney. § 2 . But if it is someone who should have observed the form of marriage celebration prescribed by law, but attempted to contract marriage in the presence of a civil official or a non-Catholic minister, the premarital investigation, mentioned in Can. 784, is sufficient to verify his free status.

Can. 1373 . § 1 . From the ruling mentioned in Can. 1372 , § 1 , the defender of the bond, if he reasonably believes that the defects or lack of dispensation are not true, must appeal to the judge of the second degree court, to whom the minutes are sent and to whom he must be informed in writing about the documentary process. § 2 . The right of appeal remains intact for the party that considers itself aggrieved.

Can. 1374 . The judge of the second degree court will decide, with the intervention of the defender of the bond and the parties heard, whether to confirm the sentence or proceed in the case in accordance with the ordinary rule of law; in which case it returns it to the first degree court. 7° General rules
Can. 1375 . Cases to declare the nullity of a marriage cannot be processed by summary judgment.

Can. 1376 . In the others, which concern the procedural system, unless the nature of the case prevents it, the canons of sentences in general and ordinary contentious sentences will be applied, subject to special rules for cases that concern the public good.

Can. 1377 . The decision must warn the parties about the moral or even civil obligations that they may have, towards each other and towards their children, to provide them with proper support and education. Art. II OF THE CAUSES OF THE SEPARATION OF THE SPOUSES

Can. 1378 . § 1 . The personal separation of spouses, unless otherwise provided by law in certain areas, can be decided by decree of the eparchial bishop or by decision of a judge. § 2 . However, when the ecclesiastical decision has no civil effects, or if it is anticipated that the civil decision is not contrary to divine right, the eparchial bishop of the eparchy of residence of the spouses may, after considering the special circumstances, grant permission to resort to the civil forum. § 3 . If the case also concerns the purely civil effects of marriage, the judge will try to take the case from the beginning to the civil jurisdiction with the authorization of the eparchial bishop.

Can. 1379 . § 1 . Unless a party requests ordinary contentious information, summary contentious judgment will be used. § 2 . If the ordinary contentious trial is used and an appeal is filed, the second level court, after hearing the parties, will continually confirm its decree or decision or admit the case to ordinary examination of the second level of the trial.
Can. 1380 . Regarding the jurisdiction of the court, Can. 1359, nos. 2 and 3

Can. 1381 . The judge, before accepting the case and whenever he sees prospects for a good result, must use pastoral means to reconcile the spouses and lead them to reestablish the partnership of conjugal life.
Can. 1382 . The promoter of justice must intervene in cases of separation of spouses according to the Can. 1097 standard. Art. III OF THE PROCESS OF PRESUMED DEATH OF THE SPOUSE

Can. 1383 . § 1 . When the death of one of the spouses cannot be proven by an authentic ecclesiastical or civil document, the other spouse is not considered released from the marriage bond until the eparchial bishop has made a declaration of presumed death. § 2 . The eparchial bishop can only make this declaration if, after carrying out the appropriate investigations, he has obtained moral certainty about the death of the spouses from the statements of witnesses, reports or information; The mere absence of the spouse, even if prolonged, is not enough. § 3 . In uncertain and complicated cases, the eparchial bishop, exercising his power within the territory of the patriarchal Church, consults the Patriarch; but the other eparchial bishops consult the Apostolic See. § 4 . In the process of presumed death of the spouse, the intervention of the promoter of justice is required, but not of the defender of the bond. Art. 4 OF THE MODE OF PROCEDURE TO OBTAIN THE DISSOLUTION OF AN UNCONSUMED MARRIAGE OR THE DISSOLUTION OF A MARRIAGE IN FAVOR OF THE FAITH

Can. 1384 . To obtain the dissolution of an unconsummated marriage or the dissolution of a marriage in favor of the faith, the special regulations issued by the Apostolic See must be carefully observed. CHAPTER II OF THE CAUSES FOR DECLARING THE NULLITY OF THE HOLY ORDINANCE
Can. 1385 . They have the right to accuse the cleric himself or the Hierarch to whom the cleric is subordinate or in whose eparchy he is ordained the validity of the sacred ordination.

Can. 1386 . § 1 . The bill challenging the validity of a sacred order must be sent to the competent department of the Roman court, which will decide whether the case should be heard by it or by a court designated by it. § 2 . If the Department refers the case to the court, unless the nature of the case prevents it, the canons of general trials and ordinary contentious trials will be observed, but not the canons of summary contentious trials. § 3 . By sending a letter, the clergyman is legally prohibited from exercising holy orders.

Can. 1387 . After the second decision, which confirms the nullity of the sacred ordination, the cleric loses all the rights of the clerical state and is freed from all the obligations of the same state.

Can. 1388 . In the removal or transfer of pastors, cann. 1389 - 1400 will be maintained, unless a particular law approved by the Apostolic See determines otherwise. Art. I. THE MODE OF PROCEDURE IN THE EXTRACTION OF PARISHES

Can. 1389 . If the ministry of a pastor for any reason, even through his own grave fault, proves detrimental or at least ineffective, the pastor may be removed from the parish by the eparchial bishop.

Can. 1390 . The reasons why a parish priest can be legitimately separated from his parish are mainly these: 1. a way of acting that brings serious damage or disturbance to the ecclesiastical communion; 2° inexperience or permanent illness of the spirit or body, which renders the priest incapable of usefully performing his duties; 3° loss of good reputation due to poor and serious parishioners or dislike of the parish priest, which is expected not to cease soon; 4° serious negligence or violation of the priest's obligations, which persists after the reprimand; 5. The mismanagement of temporal affairs, with serious damage to the Church, provided that no other remedy can be found for this evil.

Can. 1391 . § 1 . If, after completing the instruction, it becomes clear that there is cause for removal, the eparchial bishop must discuss the matter with two parish priests chosen from the group of parish priests, which the presbyteral council proposed to the eparchial bishop had stably elected for this purpose; However, if you consider it necessary to dismiss him, you must notify the paternal priest, with the reason and arguments indicated for its validity, to present your resignation within a period of fifteen days. § 2 . A parish priest who is a member of a religious institution or of a society of common life analogous to the religious may be removed at the request of the eparchial bishop by notification to the major superior, or by the major superior of the eparchial bishop without the consent of the other being necessary.
Can. 1392 . The resignation of the parish priest can also be made under conditions, provided that it can be legitimately accepted by the eparchial bishop and is actually accepted.

Can. 1393 . § 1 . If the parish priest did not respond within the indicated days, the eparchial bishop would repeat the invitation, extending the useful time to respond. § 2 . If it is clear to the eparchial bishop that the pastor received the second invitation but did not respond, even if he was detained without any impediment, or if the pastor rejects the resignation without reason, the eparchial bishop must issue a decree of removal.

Can. 1394 . However, if the parish priest attacks the case initiated and its reasons, alleging reasons that seem insufficient to the eparchial bishop, here he must act forcefully: 1. invite him to collect his objections in a written report after having examined the records, or rather to provide evidence to the contrary, if he has any; 2.or then, completed, if necessary, with instruction together with the same two parish priests, about whom in Can. 1391, § 1, unless the others are due to their impossibility to appoint, assess the matter; 3. Finally, let him decide whether the priest should be removed or not, and he will soon make a decision on the matter.
Can. 1395 . When the parish priest is removed, the eparchial bishop consults with the grant of another office, if he is suitable for it, or with a pension, as circumstances and conditions permit.

Can. 1396 . § 1 . The removed parish priest must refrain from exercising the office of parish priest, leave the parish house free as soon as possible and hand over everything that belongs to the parish to the person to whom the eparchial bishop has entrusted the parish. § 2 . But if it is a sick person who cannot be transferred from the parish house to another without problems, the eparchial Bishop will allow him the use of the parish house, even exclusive, during the same need. § 3 . During the pending appeal against the removal decree, the eparchial bishop cannot appoint a new parish priest, but must arrange for an interim one through the parish administrator. Art. II OF THE METHOD OF PROCEDURE IN THE TRANSLATION OF PARISHES

Can. 1397 . If the safety of souls or the needs of the Church require that the parish priest be transferred from his own parish, which he governs usefully, to another parish or to another office, the eparchial bishop will propose the same transfer in writing and will advise him to accept it for the love of God and souls.
Can. 1398 . If the parish priest does not intend to follow the advice and suggestions of the eparchial bishop, he must explain the reasons in writing.

Can. 1399 . § 1 . If the eparchial bishop, despite the reasons stated, decides that he should not desist from his purpose, with two parish priests of the group, on which in Can. 1391 , § 1 , he will evaluate the reasons chosen, which favor or hinder the transfer; But if from then on he thought that the translation should be done, he repeated his fatherly exhortations to the priest. § 2 . This done, if the parish priest still refuses and the eparchial bishop thinks a transfer should be made, he must issue a decree of transfer, determining that the parish will be vacant at the end of a given day. § 3 . Having passed this day in vain, the eparchial bishop will declare the parish vacant.
Can. 1400 . In case of transfer, Can. 1396, the acquired rights and assets are preserved. TITLE XXVII OF PENALTIES IN THE CHURCH CHAPTER I CRIMES AND SANCTIONS IN GENERAL

Can. 1401 . When God enters into every reason to bring back the straying sheep, those who have received from Him the power to loose and bind, bring suitable medicine for the disease of those who have transgressed, rebuke them, supplicate them, rebuke them with all patience and teaching, nay, impose punishments, so that the wounds inflicted by the transgression may be healed in such a way that the transgressors are not driven to the precipice of despair, nor are the reins relaxed. for the dissolution of life and disregard of the law. Can. 1402 n - § 1 . The hierarch must promote the procedure for imposing penalties, when neither reprimand, nor supplication, nor reprimand can be sufficient to restore justice, to bring the guilty to repentance and reparation, and to repair the scandal and damage. § 2 . The canonical penalty must be imposed by criminal sentence prescribed in cann. 1468 - 1482 with the firm coercive power of the judge in cases expressed by law and rejected contrary to custom. § 3 . But if, in the opinion of the authority referred to in § 4, there are serious reasons why a criminal proceeding should not be carried out, and the proof of the crime is true, the crime may be punished, observing Can. 1291, by extrajudicial decree in accordance with cann. 1486 y 1487, provided that it does not involve deprivation of office, title, insignia or suspension for more than one year, reduction to a lower rank, deposition or major excommunication. § 4 . In addition to the Apostolic See, the Patriarch, the Major Archbishop, the Eparchial Bishop and the Major Superior of the Institute of Consecrated Life, who has the ordinary power of government, to the exclusion of all others, may issue this decree within the limits of their competence.

Can. 1403 . § 1 . Even if these are crimes that carry a penalty by law, the Hierarch, after hearing the promoter of justice, may abstain from criminal proceedings, or even impose sanctions, provided that, in the opinion of the Hierarch himself, all these things coincide: the criminal who has not yet been tried has confessed his crime to the Hierarch in an external forum, has sincerely repented of the movement and has been adequately provided for the reparation of the crime and the damage. § 2 . But the Hierarch cannot do this if it is a crime that carries a penalty whose remission is reserved to a higher authority, until he has obtained permission from the same authority.

Can. 1404 . § 1 . In punishments, a kinder interpretation must be made. § 2 . It is not allowed to produce punishment from person to person or from case to case, even if there is an equally or even more serious reason.

Can. 1405 . § 1 . He who has legislative power may, to the extent that it is really necessary for the most adequate provision of ecclesiastical discipline, also dictate penal laws, as well as with his own laws also the divine or ecclesiastical law extended by a higher authority to strengthen the appropriate punishment, respecting the limits of his competence in terms of territory or persons. § 2 . To the penalties established by common law for any crime, other penalties may be added by particular law; this should not be done before except for the most serious reason; But if by common law an indeterminate or optional penalty is established, a specific or mandatory penalty may be established in its place by particular law. § 3 . Patriarchs and eparchial bishops must ensure that the criminal laws of particular law in the same territory are, as far as possible, uniform. Can. 1406 n - § 1 . To the extent that someone can impose precepts as provided in cann. 1510 1520, to the extent that the issue can be weighed early and with the greatest moderation, they can be threatened with the penalties determined by the precept, except those listed in Can. 1402 , § 3 ; But the patriarch, with the consent of the permanent Synod, can also threaten these punishments by precept. § 2 . A warning with threat of punishment, by which the Hierarch enforces a non-penal law in individual cases, is equivalent to a penal precept. Can. 1407 n - § 1 . If, in the judgment of the Hierarch who may inflict the punishment, the nature of the offense permits, the punishment cannot be inflicted unless the offender has previously been warned at least once to desist from the offense, giving him adequate time to repent. § 2 . A person who has sincerely repented of the violation and who, in addition, has given, or at least seriously promised, adequate compensation for the violation and damage is said to have desisted from an infringement. § 3 . If someone has been given warnings or reprimands in vain, the Hierarch will issue a penal order, in which he will prescribe exactly what must be done or avoided. § 4 . The penalty warning, of which in Can. 1406 , § 2 , is sufficient for a penalty to be imposed.

Can. 1408 . The penalty does not declare the guilty guilty, except after the sentence or decree has been imposed, except for the right of the Roman Pontiff or the Ecumenical Council to decide otherwise. Can. 1409 n - § 1 . When applying the criminal law, even if the law uses prescriptive words, the judge may, according to his conscience and prudence: 1° defer the imposition of the sentence to a more appropriate time, if greater evils are foreseen than the anticipated sanction of the matter, unless there is an urgent need to repair the crime; 2° to refrain from imposing a sentence or to impose a lighter sentence, if the accused has been reformed and adequate measures have been taken to repair the crime and damage, or if the accused himself has been sufficiently punished by the civil authority or is expected to be so; 3° that the penalties be moderated within fair limits, if the accused has committed several crimes and the accumulation of penalties seems excessive; 4° suspend the obligation to observe the penalty in favor of whoever, with all the integrity of his life and until now entrusted, commits the first crime, as long as he does not insist on reparation for the crime; The suspended sentence ceases completely, if within the period set by the judge the guilty party does not commit the crime again, otherwise the debtor of both crimes will be punished more severely, unless in the meantime the criminal action for the previous crime has been extinguished. § 2 . If the sentence is indeterminate and the law does not provide otherwise, the judge, when determining the sentences, will choose those that are proportionate to the crime caused and the severity of the damage; however, it cannot impose the sanctions listed in Can. 1402 , § 3 . Can. 1410 n - In the penalties imposed on the clergyman, those necessary for his adequate maintenance must be certain, unless it is a matter of deposition, in which case the Hierarch will ensure that the deposit that he really needs due to the penalty is provided, in the best possible way, excluding the contribution of position, ministry or service, and always saving the rights that arise in matters of prevention and social security, as well as health care in favor of him and his family, if he is married.
Can. 1411 . No penalty may be imposed once the criminal action has expired.

Can. 1412 . § 1 . Whoever is bound by a law or a precept is subject to the punishment that it entails. § 2 . If the law is changed after the crime has been committed, the law most favorable to the accused must be applied. § 3 . But if a subsequent law abolishes the law, or at least the penalty, it, regardless of its imposition, ceases immediately. § 4 . The penalty binds the guilty everywhere, even after the repeal of the law of the person who imposed it, unless expressly provided otherwise in the common law.

Can. 1413 . § 1 . Anyone who has not reached the age of fourteen is not subject to any penalty. § 2 . But whoever commits a crime between fourteen and eighteen years of age can only be punished with penalties that do not include the deprivation of any property, unless the eparchial bishop or the judge in special cases deems that it would be better to modify it otherwise. Can. 1414 n - § 1 . Everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty. § 2 . Only those who violate a criminal law or a penal precept, whether deliberately, or by gravely culpable omission of due diligence, or by gravely culpable ignorance of the law or precept, are subject to punishment. § 3 . In the case of external violation of a criminal law or a criminal precept, it is presumed that it was done deliberately, until the contrary is proven; In other laws or precepts this is only presumed if the law or precept is violated again after a criminal reprimand.

Can. 1415 . If, according to common practice and canonical teaching, mitigating circumstances occur, as long as the crime is still considered, the judge must moderate the penalty established by law or precept; Furthermore, out of his own prudence, if he considers that it would otherwise be better to consult for the amendment and reparation of the scandal and damage, he may also abstain from the penalty imposed. Can. 1416 n - § 1 . If the crime is committed by a repeat offender, or by one who is in a state of intoxication or other mental disorder, which is deliberately sought to commit or excuse the crime, or by one who acts because of a passion voluntarily aroused or nourished, or if other aggravating circumstances occur according to common practice and canonical teaching, the judge must punish the offender more severely than that established by law or precept, without excluding the penalties listed in Can. 1402, § 3 . § 2 . In the same cases, if the penalty is established as optional, it becomes mandatory.

Can. 1417 . Those who participate in the crime with a common plan to commit it and are not expressly named in the law or order, may be punished with the same penalties as the main perpetrator, or, at the discretion of the judge, with other penalties of equal or lesser severity.

Can. 1418 . § 1 . He who has committed or omitted to commit a crime, and yet has not committed it against his will, is not subject to the penalty established for the completed crime, unless the law or precept provides otherwise. § 2 . But if the acts or omissions by their very nature lead to the commission of a crime, the perpetrator will be punished with the appropriate penalty, especially if the crime or other serious damage occurs, even if it is lighter than that established as a completed crime. § 3 . The person who, of his own free will, desisted from carrying out the commission of the crime will be free from all punishment, if no damage or scandal resulted from the attempt.

Can. 1419 . § 1 . He who can dispense from a criminal law, or exempt from a penal precept, can also forgive a penalty imposed by force of the same law or precept. § 2 . In addition, the power to remit penalties may also be conferred on others by criminal law or ordinance.

Can. 1420 . § 1 . A penalty imposed by common law may be remitted: 1° The Hierarch, who has issued a criminal sentence or has imposed a penalty by decree; 2° The Hierarch of the place where the defendant actually resides, but the Hierarch of the consultation, of which in no. 1. § 2 . These rules also apply to penalties imposed by virtue of a particular law or a penal precept, unless otherwise provided by the particular law of the independent Church. § 3 . But only the Apostolic See can remit a penalty imposed by the Apostolic See, unless the remission of the penalty is delegated to the Patriarch or others.
Can. 1421 . There is no remission of punishment by force, nor by grave fear, nor by deception, alone.

Can. 1422 . § 1 . Remission of sentence may be granted even to an innocent accused or under a condition. § 2 . Remission of the sentence must be granted in writing, unless serious reason suggests otherwise. § 3 . Care should be taken that the application for remission of the sentence, or the remission itself, is not made public, except to the extent that it is useful to protect the reputation of the matter or is necessary to repair the scandal.

Can. 1423 . § 1 . Except for the right of the Roman Pontiff to reserve the remission of any penalty for himself or for others, the Synod of Bishops of the patriarchal or archiepiscopal church may, by law approved by law, reserve the remission of penalties to the patriarch or major archbishop for subjects who have a domicile or quasi-domicile within the territory of the church over which he presides; No one else can validly reserve for himself or others the remission of penalties established by common law, without the consent of the Apostolic See. § 2 . All reservations must be strictly interpreted. Can. 1424 n - § 1 . Remission of the sentence may not be granted unless the guilty party has sincerely repented for the crime he committed and adequate provision has been made for reparation for the crime and damage; For reparation or restitution, the offender may be subject to other appropriate penalties. § 2 . But if, in the opinion of the person to whom the remission of the sentence corresponds, these conditions are met, the remission will not be denied, to the extent that it is possible taking into account the nature of the sentence.

Can. 1425 . If a person is detained for several sentences, the remission is only valid for the sentences expressed in them; but the general pardon eliminates all penalties except those which the defendant in bad faith withheld in the petition.

Can. 1426 . § 1 . Unless the law determines another penalty, penalties may be imposed according to the ancient traditions of the Eastern Churches, which are imposed to perform some serious work of religion or piety or charity, such as specific prayers, pious pilgrimages, special fasts, alms, spiritual retreats. § 2 . For those who are not willing to accept these punishments, other punishments will be imposed.

Can. 1427 . § 1 . Unless there is a special law, public correction is made in the presence of a reporter or two witnesses, or by letter, so that the receipt and content of the letter are confirmed by some document. § 2 . We must be careful, lest public correction itself give rise to greater infamy than its due.

Can. 1428 . If the case is serious, and especially if it involves repeat offenders, the Hierarch may also, in addition to the penalties imposed by sentence in accordance with the law, subject the accused to surveillance in the manner determined by administrative decree. Can. 1429 n - § 1 . It may be prohibited: 1° to remain in a certain place or territory; 2° carry out, in any place or in a certain place or territory or outside it, all or some of the duties, functions, ministries or only some works inherent to the duties or functions; 3º impose all or some acts of the power of order; 4º impose all or some acts of governmental power; 5º exercise any right or privilege or use insignia or titles; 6º enjoy an active or passive voice in canonical elections or have a part with the right to vote in councils or ecclesial colleges; 7.º Of having an ecclesiastical or religious attitude. § 2 . It may be prescribed: 1° to remain in a certain place or territory; 2° pay a sum of money for the purposes of the Church, according to the methods determined by particular law. § 3 . The prohibition to remain in a certain place or territory can only affect clerics or religious or members of the society of common life in the same way as religious, but the prescription to remain in a certain place or territory can only affect clerics registered in the eparchy, except for the law on institutes of consecrated life. § 4 . For a residence prescription to be imposed in a certain place or territory, the consent of the local Hierarch is required, unless it is a house of the institution of consecrated life of pontifical or patriarchal right, in which case the consent of the competent Superior is required, or a house intended for penitent clerics or reformers of various eparchies. Can. 1430 n - § 1 . Penal deprivations can affect both all or some of the powers, offices, ministries, functions, rights, privileges, faculties, graces, titles, insignia, as well as only some works inherent to the offices or functions, which are under the control of the authority that constitutes the sentence or the Hierarch who promotes the criminal trial or imposes it by decree; The same applies to a criminal transfer to another office. § 2 . There can be no deprivation of the power of a sacred order, but only a prohibition to exercise all or some of its acts according to the norm of common law; Likewise, the deprivation of academic titles may not occur. § 3 . Deprivation can also occur: 1st of the ability to receive or preach confessions; 2nd delegated power of government; 3º of all or part of the ecclesiastical remuneration, determined according to particular law, without prejudice also to the provisions of Can. 1410.

Can. 1431 . § 1 . Those punished with minor excommunication are deprived of receiving the Divine Eucharist; Furthermore, they may be excluded from participation in the Divine Liturgy, or even from entering the church, if divine worship is publicly celebrated there. § 2 . The sentence or decree itself by which this penalty is imposed must define the scope of the penalty itself and, where appropriate, its duration.

Can. 1432 . § 1 . The suspension may be of all or some of the acts of the power of order or government, of all or some of the acts or rights related to the position, ministry or function; but the scope of the same must be determined by the sentence or decree by which the penalty is imposed, unless it has already been determined by law. § 2 . No one can be suspended except for acts that are under the power of the authority that constitutes the penalty, or of the Hierarch, who promotes the criminal trial or imposes the suspension by decree. § 3 . The suspension never affects the validity of the acts or the right of residence, if the defendant has it by reason of position, ministry or service; But the suspension that prohibits receiving profits, remunerations or pensions entails the obligation to return what has been received illicitly, even if it is in good faith.

Can. 1433 . § 1 . A cleric reduced to a lower rank is prohibited from exercising those acts of the power of order and government that are not compatible with this rank. § 2 . But a clergyman, deposed from the clerical state, is deprived of all offices, ministries or other functions, of ecclesiastical pensions and of any delegated power; becomes unsuitable for them; it is prohibited to exercise the power of order; cannot be promoted to higher sacred and secular orders, as far as canonical effects are concerned, it is equivalent to the signature cann. 396 y 725.

Can. 1434 . § 1 . The major excommunication prohibits, in addition to all those mentioned in Can. 1431, § 1, and other sacraments, receiving sacraments, administering sacraments and sacramentals, performing any offices, ministries or functions, performing acts of government, which, if performed, are themselves null and void. § 2 .
