Punished with further excommunication, he must be prohibited from participating in the Divine Liturgy and any other public celebrations of divine worship. § 3 . Punished with further excommunication, he is prohibited from enjoying the privileges previously granted to him; He cannot validly obtain a position, office, service or other office in the Church, nor a pension, nor make his own the fruits inherent in these; It also lacks active and passive voice.

Can. 1435 . § 1: If the penalty prohibits receiving the sacraments or sacramentals, the prohibition is suspended, while the guilty person is in danger of death. § 2 . If the penalty prohibits the administration of sacraments or sacramentals or the imposition of an act of government, the prohibition is suspended whenever it is necessary to consult the faithful who are in danger of death. CHAPTER II OF THE SANCTIONS FOR EACH INFRINGEMENT Can. 1436 n - § 1 . Whoever denies believing any truth of the divine and Catholic faith, or questions it, or completely rejects the Christian faith and does not come to his senses when legally reprimanded, like a heretic or an apostate, is punished with further excommunication, the clergyman may be punished with other penalties, not excluded by deposition. § 2 . Outside of these cases, whoever obstinately rejects the teaching that is proposed to be definitively maintained by the Roman Pontiff or the College of Bishops in the exercise of the authentic magisterium, or supports the teaching that has been condemned as erroneous, and does not legitimately repent and admonish, must be punished with the appropriate penalty. § 3 . Whoever appeals to the Episcopal College against an act of the Roman Pontiff will be punished with the appropriate penalty.

Can. 1437 . He who rejects submission to the authority of the supreme Church or communion with the faithful who are subject to it, and does not guarantee obedience when legitimately warned, as a schismatic is punished with further excommunication.

Can. 1438 . Whoever deliberately omits the commemoration of the Hierarch in the Divine Liturgy and in the divine praises prescribed by law, if he does not come to his senses when legitimately admonished, will be punished with the appropriate penalty not excluded from major excommunication.
Can. 1439 . Parents, or those who act in their place, who send their children to be baptized or educated in the non-Catholic religion, will be punished accordingly.
Can. 1440 . Whoever violates the rules of the law regarding communication in sacred places may be punished with the corresponding penalty.

Can. 1441 . Whoever uses sacred things for profane use or for an evil purpose must be suspended or prevented from receiving the Divine Eucharist. Can. 1442 n - § 1 . He who rejects the Divine Eucharist, or directs it to a sacrilegious purpose, or retains it, will be punished with greater excommunication, and, if he is a clergyman, also with deposition, without excluding other penalties. § 2 . The person guilty of consecration to the sacred purpose of both sacred gifts or one of them during the celebration of the Divine Liturgy or outside of it, will be punished by the gravity of the crime not excluded by deposition. Can. 1443 n - § 1 . The following will be punished with an appropriate penalty, not excluding a major excommunication: 1° whoever feigns the celebration of the Divine Liturgy or other sacraments; 2° whoever has not been promoted to the priestly order has attempted the celebration of the Divine Liturgy; 3° who, except in the case mentioned in Can. 1457, when he cannot give sacramental absolution, has attempted to impart it or has heard a sacramental confession. § 2 . Anyone who has deliberately administered the sacrament to those who are prohibited from receiving it will be punished with suspension, to which other penalties may be added.

Can. 1444 . Whoever has committed perjury before ecclesiastical authority, or who, even though he has been wronged, has knowingly made a false statement before a legitimately questioned judge, or has concealed the truth, or who has led to these crimes, will be punished with the corresponding penalty.

Can. 1445 . § 1 . Whoever has used physical force on a bishop or has caused him some other serious injury, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, not excluded, if he is a clergyman, by deposition; but if the same crime is committed against a Metropolitan, a Patriarch or even a Roman Pontiff, the guilty person is punished with a major excommunication, the remission of which is reserved in the latter case to the Roman Pontiff himself. § 2 . Whoever does this to another clergyman, to a religious, to a member of a society of common life such as the religious, or to a layman who actually performs an ecclesiastical function, will be punished with the appropriate penalty. Can. 1446 n - § 1 . Whoever does not obey what his own Hierarch legitimately orders or prohibits, and after warning him persists in disobedience, let the offender be punished with the appropriate penalty. § 2 . Whoever violates the obligation to keep the pontifical secret will be punished with the penalties mentioned in cann. 1429 y 1430. § 3 . Whoever fails to comply with the duty to execute the sentence or executive decree by which a penalty is imposed, will be punished with the corresponding penalty, without excluding minor excommunication and suspension. § 4 . He who does not communicate knowledge of the infraction, when obliged to do so by canon law, must be punished according to the cann. 1429 y 1430 norm, along with other penalties depending on the seriousness of the infraction. § 5 . The cleric who voluntarily and illegitimately abandons the sacred ministries, for six consecutive months, with the intention of submitting to the competent authority of the Church, due to the seriousness of the offense, is punished with suspension or even with the penalties established in cann. 1429 y 1430, and in the most serious cases with deposition.

Can. 1447 . § 1 . Whoever stirs up sedition or hatred against any Hierarch, or provokes his subjects to disobey him, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, without excluding a greater excommunication, especially if this offense was committed against the Patriarch or even against the Roman Pontiff. § 2 . Whoever obstructs the freedom of office or election or ecclesiastical power, or the legitimate use of the temporal goods of the Church, or intimidates the voter or whoever exercises power or office, will be punished with the appropriate penalty.

Can. 1448 . § 1 . Whoever blasphemes, whether in a public spectacle or meeting, in a publicly published writing or in any other way using the media, or seriously damages good customs, or expresses insults against religion or the Church, or incites hatred or contempt, will be punished accordingly. § 2 . Whoever names an association that conspires against the Church must be punished with the appropriate penalty. Can. 1449 n - § 1 . The penalties mentioned in cann. 1429 y 1430 are punished with the firm obligation to repair the damage: 1st who removes the ecclesiastical property or prevents them from receiving the fruits thereof; 2nd who alienates ecclesiastical property or carries out acts of administration on them without the prescribed consultation, consent or license or without any other requirement imposed by law for its validity or legality; 3° whoever obtains illegitimate benefit from the offerings, mentioned in Can. 715, for the celebration of the Divine Liturgy or for the Liturgy of the Presanctified or for commemorations in the Divine Liturgy. § 2 . The following will be punished with the appropriate penalty, without excluding deprivation of office, with a firm obligation to repair the damage: 1. whoever, by seriously culpable omission of due diligence or by seriously culpable ignorance of the law or precept, commits the crime referred to in § 1, n. 2 commits; 2nd who has otherwise been found guilty of gross negligence in the administration of ecclesiastical property.

Can. 1450 . § 1 . He who commits murder must be punished with greater excommunication; Furthermore, the clergyman may be punished with other penalties, not excluded by the deposition. § 2 . In the same way, whoever procured an abortion must be punished with the following effect, with the signature Can. 728 , § 2 .

Can. 1451 . Whoever kidnaps or unjustly detains a person, seriously injures or mutilates him, or inflicts physical or psychological torture on him, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, without excluding further excommunication.

Can. 1452 . Whoever has caused serious harm to someone, or has seriously damaged his good reputation with slander, will be obliged to make adequate satisfaction; but if he refused, he was to be punished with excommunication or minor suspension. Can. 1453 n - § 1 . The cleric in concubinage or in another external sin against chastity will be punished with permanent suspension with scandal, to which other penalties may be gradually added until the deposition is persistent. § 2 . A clergyman who attempted to perform a prohibited marriage was deposed. § 3 . A clergyman who otherwise commits a crime against chastity, if the crime has actually been committed publicly, must be punished with appropriate penalties, without excluding, if necessary, deposition. § 4 . The same punishment, which is mentioned in § 3, must be punished by a cleric who commits a crime against chastity by force, threats, or abuse of his authority or forces someone to perform or submit to sexual acts. § 5 . With deprivation of office and other appropriate penalties, without excluding deposition, if the case requires it, the cleric will be punished: 1) who commits an offense against chastity with a minor or with a person who habitually lacks the use of reason or whose right recognizes equal protection; 2º that which forces or induces a minor or a person who habitually lacks the use of reason or who recognizes the right to equal protection, to expose themselves pornographically or participate in pornographic exhibitions, real or simulated; 3º Anyone who, contrary to good customs, acquires, possesses, presents or disseminates, in any form and by any means, pornographic images of minors or people who usually lack the use of reason. § 6 . The religious who has made a public vow of perpetual chastity and is not established in a sacred order, committing the crimes mentioned in §§ 1 and 2, will be punished with the corresponding penalty. § 7 . A religious or member of a community of common life, such as religious and lay people, anyone who enjoys any dignity or performs a position or function in the Church, if he commits the crime referred to in §§ 3 -5, will be punished with the penalty appropriate to the seriousness of the crime.

Can. 1454 . Whoever falsely informs someone of any crime will be punished with the appropriate penalty, not excluded from further excommunication, especially if he is denounced as a confessor, Hierarch, cleric, religious, member of a society of common life such as the religious, or layman established in an ecclesiastical position with the signature Can. 731.

Can. 1455 . Whoever made a false ecclesiastical document, or made a false statement in it, or who knowingly used any false or altered document in ecclesiastical matters, or who altered, destroyed or concealed a true document, will be punished with the corresponding penalty. Can. 1456 n - § 1 . The confessor, who has directly violated the sacramental seal, is punished with major excommunication, with the signature Can. 728, § 1, n. 1; but if he breaks this seal in any other way, he will be punished accordingly. § 2 . The interpreter and other persons mentioned in Can. 733 , § 2 , who violated the secrecy, and also those who tried to obtain information from the confession in any way, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, not excluding minor excommunication or suspension. § 3 . According to the provisions of §§ 1 and 2, whoever captures by any technical means or maliciously publishes in the media or in any other way what was said in the sacramental confession, true or false, by the confessor or by the penitent, will be punished according to the seriousness of the offense, not excluded, if he is a clergyman, with deposition.
Can. 1457 . The priest who absolves an accomplice of a sin against chastity will be punished with major excommunication, with firm Can. 728 , § 1 , n. 2.

Can. 1458 . The priest who, in the act, occasion or pretext of confession, asked a penitent to sin against chastity, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, not excluding deposition. Can. 1459 n - § 1 . Bishops who have ministered episcopal ordination to someone without a mandate from competent authority, and whoever has received episcopal ordination from her, must be punished with further excommunication. § 2 . The bishop who administers diaconal or presbyteral ordination to someone contrary to the provisions of the canons must be punished with the appropriate penalty. § 3 . Both he who has attempted to administer sacramental ordination to a woman, and the woman who has attempted to receive sacred ordination, will be punished with excommunication reserved for the highest Apostolic See; In addition, the secretary may be punished with deposition. § 4 . He who has come to sacred ordination under penalty of greater or lesser excommunication, or obstruction, has been voluntarily withheld, in addition to what is established in Can. 763, n. 1, is suspended from the sacred order received.

Can. 1460 . Whoever approaches civil authority directly or indirectly, in order to obtain a sacred ordination, office, service or other function in the Church, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, not excluded from further excommunication and, if it is a clergyman, also with deposition.

Can. 1461 . He who ministered or received the sacred ordination simonically must be deposed; but he who has ministered or received other sacraments simonically, must be punished with an appropriate penalty, not excluded from further excommunication.

Can. 1462 . Whoever fraudulently obtained an office, service or other function in the Church, contributed to it, or in any way usurped it, or unlawfully retained it, or transmitted it to others, or executed it, shall be punished with the appropriate penalty, without excluding further excommunication. Can. 1463 n - § 1 . Whoever has given or promised something, so that whoever exercising an office, service or other office in the Church does or omits something illegally, will be punished with the corresponding penalty; also, who accepted those gifts or promises. In both cases there remains the obligation to repair the damage. § 2 . Whoever, in the performance of a position, ministry or function, has requested a position greater than the indicated amount or additional sums or anything for his benefit, will be punished with the corresponding pecuniary penalty or other penalties, without excluding deprivation of office, and with the obligation to repair the damage. Can. 1464 n - § 1 . Whoever, in addition to the cases already provided for by law, has abused power, office, ministry or any other function in the Church by action or omission, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, not excluding deprivation thereof, unless for this abuse there is another penalty established by law or precept, with a firm obligation to repair the damage. § 2 . But whoever, through culpable negligence, illegitimately placed or omitted an act of power, office, ministry or other office in the Church with harm to others, will be punished with the appropriate penalty, with a firm obligation to repair the damage.

Can. 1465 . Whoever holds an office, ministry or other function in the Church, and is attached to any independent Church, including the Latin Church, who seeks to induce the Christian faithful against Can. 31 to move to another independent Church in any way, will be punished accordingly. Can. 1466 n - § 1 . The clergyman, religious or member of a society of common life who dedicates himself to businesses or commerce contrary to the provisions of the canons, such as religious ones, will be punished with the corresponding penalty. § 2 . The cleric, religious or member of a community of common life analogous to the religious who, outside the cases already provided for by law, commits an economic crime, or seriously violates the prescriptions listed in Can. 385 § 3, will be punished with the corresponding penalty, with a firm obligation to repair the damage. Can. 1467 n - Anyone who violates the obligations imposed by the sentence will be punished with additional penalties. TITLE XXVIII OF THE PROCEDURE IN THE IMPOSITION OF SENTENCES CHAPTER I OF THE CRIMINAL SENTENCE Art. I IN THE PRELIMINARY INVESTIGATION

Can. 1468 . § 1 . Whenever the Hierarch has even probable knowledge of a crime, he carefully investigates, himself or through another competent person, the facts and circumstances, unless this investigation seems to him completely unnecessary. § 2 . We must be careful not to endanger anyone's good with this investigation. § 3 . The person who carries out the investigation has the same powers and obligations as the auditor of the process; and he himself cannot, if a criminal proceeding is later carried out, act as a judge in it.

Can. 1469 . § 1 . Signature cann. 1403 y 1411 , if the investigation appears sufficiently informed, let the Hierarch decide whether the sentencing procedure should be brought forward and, if he decides affirmatively, whether it should be dealt with through criminal proceedings or through an extrajudicial decree. § 2 . The leader will revoke or change his decision whenever, due to new facts and circumstances, he appears to decide otherwise. § 3 . Before deciding anything on the matter, the Hierarch must hear the person accused of the crime and the promoter of justice, and, if he believes it prudent, two judges or other legal experts; Let the Hierarch also consider whether, to avoid useless lawsuits, he should have the parties come to an agreement so that he or the investigator can resolve the question of damages in a good and equitable manner.

Can. 1470 . The actions of the investigation and the decisions of the Hierarch by which the investigation is initiated or closed, and all those that precede the investigation, if they are not necessary for the procedure for imposing sanctions, will be kept in the secret archive of the court. Art. II ON THE EVOLUTION OF THE CRIMINAL SENTENCE

Can. 1471 . § 1 . Without prejudice to the canons of this title, in criminal proceedings the canons on general trials and on ordinary contentious trials apply, as well as the special rules on cases that concern the public good, unless the nature of the case prevents it. § 2 . The accused is not required to confess to the crime nor can he take an oath.

Can. 1472 . § 1 . If the Hierarch has decided to initiate a criminal process, he will deliver the minutes of the investigation to the promoter of justice, who will present the indictment to the judge in accordance with the cann. 1185 y 1187 standard. § 2 . Before the superior court, the promoter of justice appointed in that court plays the role of petitioner.

Can. 1473 . To prevent scandals, protect the freedom of witnesses and protect the course of justice, the Hierarch may, after hearing the promoter of justice and summoning the accused himself, in any state and degree of criminal proceedings, prevent the accused from exercising an order, office, ministry or other sacred function, impose or prevent his residence in any place or territory, or even prevent the public reception of the Divine Eucharist; all of which must be revoked when the case ceases, and by right end when the criminal sentence ceases.

Can. 1474 . The judge who summons the accused must invite him to choose a lawyer within a certain period; after which the same judge appointed a lawyer so that the accused would remain in office until the accused had appointed a lawyer for himself.

Can. 1475 . § 1 . At any stage of the trial, the renunciation of the case may be made by the promoter of justice by order or with the consent of the Hierarch, by whose decision the trial was promoted. § 2 . To be valid, the resignation must be accepted by the accused, unless he or she has been declared absent from court.
Can. 1476 . In addition to the defenses and observations formulated in writing, if any, the discussion of the case must be done orally.

Can. 1477 . § 1 . The discussion is attended by the promoter of justice, the accused and his lawyer, the injured party, about whom in Can. 1483, § 1 and his lawyer. § 2 . It is up to the court to call the experts who have worked on the case for a discussion, so that they can explain their experience.
Can. 1478 . In the discussion of the case, the accused always has the right to speak last, he or his lawyer.

Can. 1479 . § 1 . After discussion, the court should make a decision. § 2 . If a need arises from the discussion to gather new evidence, the court will gather new evidence by expanding the definition of the case.

Can. 1480 . The operative part of the sentence must be published immediately, unless the court decides for serious reasons that the decision must be kept confidential until formal notification of the sentence, which may never be delayed more than one month from the date on which the criminal case was resolved.

Can. 1481 . § 1 . The accused can file an appeal, even if the judge acquitted him only because the sentence was optional or because the judge used the power, which is analyzed in cann. 1409 , § 1 and 1415. § 2 . The promoter of justice may appeal if he considers that reparation for the crime or the restoration of justice has not been sufficiently provided.

Can. 1482 . At any stage and level of a criminal process, if it is evident that the crime was not committed by the accused, the judge must declare that sentence and acquit the accused, although at the same time it is clear that the criminal action has been extinguished. Art. III ACTIONS TO REPAIR DAMAGES

Can. 1483 . § 1 . The injured party may file a contentious action to recover damages for the infringement inflicted on him or her before the criminal court itself in accordance with the Can. 1276 rule. § 2 . The intervention of the injured party is no longer appropriate if it was not done at the first level of the criminal process. § 3 . The appeal in a damages case is made according to the rule of cann. 1309 - 1321 , although it cannot be appealed in criminal court; but if both appeals are filed, even if they are from different parties, the ruling on the appeal will be the same, except for Can. 1484.

Can. 1484 . § 1 . To avoid excessive delays in the criminal proceedings, the judge may postpone the ruling on damages until he has made a final decision in the criminal proceedings. § 2 . The judge who has acted in this way must, after having issued a ruling in the criminal proceedings, know the damages, even when the criminal proceedings are still pending due to the appeal filed or the accused has been acquitted for reasons that do not eliminate the obligation to repair the damages.

Can. 1485 . A sentence handed down in a criminal proceeding, even if it has become res judicata, does not in any way create a right towards the injured party, unless the injured party intervenes in accordance with the Can. 1483 rule. CHAPTER II ON THE IMPOSITION OF SANCTIONS BY EXTRAJUDICIAL DECREE

Can. 1486 . § 1 . For the validity of the decree imposing the sentence, it is required that: 1° the accused be informed of the accusation and the evidence, giving him the opportunity to fully exercise his right to defend himself, unless he has not appeared according to the rule of the cited law; 2° the oral discussion between the Hierarch or his delegate and the accused will take place in the presence of the promoter of justice and the rapporteur; 3. The decree itself explains the reasons on which the de facto and legal penalty is based. § 2 . The penalties mentioned in Can. 1426 , § 1 , may be imposed without this procedure, provided that their acceptance by the case is confirmed in writing.

Can. 1487 . § 1 . An appeal may be filed against the decree that imposes a penalty before the competent higher authority within ten working days of having been notified. § 2 . This appeal suspends the force of the decision. § 3 . There is no further appeal against the decision of a higher authority. TITLE XXIX OF THE LAW, CUSTOMS AND ADMINISTRATIVE ACTS CHAPTER I OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL LAW
Can. 1488 . Laws are established by promulgation.

Can. 1489 . § 1 . Laws approved by the Apostolic See are promulgated by publication in the official commentary of the Acts of the Apostolic See, unless in special cases another method of promulgation is prescribed; They begin to be obligatory after three months have elapsed from the day established in the number of Minutes, unless due to the nature of the matter they are immediately obligatory or more or less long vacations are expressly established. § 2 . Laws passed by other legislators are promulgated in the manner determined by these legislators and become binding on the date set by them.

Can. 1490 . Those who have been baptized in the Catholic Church or those who have been received into the same Church, and those who have sufficient use of reason and, unless otherwise expressly provided by law, have reached the seventh year of age, are bound by purely ecclesiastical laws.

Can. 1491 . § 1 . Laws passed by the supreme authority of the Church are binding on all those for whom they were given throughout the world, unless they have been established for a specific territory; Other laws only take effect in the territory in which the authority that promulgated them exercises the power of government, unless otherwise provided by law or determined by the nature of the matter. § 2 . Those who are subject to the laws approved for a specific territory, for which they are granted and who have a domicile or quasi-domicile there and effectively reside at the same time signature § 3 , n. 1. § 3 . Pilgrims: 1° are not bound by the laws of the particular law of their territory, while they are outside it, unless their transgression in their own territory is harmful or the laws are personal; 2. They are not bound by the laws of the particular territory in which they intervene, except those that consult public order or determine solemn acts or respect real estate located in the territory; 3° But they are bound by the laws of the common law and by the laws of the particular law of their own Church, although, as for the laws of the same particular law, they are not in force in their own territory, unless they are not obligatory in the place where they are exercised. § 4 . Travelers are subject to all applicable laws where they are staying.

Can. 1492 . The laws dictated by the supreme authority of the Church, in which the passive subject is not expressly indicated, respect the faithful of the Eastern Churches only to the extent that they deal with, or expressly provide for, or are favorable to the faithful, questions of faith or morals or the declaration of divine law, which do not contain anything contrary to Eastern rites.

Can. 1493 . § 1 . In addition to the legitimate laws and customs of the entire Church, in this Code the legitimate laws and customs common to all Eastern Churches are called common law. § 2 . But under the name of particular law are included all laws, legitimate customs, statutes and other norms of law that are not common to the entire Church or to all the Eastern Churches.
Can. 1494 . Laws look to the future, not to the past, unless they expressly provide for the past.
Can. 1495 . Only those laws that expressly establish that the act is void or that the person is incapacitated will be considered irritating or disabling.

Can. 1496 . Laws, even vexatious or disabling ones, do not press a question of law; but in case of doubt the Hierarchs may dispense them, provided that the dispensation, if reserved, is usually granted by the authority to whom it is reserved.

Can. 1497 . § 1 . Ignorance or error about irritating or disabling laws does not prevent the same effect, unless the law expressly establishes otherwise. § 2 . Ignorance or error is not presumed about the law or the penalty, nor about one's own act or about the notorious fact of another; It is presumed that the foreign title is not known, until the contrary is proven.

Can. 1498 . § 1 . The laws are interpreted authentically by the legislator and by the person to whom he has conferred the power to interpret authentically. § 2 . An authentic interpretation given by law has the same force as the law itself and must be promulgated; If you only declare certain words in themselves, the opposite is true; If it narrows or expands the law or clarifies a doubt, it does not retract. § 3 . However, an interpretation through a judicial decision or administrative act in a specific case does not have the force of law and only binds people and affects the things for which it was given.

Can. 1499 . Laws must be understood according to the proper meaning of the words considered in the text and the context, which if left doubtful and obscure, according to parallel passages, if any, the object of the law and the circumstances and mind of the legislator.
Can. 1500 . Laws that establish sanctions or restrict the free exercise of rights or contain an exception to the law are subject to strict interpretation.

Can. 1501 . If there is no express provision of law on a certain matter, the case, unless it is criminal, must be resolved according to the canons of the Synods and the holy Fathers, legitimate custom, the general principles of canon law observed with equity, ecclesiastical jurisprudence and common and consistent canonical doctrine.

Can. 1502 . § 1 . A subsequent law repeals the first or repeals it, if it expressly dictates it, or if it is directly contrary to it, or if it regulates all the matter of the previous law. § 2 . But the common law law, unless expressly provided otherwise in the law itself, does not repeal the particular law law, nor does a particular law law passed in the name of a Church in its own right repeal a more particular law in force in the same Church.
Can. 1503 . In doubt, the revocation of a pre-existing law is not presumed, but rather subsequent laws must approximate the previous ones and be reconciled with them to the extent possible.

Can. 1504 . Civil law, to which the law of the Church is subject, will be preserved in canon law with the same effects, to the extent that it is not contrary to divine law and unless otherwise provided in canon law.
Can. 1505 . The expression of speech in the masculine gender also refers to the feminine gender, unless otherwise provided by law or determined by the nature of the matter. CHAPTER II CUSTOMS

Can. 1506 . § 1 . The custom of the Christian community, to the extent that it corresponds to the action of the Holy Spirit in the ecclesial body, can obtain the force of law. § 2 . No custom can in any way derogate from divine law.

Can. 1507 . § 1 . Only that custom can have the force of law that is reasonable and capable of being accepted at least by the legal community, introduced through continuous and peaceful practice and during the period prescribed by law. § 2 . A custom expressly disapproved by law is not reasonable. § 3 . A custom contrary to existing canon law, or which is additional to canon law, obtains the force of law only if it has been legally observed for thirty consecutive and complete years; Contrary to canon law, which contains a clause prohibiting future customs, only a centuries-old or immemorial custom can prevail. § 4 . The competent legislator can approve the practice as legitimate even before that moment with his at least tacit consent.
Can. 1508 . Custom is the best translator of laws.

Can. 1509 . A custom, whether contrary or additional to the law, is revoked by a contrary custom or law; but unless it makes express mention of them, the law does not remember centuries-old or immemorial customs; As for the other customs, Can. 1502 , § 2 is valid. CHAPTER III ADMINISTRATIVE ACTIVITIES

Can. 1510 . § 1 . Administrative actions may be imposed by those who hold the executive power of the government, within the limits of their jurisdiction, as well as by those to whom that power is explicitly or implicitly vested, either by right or by virtue of legitimate delegation. § 2 . Administrative acts are mainly: 1° decrees, by which a special case is resolved or a canonical provision is issued; 2. Singular precepts, by which a certain person or persons must be directly and legitimately imposed to do or omit something, especially to enforce the law; 3rd rescripts to which privilege, dispensation, license or other favor is granted.

Can. 1511 . An administrative act takes effect from the moment it is summoned, or in those rewritten from the moment the letter is given; If the application of the administrative act is committed to the executor, it takes effect from the moment of its execution.

Can. 1512 . § 1 . The administrative act must be understood according to the proper meaning of the words and the common use of the word and must not be extended to other cases than those expressed. § 2 . In case of doubt, an administrative act that refers to lawsuits, threatens or imposes sanctions, restricts the rights of a person, harms the rights pursued by others or is contrary to the law in favor of individuals, receives a strict interpretation; Otherwise it is wide. § 3 . In these privileges, interpretation must always be used, so that the one to whom the privilege is granted actually obtains some grace. § 4 . Not only the dispensation, but the very power of dispensation granted to a given case is subject to strict interpretation.

Can. 1513 . § 1 . No administrative act is revoked by contrary law, unless otherwise provided in the law itself, or unless the law has been dictated by a higher authority than the one that issued the administrative act. § 2 . An administrative act is still dissolved by the right of the person who issued it, unless expressly provided otherwise. § 3 . The revocation of an administrative act by another administrative act of the competent authority only produces effects from the moment it is notified to the person for whom it was issued. § 4 . The dispensation, which has a successive course, also ceases with the definitive and total cessation of the motive cause. § 5 . A decree or precept ceases to have singular force even when the law for whose execution it was given ceases; The singular precept ceases even after the preceptor's right has been dissolved, unless it has been imposed by a legitimate document.

Can. 1514 . The administrative act, which refers to the external jurisdiction, must be submitted in writing to the signatures cann. 1520, § 2 and 1527; Likewise, if it is done in the form of a commission, of the execution of that act.

Can. 1515 . An administrative act, even by means of a written request, has no effect to the extent that it infringes rights claimed by others or is contrary to the law or legitimate custom, unless the competent authority has expressly added a derogatory clause.

Can. 1516 . The conditions in administrative acts are then only considered added to the validity, provided that they are expressed by the particles if, except, provided, or in the vernacular by another of the same meaning. Art. I OF THE PROCEDURE IN DECREES OUT OF TRIAL

Can. 1517 . § 1 . Before making an extrajudicial decision, the authority seeks the necessary information and evidence; listens to or consults those who must be heard or consulted by law; must listen to those who are directly affected by the decree and especially to those whose rights may be harmed. § 2 . To the petitioner and also to the legitimately opposing authority, the information and evidence that can be known without risk of public or private harm, and to demonstrate possible contrary reasons, with the opportunity to respond to them, also through a lawyer, within the period determined by the authority itself.

Can. 1518 . The authority must issue a decree within sixty days following receipt of the request to obtain the decree, unless the particular law of the independent Church establishes other terms; but if this has not been done and the petitioner requests the decree again in writing, counting on the thirtieth day from the receipt of this petition, if still nothing has been done, the petition is considered rejected as if on that day the rejection was made by decree in such a way that an appeal can be filed against it.

Can. 1519 . § 1 . Whoever dictates the decree must take into account and propose what seems most conducive to the salvation of souls and the public good, effectively observing legitimate laws and customs, justice and equity. § 2 . The reasons are at least briefly expressed in the decree; But if there is a danger of public or private harm that prevents the reasons from being revealed, these are expressed in a secret book, and are shown, if requested, to anyone who sees that an appeal can be filed against the decree.

Can. 1520 . § 1 . A decree has the force of law after it has been communicated to the person for whom it is intended in the most reliable manner according to local laws and conditions. § 2 . If there is a danger of public or private harm, such that the text of the decree cannot be delivered in writing, the ecclesiastical authority may order the decree to the person for whom it is intended, in the presence of two witnesses or in the presence of a notary, in a reduced verbal process signed by all those present; Once these things are done, the decree will be considered intimate. § 3 . However, if the person to whom the decree is addressed has refused to be notified, or has been called in accordance with the law to receive the decree or to be heard, without just cause appreciable by the author of the decree, has not appeared or has refused to sign the verbal process, the decree will be deemed to have been served. Art. II OF THE EXECUTION OF ADMINISTRATIVE ACTS

Can. 1521 . The executor of an administrative act performs his function invalidly, before having received the written order and recognizing its authenticity and integrity, unless the authority that issued the same act has previously communicated information about the order to him.

Can. 1522 . § 1 . The executor of an administrative act, to whom the mere execution of the same act is committed, cannot deny this execution, unless it is evident that the same act is void or cannot be sustained for other serious reasons, or that the conditions inherent to the administrative act have not been met; However, if the execution of the administrative act seems inadmissible due to the circumstances of the person or place, the executor must stop the execution and immediately notify the authority that issued the act. § 2 . If the rescript commits the granting of grace to the executor, it is up to him to grant or deny the grace according to his prudent judgment and conscience.

Can. 1523 . The executor of the administrative act must proceed in accordance with the mandate; If the conditions for the validity of the act attached to the mandate were not met or if a substantial form of the procedure was not observed, there is no execution.

Can. 1524 . The executor of an administrative act may substitute another person at his discretion, unless the substitution is prohibited or the power of the person is chosen or the person of the substitute is determined; In these cases, however, the executor may have others perform preparatory acts.
Can. 1525 . An administrative act can also be ordered executed by the successor of the executor, unless the person's energy has been chosen.
Can. 1526 . The executor may again order the execution of an administrative act, if he made an error in any way in the execution of the same act. Art. 3 OF THE RESPONSIBILITIES

Can. 1527 . § 1 . What is established in the canons on the rescripts also applies to the granting of graces to the living voice of the oracle, unless otherwise clearly established. § 2 . A person is obliged to prove orally that a grace has been granted, provided it is legally required.
Can. 1528 . The rescript can be obtained on behalf of another person, even without his or her consent, and is valid before its acceptance, unless otherwise derived from the attached clauses.

Can. 1529 . § 1 . The reluctance to the truth in the prayers does not prevent the rescript from having force, as long as they are expressed, which to be valid must be expressed according to the style of the Hierarchical Court that allows the rescript. § 2 . Nor does it prevent the exposure of a falsehood, as long as at least one of the proposed reasons is true.

Can. 1530 . § 1 . Grace denied by a higher authority cannot be validly granted by a lower authority, unless the higher authority has expressly consented. § 2 . Grace denied by any authority cannot be validly granted by another equally competent authority or by a higher authority without mentioning the facts in the request for denial. 1. About privileges

Can. 1531 . § 1 . A privilege, that is, a favor done in favor of certain natural or legal persons through a special act, can be granted by the legislator and by the person to whom the legislator has granted this power. § 2 . Centenary or immemorial possession carries the presumption of privilege granted.

Can. 1532 . § 1 . The privilege is presumed perpetual. § 2 . The privilege ceases: 1° if it is personal, by the extinction of the person to whom it was granted; 2° if it is real or local, by the absolute destruction of the thing or place; 3° upon expiration of the term or at the end of the number of cases for which it was granted; 4° if with the passage of time the circumstances change in the opinion of the competent authority in such a way that it becomes harmful or its use becomes illicit. § 3 . Local privilege, if the place is restored fifty years from now, is revived.

Can. 1533 . § 1 . No privilege ceases due to resignation, unless it has been accepted by the competent authority. § 2 . Any natural person may waive the privilege in his favor as long as it is granted. § 3 . A natural person cannot validly renounce a privilege granted to a legal person or by reason of the dignity of a place or thing; nor is the legal entity itself intact to renounce the privilege granted to it, if the renunciation results in detriment to the Church or others.

Can. 1534 . Due to non-use or contrary use, the privilege does not cease to be burdensome for others; But if the privilege cedes to the detriment of others, it is lost if a legitimate precept or tacit renunciation approaches.

Can. 1535 . He who abuses the power that gives him the privilege must be admonished by the Hierarch; The Hierarch deprives him of a privilege that he himself has granted him; but if the privilege has been granted by a higher authority, he is obliged to report it to the Hierarch himself. 2. Of the waivers

Can. 1536 . § 1 . The dispensation, that is, the relaxation of a purely ecclesiastical law in a special case, can only be granted for a just and reasonable cause taking into account the circumstances of the case and the seriousness of the law from which it is dispensed; Otherwise the dispensation is illegal and, unless it has been given by the legislator himself or by a higher authority, it is also invalid. § 2 . The spiritual good of Christians is a just and reasonable cause. § 3 . In case of doubt about the sufficiency of the cause, the dispensation is granted lawfully and validly.
Can. 1537 . The laws are not subject to exemption insofar as they determine those that are essentially constitutive of the institutions or legal acts, nor are the procedural and criminal laws.

Can. 1538 . § 1 . The eparchial bishop can dispense from both the laws of common law and the laws of the particular law of his own Church, in the special case of the Christian faithful, over whom he exercises his authority according to the law, whenever he judges that this contributes to their spiritual good, unless a reservation has been made by the authority that dictated the laws. § 2 . If it is difficult to approach the authority to whom the dispensation is reserved, and at the same time there is a risk of serious harm in the delay, each Hierarch may in a special case dispense to the faithful over whom he exercises his authority according to the law, provided that it is a dispensation that the same authority grants in the same circumstances, sign Can. 396 .

Can. 1539 . Whoever has the power of administration can exercise it, even if it exists outside the territory, over his subjects, even if they are absent from the territory, and, unless expressly provided otherwise, also over foreigners who effectively reside in the territory, as well as over himself. TITLE 30 OF THE PRESCRIPTION AND CALCULATION OF TIME CHAPTER I OF THE PRESCRIPTION

Can. 1540 . The Church accepts prescription as a way to acquire or lose a subjective right, as well as to free oneself from obligations, as occurs in civil law, unless common law establishes otherwise.
Can. 1541 . No prescription is valid unless it is based on good faith, not only at the beginning, but throughout the period required for prescription, except Can. 1152 .

Can. 1542 . The following are not subject to prescription: 1° the rights and obligations, which are divine law; 2nd rights, which can be obtained only from the apostolic privilege; 3° the rights and obligations that directly concern the spiritual life of the Christian faithful; 4° the defined and indubitable limits of the ecclesiastical circumscriptions; 5° obligations and burdens related to the celebration of the Divine Liturgy; 6° the provision of the canonical office that, according to law, requires the exercise of sacred order; 7° the right of visitation and the obligation of obedience, so that people in the Church cannot be visited by any ecclesiastical authority and are no longer subject to any authority. CHAPTER II CALCULATION OF TIME
Can. 1543 . Unless otherwise expressly provided by law, the time will be computed according to the rules of the following canons.

Can. 1544 . § 1 . It is understood that time is continuous, which does not allow interruption. § 2 . Good time is understood to be that which corresponds to those who exercise or pursue their right, so that it does not run towards the ignorant or towards those who are incapable of acting.

Can. 1545 . § 1 . In law, a day is understood to be a space made up of 24 consecutive hours and beginning at midnight; a week of 7 days; A month has 30 days, a year has 365 days, unless it is said that the month and year are taken as they are in the calendar. § 2 . If time is continuous, you should always take the month and year exactly as they are on the calendar.

Can. 1546 . § 1 . The day from which the calculation begins is not counted in the period, unless its start coincides with the start of the day or is expressly provided for by law. § 2 . The day to which the calculation is directed is counted in the period, which, if the period consists of one or more months or years, of one or more weeks, ends with the passage of the last day of the same number or, if the month lacks a day of the same number, with the passage of the last day of the month. *AAS, vol. 82 (1990), no. 11, pp. 1260-1353 ________________________________________________ (n: Indicates that the text corresponds to a new version or to a new paragraph) Cf.: Apostolic Letter given by Motu Proprio Calling sinners, in which certain canons title XXVII and canon 1152 of the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches are modified (March 20, year of our Lord 2013) © Copyright 1990 - Vatican Publishing Copyright © Dicastery for Communication of the Holy See Holy See
